Table 9. Frailty Assessment Methods in Patients With Heart Failure [Revised]
Method Characteristics
Physical frailty
  CHS criteria (Fried criteria) Five items (weight loss, muscle weakness, fatigue, slow walking speed, and low activity) were examined, 
and 3 or more items were classified as frail, and 1 or 2 points were classified as pre-frail.
Mental and psychological frailty
  MoCA · CDR · MMSE
The MoCA or MoCA-J (Japanese version of the MoCA) is a screening tool for MCI, comprising 
assessments of visuospatial and executive function, naming, memory, attention, repetition, language 
fluency, abstraction, delayed recall, and orientation.
The MMSE consists of 11 components with a maximum score of 30, including temporal orientation, 
spatial orientation, immediate and delayed recall of three words, calculation, object naming, sentence 
repetition, a three-step verbal command, written command, sentence writing, and figure copying. A score 
of 27 or below suggests possible MCI, while a score of 23 or below suggests possible dementia.
The Mini-Cog, which combines immediate and delayed recall of three words with a clock drawing test, is 
a screening tool for dementia and is not suitable as an assessment method for cognitive frailty, for which 
MCI serves as the diagnostic criterion.
  Item GDS
The 30-item GDS, a shortened version of the 15-item (15-GDS), and the 5-item (5-GDS) are used to 
assess depressive symptoms in the elderly. PHQ-2 and PHQ-9 are assessment tools used for depression 
screening; however, they are not suitable for evaluating mental, or psychological frailty, which are 
considered preclinical stages of depression.

Method Characteristics
Social frailty
   Makizako’s 5 questions, 
Yamada’s questions
Defined as living alone, frequency of going out, and social pre-frailty when two or more of the five items 
related to family and friends are applicable, and social frailty when one of the five items is applicable. 
Yamada’s questionnaire takes into account economic status, living alone, social activities, and 
relationships with neighbors.
Multidimensional frailty
  KCL · QMCOO
KCL is a 25-item questionnaire developed by the Ministry of Health, Labor and Welfare in Japan for care 
prevention. QMCOO is a health assessment questionnaire for the screening program of old-old adults

frailty, two address general health status, and one addresses smoking habits.1218a,1218b
  Frailty Index (FI-CD, FI-CGA) More than 30 elderly-specific symptoms, signs, and problems in multiple domains are considered and 
converted to a real number between 0 and 1 to determine frailty.
CFS
  CFS
Overall health screening, scale to assess degree of “frailty” (9 levels from very healthy to end of life). A 
CFS score of 4 to 6 is diagnosed as clinically significant frailty. Patients at a more advanced stage than 
frailty, who are unable to walk, are classified as CFS 7 or higher.
CDR, Clinical Dementia Rating; CFS, Clinical Frailty Scale; CHS, Cardiovascular Health Study; FI-CD, Frailty Index based on Cumulative 
Deficits; FI-CGA, Frailty Index based on Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment; GDS, Geriatric Depression Scale; KCL, Kihon checklist; 
MMSE, Mini-Mental State Examination; MCI, mild cognitive impairment; MoCA, Montreal Cognitive Assessment; PHQ, Patient Health 
Questionnaire; QMCOO, Questionnaire for Medical Checkup of Old-Old.

JCS/JHFS 2025 Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Heart Failure
Preamble
Recent advances in pharmacological and non-pharmaco-
logical therapies, supported by large-scale clinical trials, 
have transformed heart failure management. However, 
substantial challenges remain in clinical practice due to the 
diverse etiologies and complex pathophysiology of heart 
failure (HF), which necessitate individualized treatment 
strategies. Globally, this complexity is further compounded 
by the increasing prevalence of an older HF population, 
requiring a balanced focus on improving survival and 
maintaining quality of life.
Recently, the Universal Definition and Classification of 
Heart Failure was established through a collaborative 
effort between the Japanese Heart Failure Society, Heart 
Failure Society of America, and the European Heart Fail-
ure Association.
1 In addition, the European Society of 
Cardiology has published 2021 ESC Guidelines for the 
Diagnosis and Treatment of Acute and Chronic Heart 
Failure,2 as well as a 2023 focused update.3 In the US, the 
American Heart Association, American College of Cardi-
ology, and Heart Failure Society of America jointly pub-
lished guidelines for the management of heart failure in 
2022.
4
This guideline incorporates updates from these consen-
sus documents and international guidelines, along with the 
latest findings and evidence, while addressing the unique 
challenges of HF management in Japan, which has a sig-
nificant aged population, by focusing not only on core 
issues of diagnostic and therapeutic assessment and imple-
mentation, but also on considerations specific to the Japa-
nese universal healthcare system, with its distinct strengths 
and weaknesses.
This guideline consolidates the 2017 Guideline on Diag-
nosis and Treatment of Acute and Chronic Heart Failure
5 
and the 2021 Guideline Focused Update on Diagnosis and 
Treatment of Acute and Chronic Heart Failure, 6 collab-
oratively developed by the Japanese Circulation Society 
and the Japanese Heart Failure Society, incorporating the 
latest evidence. For this revision of the guidelines, an addi-
tional 6 professional societies joined as collaborators: the 
Japanese Association of Cardiovascular Intervention and 
Therapeutics, the Japanese Society of Echocardiography, 
the Japanese Association of Cardiac Rehabilitation, the 
Japanese Heart Rhythm Society, the Japanese Society for 
Cardiovascular Surgery, and the Japanese Association for 
Thoracic Surgery.
We sincerely hope that this guideline will aid in facilitat-
ing meaningful discussions between healthcare teams, 
patients, and patients’ families.

I. Introduction
PM?b??q???
Level of Evidence
In this guideline, recommendation classes and levels of 
evidence are categorized as detailed in Tables 1 and 2. To 
maintain consistency with the US heart failure (HF) guide-
lines,
4 evidence Level B is subdivided into 2 categories, 
namely B-R (randomized), representing evidence derived 
from randomized controlled trials, and B-NR (non-ran-
domized), indicating evidence from observational studies. 
Evidence Level C is also divided into 2 categories, namely 
C-LD (limited data), signifying support from small-scale 
studies, and C-EO (expert opinion), representing practices 
widely accepted in routine clinical settings or recommenda-
tions based on expert consensus in the absence of specific 
evidence.
2. Top 10 Key Revisions in the Present Guidelines
The following major revisions have been incorporated into 
this guideline:
PM???s??????????
“Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Heart 
Failure” from “Guidelines for Diagnosis and Treat-
ment of Acute and Chronic Heart Failure”, published 
in 2017 and updated in 2021. This change reflects a 
decreased emphasis on distinguishing between acute 
and chronic HF due to the difficulty in clearly differ-
entiating between these phases, instead highlighting 
the importance of seamless care across both stages.
2.   The definition and classification of HF have been 
updated in accordance with the Universal Definition 
of Heart Failure. In addition, the descriptions of Stage 
A (at risk of HF) and Stage B (pre-HF) have been 
expanded to highlight the importance of preventing 
progression to symptomatic HF and implementing 
early therapeutic interventions, with chronic kidney 
disease now included in Stage A.
3.   Guideline-directed medical therapy for HF with 
reduced ejection fraction, HF with mildly reduced 
ejection fraction (HFmrEF), and heart failure with 
preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has been updated 
to reflect major study findings published after the 2021 
focus update. Notably, the guideline now includes rec-
ommendations for sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 
inhibitors and a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist 
(finerenone) in HFmrEF and HFpEF, as well as incre-
tin-based therapies for HF with comorbid obesity.
4.   Regarding the management of cardiomyopathies, 
recent advances in the treatment of hypertrophic 
cardiomyopathy, cardiac amyloidosis, and cardiac 
sarcoidosis have been incorporated, with the addition 
of new therapeutic recommendations, including 
mavacamten for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and 
vutrisiran/acoramidis for transthyretin amyloid car-
diomyopathy.
5.   New sections have been added to address special car-
diovascular conditions, including atrial cardiomyopa-
thy, triglyceride deposit cardiomyovasculopathy, 
issues related to geriatrics/frailty, and cardio-oncology.
6.   Updated insights and recommendations have been 
incorporated regarding the roles of genetic testing, 
activities of daily living/quality of life assessments and 
patient-reported outcomes, and HF risk scores.
7.   A new chapter on community collaboration and com-
prehensive community care has been included, reflect-
ing the growing importance of social welfare 
considerations. This chapter covers topics such as the 
role of digital health in HF management, social reinte-
gration, employment support, and the contributions of 
certified HF educators.
8.   The assessment and treatment protocols for acute 
decompensated HF have been revised. This includes 
newly added definitions of worsening HF and decom-
pensation. Furthermore, the guideline now incorpo-
rates new insights and recommendations for 
transitional management from decompensated to 
compensated HF.
9.   Recommendations for exercise therapy and rehabilita-
tion during the acute phase have been added, offering 
a comprehensive overview of the role of cardiac reha-
bilitation in various phases of HF management.
10.  Non-cardiac comorbidities that are strongly linked to 
HF management are comprehensively summarized, 
with recommendations provided for conditions such 
as chronic kidney disease, obesity, diabetes, hyperka-
lemia, anemia, and iron deficiency, as well as cognitive 
dysfunction and psychiatric disorders.
II. Definitions
PM?c??r??g?e
 ▋ 1.1 Definition of Heart Failure
Heart failure (HF) is defined as a syndrome caused by 
structural and/or functional abnormalities of the heart, 
leading to congestion or elevated intracardiac pressure, as 
well as decreased cardiac output or tissue hypoperfusion, 
resulting in symptoms such as dyspnea, edema, fatigue, 
and reduced exercise tolerance.
1
 ▋ 1.2 Stages of Development and Risk of HF
It is important to view the progression of HF as a trajec-
tory to both enable the early detection of HF and facilitate 
appropriate therapeutic interventions and care (Figure 1). 
The American Heart Association/American College of 
Cardiology stages of HF are currently widely used to 
[[p9]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1283
JCS/JHFS 2025 Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Heart Failure
describe the stages of development and progression of 
HF.4
 ▋ 1.3  Definitions of Worsening Heart Failure and 
Decompensation
The use of terms to describe HF exacerbation, including 
worsening HF, decompensated HF, acute HF, and acute 
decompensated HF, is not consistent.2,4,11–13 The worsening 
of HF in Stage C can be regarded as a series of trajectories 
that deteriorate despite standard treatment. Therefore, the 
following conditions are included in the definition of wors-
ening HF.
13
•   Worsening symptoms and/or signs of HF despite stable 
and optimal HF therapy
•   Clinically significant deterioration in objective findings, 
regardless of symptom changes (including asymptomatic 
reductions in left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF],

quality of life.

worsening renal function as a sign of organ dysfunction, 
evidence of elevated intracardiac pressure, or declines in 
exercise tolerance or quality of life without prominent 
subjective symptoms)
•   Recurrent or worsening arrhythmic events.
Decompensated HF is defined as a condition character-
ized by worsening symptoms, signs, or hemodynamics that 
require intensified treatment beyond the initiation and 
optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy 
(Figure 2). Examples of specific thresholds for decompen-
sation include situations requiring the management of 
unstable hemodynamics, substantial escalation of oral 
diuretics or the administration of intravenous diuretic, 
unplanned outpatient visits, or, in some cases, hospitaliza-
tion.
11,12 Acute decompensated HF is defined as a condi-
tion requiring urgent treatment escalation, particularly 
life-saving interventions, to avert critical situations in cases 
of decompensated heart failure.
2. Classification of HF by LVEF
Based on the initial assessment of LVEF, HF is classified 
into 3 categories: HF with reduced ejection fraction 
(HFrEF), HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFm-
rEF), HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and 
HF with improved LVEF based on longitudinal assess-
ment (HFimpEF).
1
 ▋ 2.1 HF With Reduced Ejection Fraction
In this guideline, HFrEF is defined as LVEF ≤ 40%.1 In 
HFrEF, left ventricular (LV) dilation is commonly 
observed and is often accompanied not only by LV systolic 
dysfunction, as indicated by reduced LVEF, but also by 
LV diastolic dysfunction. In Japan, the primary causes of 
HFrEF have changed over time, from predominantly myo-
cardial diseases, such as dilated cardiomyopathy, to isch-
emic heart disease.
1
 ▋ 2.2 HF With Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction
It is recognized that clearly distinguishing between HFrEF 
and HFpEF based solely on LVEF can be challenging.
1 
Therefore, this guideline defines HF patients with an 
LVEF of 41–49% as having HFmrEF.1 Age and the preva-
lence of sex and atrial fibrillation in patients with HFmrEF 
are between those in HFrEF and HFpEF, but the distribu-
tion of underlying cardiac disease is similar to that of 
HFrEF, with a high proportion of patients with HFmrEF 
having ischemic heart disease.
14–16
 ▋ 2.3 HF With Preserved Ejection Fraction
In this guideline, HFpEF is defined as LVEF ≥50%.1 His-
torically, HFpEF has been considered to account for 
approximately half of all cases of HF. However, the preva-
lence of HFpEF is increasing due to population aging and 
the rising incidence of lifestyle-related diseases. 16a Epide-
miological studies in Japan report that 69% of patients 
with Stage C and 51% of patients with Stage D HF have 
HFpEF,17 indicating that it has become a major HF phe-
notype. Background factors strongly associated with 
HFpEF include advanced age, hypertension, atrial fibrilla-
tion, coronary artery disease, diabetes, and obesity. 18–23 
HFpEF represents a complex condition characterized by a 
combination of cardiac, vascular, and non-cardiovascular 
(e.g., pulmonary and skeletal muscle abnormalities) abnor-
malities.
24,25
Identifying the underlying etiology is crucial not only for 
classifying HF based on LVEF but also for diagnosing 
patients suspected of HFpEF. 26 Once HFpEF is diag-
nosed, it is essential to assess patients for specific etiologies 
that have disease-directed therapies, such as cardiac amy-
loidosis.
26–30
 ▋ 2.4 Changes in LVEF Over Time and HFimpEF
In HF patients, LVEF can change over time. 31,32 HFim-
pEF is defined as HF in patients whose initial LVEF was 
≤40%, with a subsequent increase in LVEF of ≥10% and a 
resulting LVEF >40% based on longitudinal assessment.1 
Other changes in LVEF are classified based on the LVEF 
category at the time of the longitudinal evaluation. Previ-
ous studies have reported that 20–40% of patients with 
HFrEF transition to HFmrEF or HFpEF over time and, 
similarly, 20–40% of patients with HFmrEF transition to 
HFpEF.
14,33–35
3. Classification by Etiology / Right-Sided HF
 ▋ 3.1 Etiology of HF
The causes of HF are diverse and can be classified based 
on pathophysiological mechanisms or the primary site of 
pathology.
 ▋ 3.2 Right-Sided HF
Right-sided HF is defined as a clinical syndrome character-
ized by impaired right ventricular filling or forward blood 
flow due to structural and/or functional abnormalities of 
the heart36 The importance of right ventricular function is 
increasingly being recognized, as recent studies have 
reported its association with long-term prognosis and exer-
cise tolerance in left-sided HF. 37,38 The most common 
cause of right-sided HF is backward failure due to left-
sided HF, often associated with pulmonary hypertension 
secondary to left-sided HF. In addition, there are various 
other causes of right-sided HF, including conditions in 
which structural or functional abnormalities of the right 
ventricle are the primary etiology.
36,39

III. Epidemiology and Prognosis
PM?d??g?e??i
 ▋ 1.1  Number of Heart Failure Patients in Japan 
(Figure 3)
Cardiovascular disease ranks as Japan’s second leading 
cause of death, with heart failure (HF) being the predomi-
nant cardiac-related cause of death. The burden of HF 
continues to grow as Japan experiences unprecedented 
demographic aging, creating an urgent public health chal-
lenge.
40
Recent data from the Japanese Registry of All Cardiac 
and Vascular Diseases (JROAD) showed that the number 
of HF hospitalizations in Japan reached 285,000 in 2023, 
with an in-hospital mortality rate of 9.1%. Both hospital-
ization and mortality rates show an upward trend, high-
lighting a growing public health challenge.
Projections from the Kobe University Heart Failure 
Registry in Awaji Medical Center (KUNIUMI) Registry, 
a regional cohort study conducted in Awaji, indicate that 
new HF hospitalizations in Japan will reach 210,000 by 
2025 and increase to 250,000 by 2040.
41 The burden of 
chronic HF presents appears even more challenging, with 
the total number of cases expected to surge to 1.3 million 
by 2030.42
 ▋ 1.2 Background of HF Patients in Japan
Major observational studies of both acute HF hospitaliza-
tion and chronic HF in Japan are presented in 
Table 3.
17,41,43–49 The mean age of patients enrolled in each 
study increase over time, reflecting an overall aging trend 
in the HF patient population. In addition, the proportion 
of patients with HF with preserved ejection fraction 
(HFpEF) is increasing as the population ages.
17,45 HF in 
the elderly is associated with a poor prognosis and presents 
a significant health economic challenge complicated by the 
need for caregiving and social support. Recent registry 
studies have identified ischemic heart disease as the pre-
dominant underlying cause of HF, accounting for 27–35% 
of cases, followed by valvular disease, arrhythmia, hyper-
tension, and cardiomyopathy. The complexity of HF man-
agement is further compounded by high rates of 
comorbidities: atrial fibrillation is present in 41–47% of 
patients, diabetes in 34–37%, and chronic kidney failure in 
39–45%, highlighting the systemic nature of the dis-
ease.
17,44–49 Furthermore, approximately 35% of patients 
have a history hospitalization for HF, with each subse-
quent admission strongly correlating with a poorer prog-
nosis.51
2. Prognosis of HF
The overall 1-year mortality rate in HF patients is approx-
imately 20%, and the 1-year readmission rate among hos-
pital discharge survivors is extremely high at 27–29%. 46 
The prognosis remains poor over longer periods, with only 
49% of patients surviving 4 years after hospitalization for 
HF exacerbation.
46
Cardiovascular death is a leading cause of death in HF 
with reduced ejection fraction, HF with mildly reduced 
ejection fraction, and HFpEF. Although sudden cardiac 
death occurs in all 3 types,52 the mortality pattern differs in 
elderly HFpEF patients. In those aged over 85 years, non-
cardiovascular causes become the predominant driver of 
death, suggesting the need for age-specific treatment 
approaches.
53 However, these clinical outcomes in Japan 
are comparable to or even better than in Europe, the US, 
and Southeast Asia.54,55

and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) in Japan. HF, heart failure.

3. Medical Expenses for HF
According to a 2012 survey, the global medical cost of HF is 
approximately 16 trillion yen, with the average annual medi-
cal cost per HF patient being approximately 3.5 million 
yen.56,57 In Japan, the estimated annual cost per HF patient is 
approximately 1.06 million yen.58 In addition, compared with 
other countries, hospital stays for HF patients are longer in 
Japan (with a median length of stay of 17 days in Japan vs. 4, 
7, and 9 days in the US, UK, and Taiwan, respectively), 
but the 30-day all-cause mortality rate and rehospitaliza-
tion rate are lower in Japan vs. other countries.
59
This favorable prognosis for HF patients in Japan may 
be attributed to the extended length of the hospital stay, 
which allows for comprehensive patient education and 
optimal medication management. Cost and treatment effi-
ciency remain challenging goals, requiring collaboration 
and optimization across multiple domains, including social 
systems and the healthcare workforce.
60
IV. Diagnosis and Longitudinal Evaluation
PM?c?`
Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome, and accurate 
diagnosis relies on a thorough evaluation of symptoms, 
medical history, and physical examination. Among the 
biomarkers, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and N-ter-
minal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) are the 
most critical tools in the diagnostic assessment of HF. 
Measurement of BNP/NT-proBNP is not necessarily 
required in patients with obvious signs of cardiac conges-
tion, but is recommended to differentiate HF from non-
HF causes. Echocardiography provides information on 
cardiac structure and function, and thus plays a central 
role in the evaluation of HF. Echocardiography allows 
ejection fraction (EF)-based classification and the identifi-
cation of potential causes of HF, such as valvular heart 
diseases, cardiomyopathies, or ischemic heart diseases.
The diagnosis of HF is challenging in patients with a 
preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and no 
apparent functional or structural abnormalities.
61–63 The 
H2FPEF score and the HFA-PEFF algorithm can be used 
to assess the pretest probability in patients with suspected 
HFpEF.62,64,65 However, there are phenotypic differences 
between Japanese and Western patients with HF with pre-
served ejection fraction (HFpEF), such as the prevalence 
of obesity. Therefore, a risk score specific to the Japanese 
population may be necessary.
66 Further, in patients with 
HFpEF who are euvolemic, left ventricular (LV) filling 
pressures are often normal at rest but may become abnor-
mal during exercise.63,67–70 In such cases, exercise testing is 
required to detect such abnormalities, and a physiological

2. Symptoms, Physical Examination, 
Electrocardiogram, Chest Radiograph
 ▋ 2.1 Symptoms (Medical History Taking)
A detailed medical history should be taken for the evalua-
tion of patients with HF. 1 Symptoms of pulmonary con-
gestion include dyspnea on exertion. Symptoms of systemic 
congestion include leg edema, loss of appetite, abdominal 
bloating, and postprandial fullness. Bendopnea (shortness 
of breath while bending forward occurring within 30 s) is 
less frequent, but typical for both systemic and pulmonary 
congestion.
74 This symptom is caused by a further increase 
in atrial pressure in patients with elevated atrial pressure 
and often appears within 10 s.75,76 Symptoms related to low 
cardiac output and tissue hypoperfusion include fatigue, 
malaise, dizziness, fainting, cognitive decline, and delir-
ium.
1
A thorough family history, including a 3-generation 
pedigree,77,78 is essential to diagnose hereditary cardiomy-
opathy. While obtaining a family history, it is important to 
confirm the existence of any family history of cardiovascu-
lar abnormalities with simple, non-technical language, as 
well as the family history of HF. A family history of pace-
maker or implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) 
implantation, or sudden death, should also be ascertained. 
In patients with unexplained cardiomyopathies, regular 
updates of the family history are recommended.
It is recommended a medical history is taken to identify 
exacerbating factors in patients with acute decompensated 
HF (ADHF). Assessment of social determinants of health, 
such as socioeconomic status, employment issues, educa-
tion level, health literacy, access to healthcare, and social 
support within the community, is also essential.
 ▋ 2.2 Physical Examination
  ▋ 2.2.1 Diagnosis of HF
In patients with pulmonary congestion, an S3 or S4 heart 
sound may be heard, reflecting elevated left atrial (LA) 
pressure.79 A highly specific sign of systemic congestion is 
jugular venous distention, which is associated with higher 
risk of HF hospitalization and cardiac death.80 Congestion 
scores calculated from multiple symptoms and signs 
reflecting clinical congestion can predict HF rehospitaliza-
tion and mortality.
81–87 Regular monitoring for signs of 
advanced HF88–93 is recommended to guide appropriate 
treatment.
  ▋ 2.2.2 Evaluation of HF Etiology
It is recommended that systemic diseases (e.g., amyloido-
sis, sarcoidosis, Fabry disease, connective tissue disorders) 
and conditions precipitating HF (e.g., anemia and endo-
crine disorders) are considered during physical examina-
tions to identify their characteristic signs and facilitate 
specific treatment.
94,95
 ▋ 2.3 Electrocardiography
Electrocardiography (ECG) is a fundamental tool in the 
clinical evaluation of HF. In ADHF, an ECG should be 
performed promptly to assess for acute coronary syn-
dromes and arrhythmias.
 ▋ 2.4 Chest X-Ray
A chest X-ray is useful for differentiating respiratory dis-
eases, such as pneumonia. 96,97 Although the severity of 
pulmonary congestion (i.e., pulmonary artery wedge pres-
sure) cannot be accurately determined by a chest X-ray 
alone, specific findings provide qualitative estimation of 
elevations in pulmonary artery wedge pressure.
98–103 The 
cardiac silhouette reflects the size and morphology of the 4 
cardiac chambers. An increased cardiothoracic ratio is 
associated with a poor prognosis.104

 ▋ 3.1 Natriuretic Peptides
  ▋ 3.1.1 Diagnosis of HF
BNP and NT-proBNP correlate with hemodynamics and 
are useful in diagnosing HF in both ambulatory and emer-
gency settings.106–109 In particular, their high negative pre-
dictive value (94–98%) underscores their utility in ruling

demonstrated that patients with BNP <35 pg/mL or NT-

BNP and NT-proBNP levels are influenced by non-HF 
factors.
1,2,4 Impaired renal function elevates BNP and NT-

2 show more sig-

without.
19,119–123
  ▋ 3.1.2  Prediction of Prognosis Based on Measurements at 
Admission and Discharge
Natriuretic peptides are useful for assessing disease sever-
ity and predicting prognosis.
19,124 BNP and NT-proBNP 
levels are correlated with prognosis. 125–129 Elevated BNP/
NT-proBNP levels at admission are associated with short-
term clinical outcomes (e.g., in-hospital mortality), regard-
less of LVEF. 113,130,131 BNP/NT-proBNP levels at 
discharge, as well as changes during decongestion therapy, 
are associated with long-term outcomes (e.g., post-dis -
charge death or HF rehospitalization).132–138
 ▋ 3.2 Other Biomarkers
HF encompasses diverse pathophysiological aspects, mak-
ing it challenging to capture a complete clinical picture of 
an HF patient with a single biomarker. 143 Therefore, to 
better understand the underlying pathophysiology and 
personalize treatment, a comprehensive approach that 
integrates multiple biomarkers reflecting different patho-
physiological pathways is essential.
  ▋ 3.2.1 Representative Biomarkers of HF
a. Myocardial Troponin I/T
High troponin levels reflect myocardial injury and are 
associated with poor prognoses in both ischemic and non-
ischemic HF.
144–146
b. High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein, Interleukin-6
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 are 
important biomarkers of inflammation and predictors of 
all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization.147–150
c. Soluble Suppression of Tumorigenicity-2
Soluble suppression of tumorigenicity-2 (sST2) is produced 
in the vascular endothelium and lungs in response to con-
gestion and inflammation and promotes inflammation and 
fibrosis.
151,152 sST2 is a predictor of all-cause mortality, 
cardiovascular death, and HF hospitalization in both 
chronic153 and acute HF.154,155
d. Growth Differentiation Factor-15
Growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15) levels increase 
with hypoxia, mechanical stress, oxidative stress, inflam-
mation, and metabolic dysregulation.
152 GDF-15 is a prog-
nostic biomarker of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular 
death, and HF hospitalization in various patient popula-
tions.156–158
e. Galectin-3
Galectin-3 (GAL-3) is a mediator of cardiac fibrosis and 
inflammation.
151 GAL-3 is a predictor of all-cause mortal-
ity and HF hospitalization.159
f. Carbohydrate Antigen-125
Carbohydrate antigen-125 (CA125) is released by mesothe-
lial cells in the pleura, peritoneum, and pericardium
151 and 
has been reported to be associated with congestion in HF 
in studies such as the Biology Study to Tailored Treatment 
in Chronic Heart Failure (BIOSTAT-CHF).
160,161 CA125-
guided use of intravenous diuretics reduced HF hospital-
izations162 and improved renal function in acute HF 
patients with renal dysfunction.163
g. Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Protein-7
Levels of insulin-like growth factor binding protein-7 
(IGFBP-7), produced by a wide range of human tissues 
including the heart, are elevated in response to renal injury 
and inflammation.
164 IGFBP-7 improves the prediction 
accuracy of all-cause mortality and HF hospitaliza-
tion.164,165
4. Echocardiography
 ▋ 4.1  Cardiac Function, Morphology and 
Hemodynamic Assessment
  ▋ 4.1.1 Evaluation of Cardiac Function and Morphology
In patients with suspected HF, echocardiography is recom-
mended for the assessment of cardiac function and mor-
phology, as well as coexisting conditions such as valvular 
heart disease or cardiomyopathy.
a. Evaluation of LV Systolic Function
Evaluation of LVEF is recommended for all patients with 
HF to ensure EF-based classification of HF and to deter-
mine the treatment strategy.
166–168 Although the 2-dimen-

sional disk summation method is the standard for 
measuring LVEF, 3-dimensional analysis may offer higher 
accuracy and reproducibility when feasible with good 
image quality. 169 In recent years, artificial intelligence-
based automated measurement has become a highly repro-
ducible and objective option when image quality is 
sufficient.170,171
Global longitudinal strain using a speckle tracking 
method may be considered for risk stratification regardless 
of the type of HF. Global longitudinal strain captures 
early myocardial dysfunction, has good reproducibility, 
and provides better prognostic value than LVEF.
172,173 
However, variations in strain values among analysis soft-
ware and susceptibility to image quality remain challenges.
b. Evaluation of LV Diastolic Function
LV diastolic function consists of LV relaxation and stiff-
ness. Thus, echocardiographic evaluation of diastolic func-
tion aims to detect increased LV filling pressure caused by 
impaired LV relaxation and increased LV stiffness. 174,175 
Elevated filling pressure serves as a useful prognostic factor 
in HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
176 and is 
central to the diagnosis in HFpEF.26,177–180 
In the American Society of Echocardiography and 
European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging guide-
lines181,182 and the JCS 2021 Guideline on the Clinical 
Application of Echocardiography, LV diastolic function is 
evaluated using an algorithm based on several parameters. 
However, its limitations of adopting uniform cutoff values 
of the parmeters without considering a patient’s age or 
underlying conditions should be acknowledged.
c. Evaluation of Right Ventricular Function
Right ventricular (RV) function is an important prognostic 
factor in both HFpEF and HFrEF.
183,184 It is especially 
important in conditions that primarily affect the RV, such 
as pulmonary hypertension and tricuspid valve regurgita-
tion.185,186
Among individual parameters, tricuspid annular plane 
systolic excursion (TAPSE) and the peak systolic velocity 
at the tricuspid annulus (s′ ) are simple and widely used 
indices, but these metrics assess only the motion of the RV 
annulus. RV fractional area change incorporates RV free 
wall motion; however, it is highly dependent on the imag-
ing plane and are prone to reproducibility issues.
3-Dimensional RVEF can evaluate the entire RV and is 
considered the most reliable when feasible. Speckle-track-
ing-derived longitudinal strain of the RV free wall has been 
shown to be strongly correlated with prognosis across 
various conditions.
187,188 However, these indices are com-
plicated and are not widely used in clinical practice.
In conclusion, no single parameter is both simple and 
comprehensive enough to serve as a standalone metric, 
highlighting the importance of a multiparametric evalua-
tion of RV function.
d. Assessment of Atrial Function
Atrial function is increasingly recognized as an important 
prognostic factor both in HFrEF and HFpEF.
189 LA vol-
ume index, in addition to the LA diameter, should be 
measured in patients with HF. LA longitudinal strain, a 
parameter gaining attention as a sensitive indicator of LA 
function, may be useful for differentiating between HFpEF 
and non-cardiogenic causes of dyspnea in challenging 
cases.
190
  ▋ 4.1.2 Hemodynamic Evaluation
Another important role of echocardiography in HF is 
hemodynamic assessment, with a focus on flow and pres-
sure estimation.
a. Evaluation of Cardiac Output
The diameter of the LV outflow tract and the velocity–time 
integral obtained by the Doppler method can be used to 
evaluate stroke volume. In addition, serial changes in the 
velocity–time integral have been reported to reflect HF 
prognosis.
191,192
b. Estimation of Intracardiac Pressure
Although echocardiography cannot directly measure pres-
sure, it provides useful estimates of LV filling pressure 
based on several indices. 192a In HF, elevated pulmonary 
arterial pressure is typically secondary to increased LV 
filling pressure. However, significant deviations from LV 
filling pressure indices may suggest increased pulmonary 
vascular resistance, necessitating consideration of pulmo-
nary arterial hypertension. Systolic pulmonary arterial 
pressure is often estimated using the maximum tricuspid 
regurgitation velocity. However, this measurement can be 
inaccurate in cases of minimal or massive regurgitation, 
where laminar flow may distort the velocity.
193 In such 
scenarios, additional indices, such as the acceleration time 
of the RV outflow or the presence of an LV D-shape can 
be informative.194

Right atrial (RA) pressure reflects not only RV diastolic 
pressure but also systemic fluid volume, as represented by 
central venous pressure. Estimating RA pressure is impor-
tant for assessing the need for diuretics. RA pressure is 
commonly estimated by measuring the diameter of the 
inferior vena cava in a long-axis image and evaluating its 
respiratory variability.
195,196 Body size adjustment or the 
long-to-short axis ratio in the short-axis view may be use-
ful.195,196
  ▋ 4.1.3 Evaluation in Atrial Fibrillation
Evidence for echocardiographic evaluation in patients with 
atrial fibrillation is limited. Measuring beats with stable 
RR intervals or averaging 5–10 beats may be useful for 
prognostic assessment.
196a
  ▋ 4.1.4 Timing of Evaluation
Echocardiography, as a non-invasive and repeatable diag-
nostic tool, provides valuable insights into the dynamic 
changes associated with HF. In patients undergoing phar-
macological or device therapy for HF, echocardiographic 
evaluation before the intervention is recommended. Echo-
cardiographic evaluation can be repeated if there are 
changes in the patient’s condition or after therapeutic 
intervention. Although evidence regarding the optimal 
timing for echocardiographic evaluation is limited, follow-
up echocardiography can be considered 6–12 months after 
cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) or the initiation 
of pharmacological treatment aimed at reverse remodeling, 
because it generally occurs within this time frame.
197–203
In patients receiving non-pharmacological therapy for 
structural heart disease, echocardiography can be consid-
ered before discharge to assess acute therapeutic effects 
and establish a baseline for follow-up. Conversely, routine 
echocardiography without a clear purpose is often unnec-
essary for stable patients without significant clinical 
changes.
In patients with suspected HF exacerbations, echocar-
diography is recommended for assessment of the underly-
ing cause or hemodynamic status, as needed.
204,205 It has 
been reported that echocardiographic findings at discharge 
are more strongly associated with outcomes, such as rehos-
pitalization, than those on admission.
206,207 Evaluating 
residual congestion at discharge using echocardiography 
has also been shown to be beneficial.208,209 Thus, echocar-
diography may be considered before discharge from HF 
hospitalization to evaluate residual congestion and help 
with risk stratification.
 ▋ 4.2 Stress Echocardiography
  ▋ 4.2.1  Exercise Stress Echocardiography for HFpEF 
Diagnosis
The diagnosis of HFpEF is more challenging than the 
diagnosis of HFrEF.
1,63,68,71 Exercise stress echocardiogra-
phy is a useful tool to detect impaired LV diastolic reserve 
that appears only during exertion and subsequent eleva-
tions in LA and pulmonary pressures.63,70,71,210,211 Exercise 
stress echocardiography is indicated when resting assess-
ments do not explain the symptoms of dyspnea. The most 
appropriate patient population for exercise stress echocar-
diography is the group of patients with an intermediate 
pre-test probability of HFpEF.
62,63,72,213 The H2FPEF score 
or the HFA-PEFF algorithm can be used to evaluate the 
pre-test probability of HFpEF.
61,62,64
There are 2 types of stress echocardiography: exercise 
stress and pharmacological stress. In general, exercise 
stress is a preferred approach because it is more physiolog-
ical than pharmacological stress. Exercise stress includes 
isometric exercises (e.g., handgrips) and isotonic exercises 
(e.g., treadmills, ergometers). Supine ergometer exercise is 
recommended for the diagnosis of HFpEF.
210 This is 
because it allows continuous image acquisition throughout 
the test, is safer than a treadmill (lower risk of falls), and 
can be performed at low intensity even in elderly patients.214
Mitral inflow E and A velocities, mitral annular early 
diastolic wave (e′), E/e′, and tricuspid regurgitation veloc-
ity (TRV) should be assessed at baseline and during exer-
cise for the evaluation of HFpEF. According to the 
guidelines from the American Society of Echocardiogra-
phy and the European Society of Cardiovascular Imaging, 
elevated LA pressure is defined when patients meet all 3 of 
the following criteria: (1) an average E/e′ ratio >14 or sep-
tal E/e′ ratio >15 with exercise; (2) peak exercise TRV >2.8 
m/s; and (3) resting septal e′  <7 cm/s (or lateral e′  < 
10 cm/s).
182 The European Heart Failure Association rec-
ommends the addition of exercise E/e′  ratio and TRV to 
resting assessments.62 However, the primary limitation is 
that the criteria for diagnosing HFpEF by exercise stress 
echocardiography have not been standardized.67,211,215–217
  ▋ 4.2.2 Stress Echocardiography for Other Conditions
In mitral regurgitation (MR), exercise stress echocardiog-
raphy is mainly used to confirm equivocal symptoms and 
predict clinical outcomes. Exercise stress echocardiogra-
phy can be considered in asymptomatic patients with 
severe MR or symptomatic patients with moderate MR on 
resting echocardiography.
213 Symptoms, MR severity, sys-
tolic pulmonary artery pressure, and LV and RV systolic 
reserve should be evaluated during exercise.218–221 MR can 
worsen not only when exercising on ergometer or tread-
mills, but also when exercising with handgrips.
222,223 How-
ever, there is no evidence supporting the utility of exercise 
stress echocardiography in helping guide treatment deci-
sions.
Exercise stress echocardiography is reasonable for

stress should not be performed in symptomatic patients 
with severe AS. Dobutamine stress echocardiography can

224,226–229 If stroke volume is increased by ≥20% by

gradient ≥30–40 mmHg with an aortic valve area <1.0 cm2 
are considered to have true severe AS. Pseudo-severe AS is 
defined as a peak mean pressure gradient <40 mmHg and 
a peak stress aortic valve area ≥1.0 cm2.224,226 The presence 
of LV contractile reserve is generally defined as a relative 
increase in stroke volume >20% during dobutamine 
stress.

 ▋ 4.3 Other Echocardiographic Indicators
  ▋ 4.3.1 Point-of-Care Ultrasound
Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), a focused bedside 
imaging technique used to rapidly evaluate essential signs, 
is becoming increasingly widespread.234–237 In HF, POCUS 
has proven useful for excluding conditions like myocardial 
infarction and pulmonary embolism, as well as for assess-
ing congestion.238
  ▋ 4.3.2 Evaluation of Multiorgan Congestion in HF
a. Lung Ultrasound
B-lines are indicative of interlobular septal thickening due 
to pulmonary congestion, and the presence of 3 or more 
B-lines within a single field of view is considered abnor-
mal.
239–241 Lung ultrasound assessing B-lines is simple, 
extremely quick to perform, and has a high negative pre-
dictive value.
240,242–245 Evaluating residual congestion 
through B-lines prior to discharge has been reported to be 
useful for risk stratification.
209,246
b. Intrarenal Doppler Ultrasound
Intrarenal Doppler ultrasound may be considered to eval-
uate renal congestion in HF patients. In HF patients, prog-
nosis worsens as the waveform of intrarenal venous flow 
progresses from continuous to biphasic and eventually to 
monophasic.
239,247–250 These patterns can be correlated with 
lowering central venous pressure and can improve with 
appropriate HF management.
250–254
  ▋ 4.3.3  Unique Echocardiographic Findings in HF-Related 
Conditions
a. Echocardiographic Findings Related to CRT
Echocardiographic assessment of LV dyssynchrony is an 
important prognostic indicator in patients undergoing 
CRT. Specific markers of LV dyssynchrony, such as septal 
flash and apical rocking, have been shown to improve after 
CRT device implantation, and these improvements are 
associated with better clinical outcomes.
255,256 Although 
optimization of atrioventricular and interventricular delay 
settings following CRT device implantation is not rou-
tinely necessary, it may be considered in specific cases to 
further enhance therapeutic outcomes.
257,258
b.  Echocardiographic Findings Suggestive of Cardiac 
Amyloidosis
Echocardiographic findings suggestive of cardiac amyloi-
dosis include LV wall thickening ≥12 mm, RV wall thick-
ening, atrial septal thickening, severe diastolic dysfunction, 
granular sparkling of the myocardium, thickening of the 
aortic valve, small pericardial effusion, and reduced basal 
LV strain with preserved apical strain (apical sparing) on 
speckle tracking echocardiography.
259,260 Although apical 
sparing was originally reported with high sensitivity and 
specificity, it is not entirely specific to cardiac amyloido-
sis.
261 Therefore, screening for cardiac amyloidosis using 
echocardiography should involve the comprehensive eval-
uation of multiple parameters. In addition, findings such 
as reduced LVEF, diastolic dysfunction, an impaired RA 
and RV function pattern (e.g., TAPSE), and the apical 
sparing pattern are prognostic indicators.
262–267
c.  Echocardiographic Findings Suggestive of Constrictive 
Pericarditis
Hemodynamic features of constrictive pericarditis include 
severe impairment of ventricular filling, represented by 
enlargement of the atrium and inferior vena cava, and 
ventricular interdependence.
268 In addition, the pericar-
dium on the lateral wall of the LV often adheres to sur-
rounding tissues, which can be visualized on B-mode 
imaging as pericardial tethering; this adhesion limits dia-
stolic motion of the lateral mitral annulus, decreasing the 
lateral e′. In contrast, the septal mitral annulus typically 
exhibits exaggerated motion as a compensatory mecha-
nism, and the septal e′ becomes larger than the lateral e′.
268
5. Other Diagnostic Imaging
 ▋ 5.1 Computed Tomography
Cardiac computed tomography (CT) can evaluate cardiac 
morphology and function in addition to coronary anat-
omy.
  ▋ 5.1.1 Evaluation of Coronary Artery Disease
Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) is useful in differenti-
ating between ischemic and non-ischemic cardiomyopa-
thy.
269,270 Given its high specificity for the diagnosis of 
ischemic heart disease, CCTA can be useful in ruling out 
coronary artery disease in HF patients with a low to inter-
mediate pre-test probability of ischemic heart disease or in 
those with equivocal results on non-invasive stress 
tests.
271,272

  ▋ 5.1.2 Evaluation of Cardiac Morphology and Function
Electrocardiogram-gated cardiac CT provides highly 
reproducible assessment of ventricular volumes and can be 
beneficial when echocardiography and cardiac magnetic 
resonance imaging (CMR) are unable to provide the 
required diagnostic information.
273,274 In addition, delayed 
enhancement cardiac CT with iodine contrast enables eval-
uation of myocardial tissue,
275 and can be considered as an 
alternative when CMR is not feasible.276–279 Furthermore, 
extracellular volume (ECV) can be evaluated with late 
enhancement cardiac CT.
280 Table 4 summarizes the pur-
pose and findings of CT for conditions associated with HF.
  ▋ 5.1.3 Evaluation of Extracardiac Abnormalities
CT is frequently performed to determine the cause of dys-
pnea, especially in patients presenting with respiratory 
failure. It is particularly useful for differentiating condi-
tions such as pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syn-
dromes, aortic dissection, and respiratory infections.
283 
Moreover, chest CT scans are valuable in detecting signs 
associated with HF, such as bilateral ground glass opacifi-
cation, interlobular septal thickening, bilateral peribron-
chovascular interstitial thickening (bronchovascular 
bundle thickening), increased vascular diameter, thicken-
ing of the interlobular fissures, and bilateral pleural effu-
sions.
284,285
 ▋ 5.2 Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) is an 
excellent tool for evaluating cardiac morphology, as well 
as LV and RV function, due to its high tissue contrast and 
reproducibility.
2,4 CMR is recommended for evaluating 
cardiac morphology and function in patients in whom 
echocardiographic evaluation is difficult. CMR can also 
evaluate myocardial tissue characteristics using various 
imaging techniques, such as late gadolinium enhancement 
(LGE) and T
1 and T2 mapping. These features are useful 
in differentiating cardiomyopathy and may be helpful 
when cardiomyopathy is suspected as the underlying cause 
of HF.
287
  ▋ 5.2.1 Evaluation of Cardiac Morphology and Function
Evaluation of LV mass and EF using the Simpson method 
with CMR is accurate and reproducible, and is considered 
the gold standard for the evaluation of LV function.288 It 
is therefore recommended when echocardiographic assess-
ment is difficult or when accurate assessment of LVEF is 
needed to decide on a therapeutic plan for patients with 
HF. Furthermore, strain analysis using the feature track-
ing method can now be performed on CMR cine images, 
allowing accurate assessment of RV function.
289,290
Because cine images can evaluate morphological

changes during a single heartbeat in any plane, they are

to accurately depict the apex of the heart with high tissue

291,292
  ▋ 5.2.2 Evaluation of Myocardial Histology
CMR can evaluate myocardial histology using LGE 
CMR, and T 1 and/or T 2 mapping, and is useful in the 
detailed evaluation of patients with HF in whom no under-
lying disease has been identified. LGE shows high signal 
intensity consistent with myocardial fibrosis, and its distri-
bution pattern can be used to differentiate between isch-
emic and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, as well as to 
assess myocardial viability.
293 For example, cardiac amy-
loidosis294,295 and HCM,296 which are frequently observed 
in patients with HFpEF, can be differentiated by the rela-
tively specific LGE pattern. Idiopathic dilated cardiomy-
opathy and cardiac sarcoidosis cannot be differentiated on 
the basis of morphology or cardiac function alone, but can 
be differentiated to some extent by the LGE pattern. Con-
versely, the LGE pattern in patients with ischemic heart 
disease is characteristic, dominant on the endocardial side, 
and can be easily differentiated from other cardiomyopa-
thies.
T
1 and T2 mapping is a pixel-by-pixel image of measured 
T1 (longitudinal relaxation time) and T2 (transverse relax-
ation time) values of the myocardium at a constant mag-
netic field. 297,298 T 1 mapping is useful for evaluating 
myocardial tissue characteristics, 299–301 whereas T 2 map-
ping can be used to assess tissue edema and inflammation 
in the hyperacute phase of myocarditis and myocardial 
infarction. In general, myocardial edema, fibrosis, and 
amyloid protein deposition prolong T
1 values, whereas 
lipid and iron deposition shorten them. T 1 mapping can 
also be used to determine the ECV from pre- and post-
contrast T1 values. Elevated T 1 values and ECV are par-
ticularly useful in diagnosing HF patients with cardiac 
amyloidosis.
300,301 In contrast, T 1 values are decreased in 
patients with cardiac Fabry disease302 and hemochromato-
sis.303
T2 mapping is a pixel-by-pixel image of measured tissue 
T2 values, similar to T1 mapping, but reflecting myocardial 
water content. T2 mapping is useful for evaluating inflam-
mation after acute myocarditis or myocardial infarction. 
Myocardial edema in cardiac sarcoidosis can also be 
assessed. Conversely, T2* (T2 star) values reflect the trans-
verse relaxation time and the signal attenuation process 
caused by magnetic field inhomogeneity, and T2* mapping 
is useful for the evaluation of local iron content and hem-
orrhage.
304 Table 5 summarizes causative diseases of HF, 
the purpose of magnetic resonance imaging examination, 
and characteristic findings.
 ▋ 5.3  Nuclear Medicine Imaging/Positron Emission 
Tomography
Nuclear medicine tests have wide-ranging roles in patients 
with HF, including in assessing the severity of HF, evaluat-
ing cardiac function if other modalities are insufficient, and 
identifying the cause of HF.
272
  ▋ 5.3.1 Evaluation of Ventricular Function
Electrocardiogram-gated single photon emission com-
puted tomography (SPECT) with technetium-99 m (99 mTc) 
or thallium-201 (201Tl) for myocardial blood flow imaging 
can be used to assess LV volume and EF.306 Cardiac blood 
pool scintigraphy using 99 mTc-labeled red blood cells has 
been reported to have high reproducibility in the determi-
nation of LVEF,
272,307 and may be considered when other 
methods are inadequate.
  ▋ 5.3.2 Myocardial Perfusion Imaging (99 mTc, 201Tl)
Myocardial perfusion imaging with 99 mTc or 201Tl SPECT 
can be used to assess myocardial ischemia and myocardial 
viability in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy.
272,308,309 
In patients with coronary artery disease, many observa-
tional studies have reported improved survival with revas-
cularization in patients with myocardial viability.
272,308–310 
Conversely, a prespecified viability substudy of the Surgi-
cal Treatment for Ischemic Heart Failure (STICH) trial 
showed that the beneficial effects of coronary artery bypass

313 The Positron Emission Tomography and 
Recovery Following Revascularization-2 (PARR-2) trial, 
an RCT comparing the treatment group based on viability 
assessment with 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron

also found no significant reduction in cardiovascular 
events.314 A post hoc analysis of the PARR-2 trial showed 
improved outcomes with revascularization in patients with 
a larger extent of myocardial perfusion–metabolism mis-
match.315 A substudy of the REVIVED-BCIS2 trial 
showed that the extent of non-viable myocardium was 
associated with prognosis and improvement in LV func-
tion.313 Based on these findings, viability evaluation is not 
recommended for all patients, but should be considered in 
patients at high risk of revascularization or in those with 
HF refractory to conservative treatment.
  ▋ 5.3.3  Myocardial Fatty Acid Metabolism Imaging 
(
123I-BMIPP Scintigraphy)
123I-β-Methyl-p-iodophenyl-pentadecanoic acid (BMIPP) 
scintigraphy is used to evaluate myocardial fatty acid metab-
olism. In the acute phase of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, it 
has been reported that fatty acid metabolism is more 
severely impaired than myocardial perfusion; metabolism 
imaging can be used as a non-invasive test in combination 
with perfusion evaluation to differentiate Takotsubo cardio-
myopathy.
316 In patients with triglyceride deposit cardiomyo-
vasculopathy, a decrease in the BMIPP washout rate due 
to impaired triglyceride metabolism has been reported, and 
is considered an important clinical finding for diagnosis.317
  ▋ 5.3.4  Cardiac Sympathetic Neuroimaging (123I-MIBG 
Scintigraphy)
Cardiac sympathetic nerve activity can be assessed with 
123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG). In patients with 
HF, regardless of the underlying cause, the MIBG wash-
out rate increases and the late heart-to-mediastinum ratio 
decreases, consistent with reduced LV function and 
increased sympathetic activity, and H/M ratio can be used 
to assess HF severity and prognosis.
318–321
  ▋ 5.3.5  Bone Scintigraphy (99 mTc-PYP Scintigraphy, 99 mTc-
HMDP Scintigraphy)
99 mTc-pyrophosphate (PYP) is useful for detecting myocar-
dial necrosis and has been used in the diagnosis and prog-
nostic evaluation of myocardial infarction and 
revascularization procedures.322 Recently, bone scintigra-
phy using 99 mTc-PYP was reported to play an important 
role in the diagnosis of hereditary and wild-type trans-
thyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM). 322–326 
Bone scintigraphy tracers other than 99 mTc-PYP have been 
reported to have a similar diagnostic performance to 
99 mTc-PYP,323,326 and 99 mTc-hydroxymethylene diphospho-
nate (HMDP) has been approved for the diagnosis of 
ATTR-CM in Japan since 2022.
  ▋ 5.3.6 Gallium Scintigraphy
Gallium scintigraphy is used to detect inflammatory dis-
eases (e.g., cardiac sarcoidosis, myocarditis, infective endo-
carditis) and cardiac lesions of malignant lymphoma.
327,328 
However, in the detection of cardiac sarcoidosis, the sensi-
tivity of gallium scintigraphy is considered inferior to that 
of FDG-PET.
  ▋ 5.3.7 Positron Emission Tomography
PET can be used for myocardial glucose metabolism imag-
ing with 18F-FDG and myocardial perfusion imaging with 
13N-ammonia. In Japan, the use of 18F-FDG to evaluate 
myocardial viability and diagnose inflammatory sites in 
cardiac sarcoidosis or large vessel vasculitis, as well as the 
use of 
13N-ammonia to evaluate myocardial perfusion, is 
covered by insurance. 18F-FDG assessment of myocardial 
viability may be used to predict the impact of revascular-
ization in patients with ischemic heart disease and reduced 
LV function.272,308–310,314,315 In patients with HF due to cor-
onary artery disease, 18F-FDG assessment of viability is 
covered by insurance when SPECT assessment of myocar-
dial perfusion is inconclusive. The evaluation of myocar-
dial perfusion with 13N-ammonia is covered only when it is 
difficult to determine myocardial perfusion using other 
modalities. The diagnostic performance of PET has been 
reported to be superior to that of SPECT.329,330
6. Invasive Examinations
 ▋ 6.1  Clinical Indications for Right Heart 
Catheterization
In patients with HF, hemodynamic evaluation by right 
heart catheterization (RHC) should be considered in cases 
of insufficient assessment of cardiac output, stroke volume, 
LV end-diastolic pressure, or fluid volume.331 RHC is rec-
ommended for evaluating heart transplant candidates 332 
and for suspected constrictive pericarditis, restrictive car-
diomyopathy, congenital heart disease, high-output HF, 
or concomitant pulmonary hypertension. 333,334 However, 
routine hemodynamic evaluation by RHC in patients with 
HF is not recommended due to its invasiveness and limited 
clinical benefit.335
In cases of suspected cardiogenic shock or anticipated 
progressive deterioration of cardiac function, such as ful-

The importance of exercise stress testing (exercise stress 
echocardiography and exercise RHC) in the diagnosis of 
HFpEF is increasingly being recognized.
337 In cases of 
inconclusive results by exercise stress echocardiography, 
exercise stress RHC may be considered.
62 Although exer-
cise stress RHC is useful for diagnosing patients with 
HFpEF who have normal LV filling pressure at rest, it can 
only be performed at limited facilities and is not yet com-
mon in clinical practice.
 ▋ 6.2  Coronary Angiography and Left 
Ventriculography
In patients with HF, the indication for early evaluation of 
coronary artery disease should be considered given the 
potential benefit of initial revascularization for cardiovas-
cular outcomes.338 In patients with low to moderate pre-
test probability, non-invasive imaging should be performed 
first to identify those patients likely to have coronary 
artery disease.
339 Invasive coronary angiography can be 
considered if coronary artery disease is suspected or non-
invasive testing is inadequate.
340 Invasive coronary angiog-
raphy can also be considered when myocardial ischemia is 
a potential contributing factor to HF and revasculariza-
tion is expected to be beneficial for HF treatment.
Indications for left ventriculography are limited; it may 
be considered in patients suspected of Takotsubo cardio-
myopathy or patients with MR if echocardiography is 
unable to accurately evaluate MR severity.
 ▋ 6.3 Endomyocardial Biopsy
Endomyocardial biopsy is useful for diagnosing underly-
ing diseases, particularly when assessing secondary cardio-
myopathies such as myocarditis, cardiac sarcoidosis, 
cardiac amyloidosis, and Fabry disease; in these cases, the 
biopsy results may directly influence treatment decisions.
341 
At facilities in which myocardial biopsy is readily avail-
able, endomyocardial biopsy is strongly recommended in 
cases of suspected acute myocarditis with severe HF or 
cardiogenic shock, acute HF, ventricular arrhythmias, or 
advanced atrioventricular block.
342–345 This procedure is 
also strongly recommended in cases of progressively wors-
ening ventricular dysfunction and HF despite appropriate 
treatment.
341,343 In addition, it is valuable for the diagnosis 
and evaluation of acute rejection after cardiac transplanta-
tion and for the diagnosis of cardiac tumors. 341,343,346 
Although some studies suggest that myocardial pathologi-
cal findings may be useful in predicting reverse remodel-
ing,348–350 sufficient evidence has not yet been established. 
Due to its invasiveness and risk, endomyocardial biopsy is 
not routinely recommended for HF patients.341,343,351,352 In 
Japan, endomyocardial biopsy is mandated for the differ-
ential diagnosis of cardiomyopathy to determine candi-
dacy for heart transplantation, except in cases of definite 
ischemic cardiomyopathy.

and Physical Function
In the evaluation of physical activity capacity, both exer-
cise tolerance and physical function should be assessed.

Exercise tolerance is defined as the ability to increase car-
diac output and utilize oxygen in peripheral skeletal mus-
cles during physical activity. 361 Physical function is an 
assessment parameter that reflects exercise capacity, which 
involves the use of peripheral skeletal muscles, and its 
relationship to activities of daily living (ADL).
 ▋ 7.1  New York Heart Association Functional 
Classification
New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional classifi-
cation demonstrates a reasonable correlation with peak 
V˙ O2 and 6-min walk distance (6MWD). 353–355 It is useful 
for prognostic stratification in patients with compensated 
HF regardless of LVEF,356 and is also useful for prognostic 
evaluation for decompensated HF.357 Evaluation and doc-
umentation of NYHA functional classification is recom-
mended for assessing treatment indications and 
effectiveness, as well as for evaluating the quality of care at 
a facility.
4,358
A disadvantage of NYHA functional classification is the 
lack of quantifiability and objectivity.353,359,360 For instance, 
in cases of short-term changes in disease status, such as 
during the decompensated (acute) phase, the assessment of 
NYHA class has limited clinical significance. Most patients 
with decompensated HF are categorized as NYHA Class 
II or III, and this classification shows weak correlation with 
objective measures of disease severity.
361 In patients with

severe HF (e.g., NYHA Class III–IV), the Interagency

362,363 In addition, the specific inten-

364
 ▋ 7.2. Evaluation of Exercise Tolerance
  ▋ 7.2.1 Significance of Assessing Exercise Tolerance
Decreased exercise tolerance is one of the main signs of HF 
and is closely related not only to the severity of HF, but 
also to decreased ADL and worsened quality of life (QOL). 
Improved exercise tolerance is one of the main goals of 
treatment for HF. An algorithm for the evaluation of exer-
cise tolerance and physical function in HF patients  is 
shown in Figure 4. Exercise tolerance should be evaluated 
comprehensively, not only by test results but also by infor-
mation obtained from medical interviews about the pres-
ence of clinical signs (e.g., shortness of breath and 
palpitations in daily life) or symptom thresholds for those 
signs.
5
  ▋ 7.2.2 Six-Minute Walk Test
The 6MWD is a simple submaximal exercise test used to 
evaluate exercise tolerance in walking, an important com-
ponent of ADL.
365,366 A 6MWD <300 m is considered an 
indicator of a poor prognosis. 367,368 In a retrospective 
observational study of elderly HF patients in Japan, a 
6MWD <242 m was reported as a cut-off value associated 
with poor prognosis.369 An increase in the 6MWD >50 m 
after treatment is an indicator of treatment efficacy and 
good prognosis.
370
  ▋ 7.2.3 Cardiopulmonary Exercise Test
The aims of cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPX) are var-
ious and include: (1) objective evaluation of dyspnea dur-
ing exertion and assessment of exercise tolerance;
371–373 (2) 
determination of surgical indications, prognosis, and treat-
ment efficacy; and (3) formulation of exercise prescriptions 
and implementation of exercise therapy in cardiac reha-
bilitation. Peak oxygen consumption (V˙ O
2) is the most 
objective evaluation index in CPX. 353,361,374–376 However, 
age-specific reference values for peak V˙ O2 (%peak V˙ O2) 
based on measured data are not provided for older adults 
aged over 80 years. The anaerobic threshold provides 
information of the intensity of activity that can be per-
formed without overloading in daily life and is used in 
exercise prescription.
377,378
  ▋ 7.2.4  Prediction of Prognosis and Determination of 
Indication for Heart Transplantation in Patients 
With Advanced HF Using CPX
Peak V˙ O2 <14 mL/kg/min obtained by CPX is used as one 
of the eligibility criteria for heart transplantation. In addi-
tion, peak V˙ O
2 <12 mL/kg/min is considered as one of the 
objective criteria for NYHA Class IV, and can be used for 
assessing the INTERMACS profile. Prognosis is particu-
larly known to be poor for patients with HFrEF who have 
peak V˙ O
2 <10 mL/kg/min.379–382 Indices such as minute 
ventilation/carbon dioxide production (V˙ E/V˙ CO2) slope, 
oscillatory ventilation, and oxygen uptake efficiency slope 
should also be considered when maximum load cannot be 
obtained with CPX.383–385 In serial monitoring, a change in 
peak V˙ O2 >6% is associated with better prognosis com-
pared with no improvement in peak V˙ O2.383,386–389
 ▋ 7.3 Evaluation of Physical Function
  ▋ 7.3.1  Comprehensive Lower Extremity Functional 
Assessment (Short Physical Performance Battery, 
4-m Walk Test)
The Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) is a com-
prehensive method for assessing physical functional, focus-
ing on lower extremity function, in the elderly.
390 In elderly 
patients hospitalized for HF, SPPB scores of <4 points 
have been shown to predict difficulty of being discharged 
from hospital to home, and SPPB scores of <7 points are 
associated with increased events after discharge.
369
  ▋ 7.3.2 Gait Speed Per Second
The walking speed at one’s usual gait has prognostic value 
equivalence to the 6MWD41 and is recommended for eval-
uation in patients who are unable to perform a 6-min walk 
test or CPX. Older HF patients often have reduced walk-
ing speed,
391 and reductions in both walking speed and

  ▋ 7.3.3  Muscle Strength Evaluation (Grip Strength 
Measurement)
Grip strength is also an independent prognostic factor in 
patients with cardiac diseases
393 and is associated with life 
expectancy, especially in male patients with chronic HF in 
Japan.394 In addition, combining grip strength with other 
indices (6MWD and QOL) enables stratification of cardio-
vascular event risk and is useful for the assessment of 
overall physical function.395
  ▋ 7.3.4  Assessment and Diagnosis of Frailty and 
Sarcopenia
Sarcopenia is a condition characterized by a decline in 
physical function due to reduced skeletal muscle mass 
associated with aging. Patients with chronic diseases, espe-
cially HF, are more likely to have sarcopenia due to low 
activity, low nutrition, and chronic inflammation associ-
ated with HF.
396 The Asian Working Group for Sarcope-
nia 2019 sarcopenia diagnostic criteria include evaluation 
of the following: (1) muscle mass (measured using dual-
energy X-ray absorptiometry or bioelectrical impedance); 
(2) muscle strength (grip strength); and (3) physical func-
tion (6-min walk test, 5-repetition chair stand test, or 
SPPB).
396
Frailty is a concept that refers to a “fragile” state that 
precedes the need for nursing care, and includes physical, 
psychological, and social frailty. In Japan, the standard 
method for assessing frailty is to use the revised version of 
the Japanese version of the Cardiovascular Health Study 
(J-CHS) criteria,
397 and typically requires 3 or more of the 
following 5 criteria to be met for frailty to be diagnosed: 
(1) weight loss; (2) muscle weakness (low grip strength); (3) 
tiredness (low energy); (4) slowed usual walking speed; and 
(5) reduced physical activity.
8. Genetic Testing
 ▋ 8.1 Significance of Genetic Testing
Genetic testing is performed to confirm the diagnosis, lead 
to disease-specific treatment based on causative genetic 
mutations, and lead to the early diagnosis and treatment 
of relatives through cascade screening.
276,398,399 The identi-
fication of causative genetic mutations by genetic testing 
provides a strong basis for the definitive diagnosis of 
underlying disease, predicting prognosis, and implement-
ing precision medicine in patients with HF. If genetic test-
ing identifies a causative variant in the proband, the genetic 
risk should be examined in the proband’s relatives, allow-
ing for early diagnosis and therapeutic intervention in fam-
ily members (Figure 5).

significance.

 ▋ 8.2 Genetic Testing for HF Patients
When genetic heart disease is suspected based on charac-
teristic clinical findings, it is recommended that genetic 
evaluation is conducted, including genetic testing of the 
affected individual and pre- and post-test genetic counsel-
ing at a facility capable of providing genetic counsel-
ing.
400–402 In patients with HF, after making a general 
diagnosis of the underlying cardiac condition, it is impor-
tant to check for any characteristic findings that warrant 
consideration of genetic testing (Figure 6).
403,404 Genetic 
testing should be performed for genes corresponding to the 
characteristic findings of each patient, and the results 
should be integrated to diagnose the underlying disease 
and provide appropriate treatment.
322,399,405–407
The causal genetic variants of non-ischemic cardiomy-
opathies, such as alcoholic cardiomyopathy, 409 perinatal 
cardiomyopathy,410 myocarditis,411 and cancer treatment-
related cardiac dysfunction,412 overlap with those found in 
dilated cardiomyopathy, HCM, and neuromuscular dis-
eases. In these diseases, it is considered that the combina-
tion of genetic and acquired factors contributes to surpass 
the threshold for onset, leading to the development of the 
condition. Therefore, genetic testing should also be consid-
ered in the context of these diseases. Furthermore, if a 
causative genetic variant is detected in the proband, genetic 
cascade screening of the proband’s relatives should also be 
considered (Figure 5). It is necessary to conduct regular 
follow-up while considering the penetrance of each genetic 
variant and the age of onset of the phenotype.

 ▋ 8.3 HF Treatment Based on Genetic Testing
Some of the important roles of genetic testing in HF are to 
identify the cause of disease onset, stratify the pathophysi-
ology, and infer the clinical course, leading to the provision 
of precision medicine. For example, HCM patients with 
pathogenic sarcomere gene variants have a higher fre-
quency of HF and ventricular arrhythmias than those 
without and can be considered for treatment with an 
ICD.
413–415 In dilated cardiomyopathy, the sarcomere 
mutation is associated with a higher incidence of HF and 
ventricular arrhythmia compared with the absence of such 
mutations. In addition, dilated cardiomyopathy patients 
with lamin A/C (LMNA) gene variants are refractory to 
treatment and have a high risk of progression to severe HF 
and fatal arrhythmias;
416–418 therefore, treatment with an 
ICD should be considered.400,416–419
9. Assessment of ADL/QOL
 ▋ 9.1 Importance of ADL/QOL Assessment in HF
Improving ADL and QOL is an important treatment goal 
for patients with HF, as is improving prognosis. ADL 
assessment is an important measure in determining the 
level of need for daily living support and nursing care. 
Various tools are available to assess ADL, such as the 
Functional Independence Measure, Barthel Index, and 
Katz Index. A decline in ADL has been identified as an 
independent risk factor for HF rehospitalization and 
death.
422–424 Conversely, QOL reflects the overall wellbeing 
and life satisfaction derived from various factors. In the 
medical field, QOL is often evaluated as health-related 
QOL, which focuses on the impact of health status while 
excluding socioeconomic and environmental status.
Both ADL and QOL are important outcome measures 
for patients with HF and are increasingly used as key end-
points in clinical trials.
425–430 Furthermore, QOL assess-
ment necessitates self-evaluation by the patient. Against 
this background, the concept of patient-reported outcomes 
(PROs) has recently been proposed.
 ▋ 9.2 Patient-Reported Outcomes
A PRO is defined as a report on a patient’s health status 
obtained directly from the patient, without interpretation 
by health care providers or anyone else, and is an indicator 
based on a patient’s subjective evaluation from their per-
spective. The tools used to measure PROs are referred to 
as patient-reported outcome measures and include generic 
instruments, such as the 36-Item Short Form Survey and 
the EuroQoL 5-dimensions 5-levels, both of which are 
designed to measure health-related QOL regardless of spe-
cific diseases. In addition to these generic measures, dis-
ease-specific instruments for patients with HF are used to 
assess health status, including the Kansas City Cardiomy-
opathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) and the Minnesota Living 
with Heart Failure Questionnaire.
431 Among these tools, 
the KCCQ is frequently used as a key outcome measure in 
clinical trials for HF.432,433
 ▋ 9.3 Clinical Significance of Evaluating PROs
Recent research has shown the clinical usefulness of assess-
ing PROs to bridge gaps in the perception of symptoms 
and health status between patients and health providers, as 
well as to optimize treatment.434,435 Continuous assessment 
of PROs using tools such as the KCCQ and the Minnesota 
Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire improved HF 
care by facilitating patient–provider communication and 
allowing for timely interventions, including referrals to 
specialized HF facilities or the introduction of more inten-
sive palliative care.
436 An observational study of patients 
with HFrEF (Change the Management of Patients with 
Heart Failure [CHAMP-HF] registry) demonstrated that 
self-reported improvements in KCCQ scores were indepen-
dently associated with a lower risk of mortality and the 
composite of mortality or HF rehospitalization, whereas 
no such association was seen for changes in NYHA func-
tional class, as assessed by healthcare providers.
434 These 
findings suggest that changes in KCCQ scores offer more 
robust prognostic value than changes in NYHA functional 
class.434
Although the clinical use of PROs has significant poten-
tial,435 very few facilities have successfully introduced 
PROs into routine practice.436 In addition, evidence sup-
porting the effectiveness of PROs in clinical practice is still 
emerging.437 The burden on patients and physicians to 
collect PRO information, as well as patients’ cognitive 
function and health literacy, are significant issues. In the 
future, it is expected that PROs could be evaluated in the 
home using digital health monitoring tools,
438 and, if these 
systems enable the integration of PRO data with timely 
treatment interventions that lead to improved clinical out-
comes, the use of PROs in routine practice is expected to 
expand.
10. Risk Score
 ▋ 10.1 Significance of Risk Scores in HF
The use of risk scores in HF has an important role in diag-
nosis, treatment, and prognostic evaluation.
 ▋ 10.2 Acute Decompensated HF
The practical applications of risk scores in ADHF include:
•   Prognostic  assessment  in  the  acute  setting,  with  more 
intensive treatment and monitoring for high-risk patients 
and disposition after initial treatment for low-risk 
patients
•   Post-discharge management, with individualized treat-
ment plans during hospitalization and follow-up care 
strategies after discharge based on risk scores to reduce 
the risk of rehospitalization.
Recommendation and Level of Evidence for Patient-
Reported Outcomes in the Assessment of Symptoms, 
Activities of Daily Living, and Quality of Life in Heart Failure
Recommendation COR LOE
 To assess the health status, symptoms, and 
prognosis of HF patients, the use of  
standardized questionnaires to evaluate 
patient-reported outcomes can be  
considered.
