The Comparison of Outcomes and Access to Care for 
Heart Failure Trial (COACH) was the first study to pro-
vide evidence that the implementation of a risk score-based 
approach could improve clinical outcomes in patients with 
HF.
444 The cluster randomized trial (10 hospitals in 
Ontario, Canada) used an algorithm for risk stratification 
based on mortality risk during the intervention period. The 
results showed that the introduction of the algorithm sig-
nificantly reduced 30-day mortality and rehospitaliza-
tion.
444 In Japan, the Get With The Guideline–Heart 
Failure risk score has been validated, 445 and some of our 
own risk scores have been proposed.446–448
 ▋ 10.3 Compensated HF
The practical applications of risk scores in chronic HF 
include:
•   Long-term  prognostic  assessment,  which  predicts  sur-
vival over several years, providing useful information for 
the planning of long-term treatment
•   Patient  education  and  self-management enhancement, 
which help patients understand their condition and 
engage in self-management, with the potential of improv-
ing future treatment adherence
•   Treatment selection, helping identify suitable candidates 
when considering advanced therapies, such as device 
therapies, mechanical circulatory support, or heart 
transplantation.
The Seattle Heart Failure Model (SHFM) has been widely 
used in this field.449 The SHFM is a tool to predict 1-, 2-, 
and 3-year survival probabilities, and is used in clinical 
decision making regarding prognosis, the development of 
optimal treatment strategies, and the design of clinical tri-
als. Specifically, patients with an estimated 1-year survival 
<85% are generally considered candidates for LV assist 
device implantation or heart transplantation.
450 The 
SHFM has been validated in a Japanese registry.451 Similar 
validation has been conducted for the Meta-Analysis 
Global Group in Chronic (MAGGIC) Heart Failure risk 
score, a tool developed in Europe.452 The method of imple-
menting risk scores is also being validated through ran-
domized trials, 444,453 and it is anticipated that further 
evaluation and integration of these tools within Japan’s 
healthcare system will facilitate more effective and indi-
vidualized care for patients with HF.
V. Heart Failure Prevention
Heart failure (HF) can be prevented through multifaceted 
interventions, including lifestyle management, such as diet 
and exercise, as well as management of HF risk factors and 
therapeutic intervention for structural/functional cardiac 
abnormalities (Figure 7). HF Stages A and B represent 
critical periods for preventing the onset of symptomatic 
HF. However, their subclinical presentation often leads to 
underdiagnosis, potentially compromising therapeutic 
adherence and optimal intervention strategies.
PM?r?`Y?`?q??ge
Stage A, defined as patients at risk of HF, requires targeted 
management of established cardiovascular risk factors 
(hypertension, diabetes, chronic kidney disease [CKD], 
obesity) to prevent the development of structural/func-
tional cardiac abnormalities. To facilitate the early detec-
tion of progression from Stage A to Stage B, screening 
protocols using natriuretic peptide biomarkers are clini-
cally useful.
 ▋ 1.1 Lifestyle Management
Comprehensive lifestyle modifications, encompassing reg-
ular exercise and physical activity, weight optimization, 
healthy diet, smoking cessation, and limited alcohol con-
sumption, have been associated with a lower risk of 
HF.
453a–453n
 ▋ 1.2 Hypertension Treatment
Effective hypertension management plays a crucial role in 
preventing HF and extending patient survival, as demon-
strated by multiple landmark clinical trials.
454–460 The Sys-
tolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial (SPRINT) 
demonstrated that intensive treatment targeting a systolic 
blood pressure (SBP) of <120 mmHg reduced the incidence 
of HF and mortality compared with the standard treat-
ment targeting an SBP of 140 mmHg.
457,458,460 In the Strat-
egy of Blood Pressure Intervention in the Elderly 
Hypertensive Patients (STEP) trial, which included elderly 
hypertensive patients aged 60–80 years, targeting an SBP 
of 110–129 mmHg reduced the incidence of HF and mor-
tality compared with targeting an SBP of 130–
149 mmHg.
459 Based on these evidences, the Japanese 
Society of Hypertension Guidelines for the Management 
of Hypertension (JSH2019)461 advocate for a comprehen-
sive treatment approach, combining appropriate antihy-
pertensive medication with essential lifestyle modifications, 
such as salt reduction and weight management, to achieve 
optimal blood pressure control. As for the choice of medi-
cations, thiazide diuretics are considered highly effective in 
the prevention of HF,
462–464 and have been shown to reduce 
the incidence of HF compared with calcium channel block-
ers and α-blockers.465

Heart Failure Management
Recommendation COR LOE
 To improve the prognosis of HF patients, the 
use of standardized risk scores for prognostic 
prediction during the acute phase can be 
considered.
444

 ▋ 1.3 Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors
A meta-analysis of 3 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) 
in patients with stable coronary artery disease without left 
ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction or symptomatic HF 
demonstrated that angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) 
inhibitors reduced the incidence of all-cause mortality, 
non-fatal myocardial infarction, and stroke, as well as 
hospitalization for HF.
466 However, because these trials 
included a high proportion of patients with previous myo-
cardial infarction (55–65%) and concurrent hypertension 
(27–46%), it remains unclear whether ACE inhibitors are 
effective in preventing HF in Stage A independent of their 
antihypertensive effects.
 ▋ 1.4 Sodium–Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors
In patients with type 2 diabetes and a history of cardiovas-
cular disease (coronary artery disease, stroke, or peripheral 
artery disease), empagliflozin reduced the rate of hospital-
ization for HF and HF mortality. 467 Canagliflozin and 
dapagliflozin have also been shown to reduce the rate of 
hospitalization for HF in patients with type 2 diabetes with 
high cardiovascular risk. 468,469 Because only 10–14% of 
patients in these trials had a history of HF at baseline, 
these findings suggest a preventive effect of sodium–glu-
cose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors against the initial 
development of HF. Based on these findings, the use of 
SGLT2 inhibitors is recommended for the prevention of 
HF in patients with type 2 diabetes with established car-
diovascular disease or at high cardiovascular risk. How-
ever, only 11–43% of patients using glucose-lowering 
medications in the Japanese National Health Insurance 
database met the inclusion criteria for these clinical tri-
als,
470 suggesting that SGLT2 inhibitors are not indicated 
for all patients with diabetes.
In patients with CKD with or without diabetes, dapa-
gliflozin reduced the incidence of a composite renal end-
point or the composite endpoint of hospitalization for HF 
or cardiovascular death,471 whereas empagliflozin reduced 
the composite endpoint of progression of kidney disease or 
cardiovascular death.
472 Notably, in these trials, renin–
angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors were used as the stan-
dard treatment for CKD in 85–97% of participants. A 
meta-analysis including these trials showed a significant 
reduction in the composite endpoint of hospitalization for 
HF or cardiovascular death with SGLT2 inhibitors in the 
diabetes group.
473 Based on these findings, the use of 
SGLT2 inhibitors is recommended for the prevention of 
HF or cardiovascular death in patients with type 2 diabetes 
and CKD.
 ▋ 1.5 Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
Most individual RCTs have not shown a preventive effect 
of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists on 
HF hospitalization in patients with type 2 diabetes who 
either have atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or are at 
high risk of developing it.
474,475 Conversely, a meta-analysis 
of 7 trials (baseline prevalence of HF: 9–24%) showed that 
GLP-1 receptor agonists moderately reduced the incidence 
of cardiovascular death and the rate of hospitalization for 
HF, and that the effect was more pronounced in the group

prevention effect remains to be identified.
 ▋ 1.6 Finerenone
In patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, finerenone, a 
non-steroidal selective mineralocorticoid receptor antago-
nist (MRA), reduced hospitalization for HF when added 
to standard therapy (including glucose-lowering therapy 
and treatment with the maximum tolerated dose of RAS 
inhibitors).
478,479 The Efficacy and Safety of Finerenone in 
Subjects With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Diabetic Kid-
ney Disease (FIDELIO-DKD) trial demonstrated that, in 
patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD who had either 
moderately increased persistent albuminuria (urinary albu-

 ▋ 1.7  HF Screening Using B-Type Natriuretic Peptide/
N-Terminal Pro B-Type Natriuretic Peptide
In the St. Vincent’s Screening To Prevent Heart Failure 
Study (STOP-HF), the effectiveness of a B-type natriuretic 
peptide (BNP) screening program (annual measurement) 
and collaborative care between primary care physicians 
and specialists was evaluated in individuals aged 40 years 
or older who had risk factors for HF (hypertension, dys-
lipidemia, obesity, vascular disease, diabetes, arrhythmias 
requiring treatment, or moderate to severe arrhythmias). 
In the intervention group, echocardiography and collab-
orative care were implemented when BNP levels were 
50 pg/mL or higher, which reduced the incidence of asymp-
tomatic LV dysfunction (systolic or diastolic dysfunction) 
or emergency hospitalization due to HF.
482 Furthermore, 
a small, single-center RCT demonstrated that aggressive 
dose titration of RAS inhibitors and β-blockers reduced 
cardiac events in patients with diabetes and elevated N-ter-
minal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels 
(>125 pg/mL), but free of established heart disease.483
The American Diabetes Association consensus report 
recommends annual natriuretic peptide screening for 
patients with diabetes to detect early-stage HF and enable 
interventions to prevent symptomatic HF.
484 Based on the 
above, in asymptomatic patients at risk of developing HF 
(including hypertension, atherosclerotic disease, diabetes, 
obesity), team interventions, including optimization of 
guideline-recommended treatments based on natriuretic 
peptide screening, can be considered for the prevention of 
HF.
2. Stage B: Pre-HF
In Stage B (pre-HF), the focus is on preventing the pro-
gression of structural/functional cardiac abnormalities and 
the development of symptomatic HF. Appropriate treat-
ment of these conditions is crucial to prevent disease pro-
gression. Management of HF risk factors in Stage B

 ▋ 2.1 ACE Inhibitors
ACE inhibitors have been shown to be useful for the pre-
vention of HF in patients with asymptomatic left ventricu-
lar ejection fraction (LVEF) reduction. According to the 
Survival and Ventricular Enlargement (SAVE) and Tran-
dolapril Cardiac Evaluation (TRACE) trials, ACE inhibi-
tors reduced rehospitalization for HF and improved 
overall survival in patients with asymptomatic LV systolic 
dysfunction (LVEF <35–40%) after acute myocardial 
infarction (AMI).
485,486 Furthermore, the Studies of Left 
Ventricular Dysfunction (SOLVD) prevention trial dem-
onstrated that enalapril reduced hospitalization for HF 
and improved overall survival in patients with asymptom-
atic LV systolic dysfunction (approximately 20% of whom 
had non-coronary artery disease).
487,488
 ▋ 2.2 Angiotensin Receptor Blockers
In patients after myocardial infarction, angiotensin recep-
tor blockers (ARBs) have been compared with ACE inhib-
itors. In the Valsartan in Acute Myocardial Infarction 
(VALIANT) trial, valsartan was shown to be as effective 
as captopril in improving prognosis and preventing other 
cardiovascular events in patients with LV systolic dysfunc-
tion after myocardial infarction (approximately 25% of 
whom were asymptomatic).
489 In the Optimal Therapy in 
Myocardial Infarction with the Angiotensin II Antagonist 
Losartan (OPTIMAAL) trial, losartan did not exhibit 
non-inferiority to captopril.490 This may be attributed to 
the low maximum dose of losartan (50 mg) used in the 
study.491 The efficacy of ARBs in patients with LV systolic 
dysfunction without a history of myocardial infarction has 
not been investigated.
 ▋ 2.3 Beta-Blockers
Beta-blockers have been shown to improve LV remodeling 
and prognosis in patients with asymptomatic reduced 
LVEF after myocardial infarction. According to the 
Carvedilol Post-Infarct Survival Controlled Evaluation 
(CAPRICORN) trial, carvedilol inhibited progression of 
LV remodeling and improved prognosis
492,492a in patients 
with reduced LVEF after myocardial infarction. Further-
more, secondary analyses of patients with asymptomatic 
LV systolic dysfunction in the SOLVD prevention trial 
(80% of whom had a history of myocardial infarction) and 
the SAVE trial showed that the use of β-blockers was asso-
ciated with reduced mortality and rehospitalization 
rates.
493,494
Even in patients with asymptomatic LVEF reduction, 
evidence supporting the efficacy of β -blockers in those 
without a history of myocardial infarction is limited. In 
141 patients with asymptomatic LV systolic dysfunction, 
including those with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, 
β-blockers reduced LV remodeling.
495 A post hoc analysis 
of the SOLVD prevention trial (in which 20% of patients 
had non-ischemic cardiomyopathy) showed that the use of 
β-blockers was associated with reduced mortality and a 
lower incidence of death or hospitalization for symptom-
atic HF.
493 Given the efficacy of β -blockers in reducing 
hospitalization for HF in patients with HF with reduced 
ejection fraction (HFrEF), they are recommended in 
patients with reduced LVEF to prevent the development 
of symptomatic HF.
Recent clinical trials have evaluated the role of 
β-blockers in myocardial infarction patients with preserved 
LVEF. In the Carvedilol Post-Intervention Long-Term 
Administration in Large-scale Randomized Controlled 
Trial (CAPITAL-RCT), which enrolled 801 patients with 
ST-elevation myocardial infarction who underwent percu-
taneous coronary intervention, there was no significant 
difference in the incidence of the composite endpoint of 
all-cause death, myocardial infarction, or hospitalization 
for HF or acute coronary syndrome between the carvedilol 
and control groups.
496 Similarly, in the Randomized Eval-
uation of Decreased Usage of Beta-Blockers after Acute 
Myocardial Infarction (REDUCE-AMI) trial, which 
enrolled myocardial infarction patients with preserved 
LVEF, there were no significant differences between the 
β-blocker and non-β-blocker groups in the composite end-
point of all-cause death or new myocardial infarction, or 
hospitalization for HF.
497 These findings were further sup-
ported by the Beta Blocker Interruption After Uncompli-
cated Myocardial Infarction (ABYSS) trial, in which 
discontinuing β-blockers did not increase the risk of death, 
non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, or car-
diovascular hospitalization compared with continuing 
therapy among myocardial infarction patients with pre-
served LVEF.
498 Further verification from ongoing large-
scale RCTs is awaited.499

 ▋ 2.5 Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibitor
In the Prospective ARNI vs ACE Inhibitor Trial to Deter-
mine Superiority in Reducing Heart Failure Events After 
MI (PARADISE-MI), which included patients with HF or 
an LVEF of 40% or less between 1 and 7 days after myo-
cardial infarction, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibi-
tor (ARNI) did not reduce the incidence of the composite 
cardiovascular endpoint (cardiovascular death or HF) 
compared with ramipril.
502
 ▋ 2.6 SGLT2 Inhibitors
In the Dapagliflozin Effects on Cardiometabolic Outcomes 
in Patients With an Acute Heart Attack (DAPA-MI) trial, 
which included patients with LV systolic dysfunction after 
AMI who had no history of diabetes or chronic HF, dapa-
gliflozin improved cardiometabolic outcomes, such as the 
diagnosis of diabetes and weight loss.
503 However, the inci-
dence of cardiovascular events, including hospitalization 
for HF, was lower than expected, and the preventive effect 
of SGLT2 inhibitors initiated after AMI on HF remains 
unclear.
503 In the Study to Evaluate the Effect of Empa-
gliflozin on Hospitalization for Heart Failure and Mortal-
ity in Patients with Acute Myocardial Infarction 
(EMPACT-MI) trial, empagliflozin did not reduce the 
incidence of a composite endpoint of all-cause death or 
hospitalization for HF in patients with AMI and increased 
risk of HF (patients with LVEF <45% or those who had 
congestion requiring treatment during hospitalization).
504 
Furthermore, in the Impact of Empagliflozin on Cardiac 
Function and Biomarkers of Heart Failure in Patients 
With Acute Myocardial Infarction (EMMY) trial, which 
investigated the effect of early initiation of empagliflozin 
after percutaneous coronary intervention for AMI, the 
changes in NT-proBNP levels and the degree of improve-
ment in LVEF up to 26 weeks after the start of administra-
tion were significantly better in the empagliflozin than 
placebo group.
505
 ▋ 2.7 Statins
Statins have been shown to reduce the incidence of coro-
nary artery disease events in patients with myocardial 
infarction, acute coronary syndrome, or at high risk of 
cardiovascular disease.
506,507 Furthermore, they have also 
been shown to reduce the incidence of HF. 506,507 A meta-
analysis of patients with acute coronary syndrome showed 
that statin therapy reduced hospitalization for HF. 506 
Moreover, a meta-analysis of 17 RCTs of statins for pri-
mary or secondary prevention demonstrated that statins 
moderately reduced hospitalization for HF.
508
 ▋ 2.8 Current Status and Future Perspectives
Based on current evidence, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and 
β-blockers are recommended for preventing HF in all 
patients with asymptomatic LV systolic dysfunction, par-
ticularly those with an LVEF of ≤40%, unless contraindi-
cated. Conversely, the effectiveness of these medications in 
preventing HF among patients with preserved LVEF fol-
lowing myocardial infarction remains unclear. The Euro-
pean Society of Cardiology guidelines for acute coronary 
syndrome explicitly acknowledge this evidence gap,
509 with 
several studies indicating that β-blockers may not be effec-
tive in this patient population. This critical uncertainty 
warrants further research.
The evidence supporting MRA use in patients with 
asymptomatic LV systolic dysfunction is currently limited. 
Recent trials investigating ARNIs and SGLT2 inhibitors 
in post-myocardial infarction patients have faced chal-
lenges in demonstrating efficacy, largely due to improved 
outcomes from modern reperfusion therapy. Conse-
quently, the routine use of MRAs, ARNIs, and SGLT2 
inhibitors is not currently recommended for patients with 
a high risk of HF following AMI. However, future studies 
are expected to identify subgroups of Stage B patients who 
may benefit from these therapeutic agents.
VI. Treatment for Heart Failure (Stages C and D)

 ▋ 1.1 Goals of Heart Failure Treatment
The goal of heart failure (HF) treatment is to improve 
prognosis and quality of life (QOL). At every stage, pre-
venting disease progression and preventing complications 
are essential priorities. In Stage C (symptomatic HF), the 
goals are to improve prognosis, alleviate symptoms, 
improve QOL, and maintain these conditions in stable 
manner over time. In Stage D (advanced HF), although 
the overall goals remain similar to Stage C, there are peri-
ods when symptom management becomes the primary 
focus of care (Figure 8).
 ▋ 1.2 Algorithm for HF Treatment
In all stages, comprehensive disease management should 
be delivered through a multidisciplinary team approach, 
incorporating exercise therapy, patient education on HF, 
and palliative care. This comprehensive approach reflects 
the core principles of effective HF management. For Stage 
[[p32]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1306
KITAI T et al.
C patients, early consideration should be given to advance 
care planning and palliative care integration to enhance 
overall QOL and facilitate shared decision making. In 
Stage D, the full range of pharmacological and non-phar-
macological treatments used in Stage C is also applicable 
(Figure 8).
Pharmacological therapy in Stage C, particularly guide-
line-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for patients with 
HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), centers on 4 
foundational medications: angiotensin-converting enzyme 
(ACE) inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)/
angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), 
β-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), 
and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibi -
tors.
510–518 It is recommended medications are initiated with 
initial (low) doses as needed, and they can be administered 
simultaneously
142,519,520 or sequentially with close monitor-
ing. The sequence of medication initiation can be tailored 
based on clinical factors and, importantly, it is not neces-
sary to achieve the target dose of one medication before 
starting another.521,522 Dosages should be uptitrated to tar-
get levels as tolerated by the patient, 510–518 with ongoing 
optimization of pharmacological treatment based on the 
patient’s clinical status to ensure appropriate and sufficient 
therapy.
142,519
Diuretics play a pivotal supportive role in managing 
congestion in the majority of patients with HF. Although 
diuretics have not been shown to improve survival, recent 
evidence suggests that guided “diuretic therapy and adjust-
ment” with hemodynamic monitoring, combined with the 
intensification of other HF medications, can effectively 
prevent HF exacerbations.
523–525 Therefore, careful titra-
tion of diuretic doses based on individual patient conges-
tion status remains an essential component of management.
The implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) is indi-
cated based on established risk stratification criteria for 
primary and secondary prevention of sudden cardiac death 
(SCD). Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) and 
catheter ablation are considered for patients with atrial 
fibrillation. In cases of residual severe functional mitral 
regurgitation with an left ventricular ejection fraction 
(LVEF) ≥20%, percutaneous mitral valve repair should be 
considered. For HF with improved ejection fraction 
(HFimpEF), the treatment strategy is generally to continue 
the medications used for HFrEF.
526
Treatment goals should be individualized, because 
symptom palliation and improving QOL may be priori-
tized over life prolongation depending on the patient’s

values, goals, and preferences. Palliative care is considered

Stage D is defined as a state in which a patient remains 
at New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III or 
higher despite receiving or being considered for all estab-
lished medical and non-medical therapies, and generally 
experiences repeated HF hospitalizations 2 or more times 
per year. It is recommended that patients be referred to a 
specialized HF center so that treatment options, including 
mechanical circulatory support, ventricular assist devices, 
and heart transplantation, are discussed with patients and 
their family and that patients are followed up at appropri-
ate intervals before the progression of multiple organ dys-
function.
 ▋ 1.3 Diuretics for Managing Congestion
Diuretics are effective in alleviating HF symptoms caused 
by congestion, regardless of LVEF, with loop diuretics 
serving as the cornerstone of therapy. Multiple random-
ized controlled trials (RCTs) and registry studies in HF 
with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) have reported 
that 70–80% or more of enrolled patients were using 
diuretics.
527–532 Although evidence for loop diuretics in 
compensated HF is limited, a Japanese trial comparing the 
long-acting loop diuretic azosemide with furosemide dem-
onstrated that the azosemide group had a lower rate of the 
primary endpoint (a composite of cardiovascular death or 
hospitalization for worsening HF).
533 However, in the US, 
the Torsemide Comparison With Furosemide for Manage-
ment of Heart Failure (TRANSFORM-HF) trial did not 
demonstrate the superiority of torsemide over furose-
mide.
534 Furthermore, it has been reported that loop 
diuretic monotherapy was associated with worse outcomes 
in higher doses compared with combination therapy 
with renin–angiotensin system inhibitors, MRAs, and 
β-blockers.
535 Therefore, caution is needed when using 
loop diuretics as monotherapy in the treatment of HF.535
For patients with congestion refractory to loop diuret-
ics, the use of thiazide diuretics can be considered for effec-
tive decongestion.536 The randomized Safety and Efficacy 
of the Combination of Loop With Thiazide-type Diuretics 
in Patients With Decompensated Heart Failure 
(CLOROTIC) trial demonstrated that the addition of 
hydrochlorothiazide to furosemide significantly enhanced 
diuretic response and facilitated weight reduction.
536 The 
efficacy of adding a vasopressin V 2 receptor antagonist 
(tolvaptan) has been demonstrated in Japanese RCTs 
(Answering the Question of Tolvaptan’s Efficacy for 
Patients With Acute Decompensated Heart Failure and 
Renal Failure [AQUAMARINE] trial, Kanagawa Aqua-
resis Investigators Trial of Tolvaptan on HF Patients with 
Renal Impairment [K-STAR]).
537,538 These trials demon-
strated significant increases in urine output and improve-
ment in congestion compared with conventional therapy 
alone, even in patients with renal dysfunction. Moreover, 
several other clinical trials and meta-analyses have shown 
the efficacy of tolvaptan in combination with conventional 
diuretics for acute decongestion.
538–542 Some studies have 
reported weight loss and increased urine output without 
improvement in dyspnea. 543,544 Although the administra-
tion of a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist can be consid-
ered for decongestion in patients with congestion refractory 
to loop diuretics,
537–539,541,542 the Efficacy of Vasopressin 
Antagonism in Heart Failure Outcome Study With 
Tolvaptan (EVEREST), an RCT comparing tolvaptan to 
placebo in patients with acute decompensated HF 
(ADHF), demonstrated that tolvaptan improved conges-
tion but did not improve long-term prognosis.
545,546 In 
Japan, the use of vasopressin V 2 receptor antagonists for 
ADHF has been increasing in recent years. 547 However, 
given the lack of evidence demonstrating improved prog-
nosis with the long-term use of tolvaptan, it should be used 
with caution, particularly in the chronic phase.
547
 ▋ 1.4  BNP/NT-proBNP-Guided Therapy: Measuring 
BNP/NT-proBNP to Guide Congestion 
Management and GDMT Adjustment
There have been attempts to use B-type natriuretic peptide 
(BNP)/N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-
proBNP) to guide HF treatment. Recent meta-analyses 
suggest potential benefits in reducing mortality and rehos-
pitalization for HF.
106,141,548 However, the results have been 
inconsistent across studies, and the effect may be limited,

be considered to achieve decongestion.

for the early detection of congestion, intensification of 
congestion treatment, and optimization of GDMT.
2. Pharmacological Therapy
 ▋ 2.1 HF With Reduced Ejection Fraction
In recent years, the therapeutic landscape for HF has 
expanded significantly with the introduction of novel phar-
macological agents targeting innovative therapeutic path-
ways. These include ARNI, which activates the natriuretic 
peptide pathway to improve HF, and SGLT2 inhibitors, 
which were originally developed for managing diabetes.
  ▋ 2.1.1 ACE Inhibitors
The effects of ACE inhibitors on survival and various car-
diovascular events in patients with HFrEF have been 
established by large-scale clinical trials, including Coop-
erative North Scandinavian Enalapril Survival Study 
(CONSENSUS) and the Studies of Left Ventricular Dys-
function (SOLVD).
512,557 ACE inhibitors should be admin-
istered to all patients with HFrEF unless contraindicated. 
In the Assessment of Treatment with Lisinopril and Sur-
vival (ATLAS) trial, although no significant difference was 
observed in mortality alone between high and low doses of 
ACE inhibitors, when HF hospitalization events were 
included, the higher dose was more effective.
558 Conse-
quently, dose uptitration is considered, when the provided 
drug is tolerated.558
  ▋ 2.1.2 Angiotensin Receptor Blockers
ARBs are used in patients with HFrEF because they pro-
vide more complete blockade of angiotensin II and have 
demonstrated comparable efficacy to ACE inhibitors in 
reducing cardiovascular events.
559–562
  ▋ 2.1.3 Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibitor
The Prospective Comparison of ARNI with ACEI to 
Determine Impact on Global Mortality and Morbidity in 
Heart Failure (PARADIGM-HF) trial demonstrated that 
ARNI significantly improves survival in patients with 
HFrEF compared with the ACE inhibitor enalapril.
514 In 
addition, several interventional studies have shown that 
ARNI induces reverse remodeling of the left ventricle 
(LV).
563,564 Furthermore, a subanalysis of the PARADIGM-
HF trial suggested that ARNI not only reduces HF-related 
deaths but also has a preventive effect against sudden 
death.565 In contrast, in the Prospective Comparison of 
ARNI With ACEi to Determine the Novel Beneficial 
Treatment Value in Japanese Heart Failure Patients 
(PARALLEL-HF) trial, a Phase III study enrolling 
Japanese patients with HFrEF, no significant difference 
was observed in the primary endpoint of cardiovascular 
death or first hospitalization for HF compared with ACE 
inhibitors. However, a significant reductions was observed 
in the secondary endpoint of NT-proBNP level.
566 Subse-
quent PARADIGM-HF trial subgroup analysis identified 
that renal dysfunction, hypotension, elevated NT-proBNP 
levels, and ischemic HF were associated with early treat-
ment discontinuation.
567
The Comparison of Sacubitril/Valsartan Versus Enala-
pril on Effect on NT-proBNP in Patients Stabilized From 
an Acute Heart Failure Episode (PIONEER-HF) trial 
evaluated ARNI initiation in patients with ADHF and 
LVEF ≤40% after achieving hemodynamic stability and 
prior to discharge. At 8 weeks after discharge, the ARNI 
group exhibited a significant reduction in NT-proBNP 
levels and HF rehospitalization rates compared with the 
enalapril group.
568 Notably, approximately half of the 
patients in the PIONEER-HF trial were not taking ACE 
inhibitors or ARBs at the time of enrollment. Based on 
these findings, ARNI can be considered as first-line ther-
apy for hemodynamically stabilized patients with NYHA 
Class II–III HF prior to discharge to reduce the risk of HF 
rehospitalization.
  ▋ 2.1.4 Beta-Blockers
The effects of β-blockers in patients with HFrEF have been 
investigated in numerous RCTs conducted during the 
1990s and 2000s.
510,569,570,571 These studies have consistently 
demonstrated the benefits of β -blockers in promoting 
reverse remodeling and reducing clinical events, including 
death and HF hospitalization. The Multicenter Carvedilol 
Heart Failure Dose Assessment Trial (MUCHA) in Japan 
demonstrated that carvedilol induced LV reverse remodel-
ing, even at a low dose (5 mg/day), significantly reducing 
the composite endpoint of death or cardiovascular event-
related hospitalization.
572
Based on these findings, β -blockers are recommended 
for all eligible patients with HFrEF to reduce mortality 
and HF events, unless contraindicated. The Japanese 
Chronic Heart Failure (J-CHF) study demonstrated com-
parable effects on reverse remodeling and clinical out-
comes across 3 carvedilol target doses (2.5, 5, or 20 mg/
day).
573 A subsequent analysis demonstrated that the

Although no specific target heart rate has been established, 
a meta-analysis of RCTs of β-blockers,
574 and the Systolic 
Heart failure treatment with the I f inhibitor ivabradine 
Trial (SHIFT) study, 575 an RCT of ivabradine, demon-
strated that patients with a heart rate <60 beats/min had 
the lowest event rate, suggesting that a heart rate 
<60 beats/min may be a reasonable target in the manage-
ment of HF. In the Cardiac Insufficiency Bisoprolol Study 
(CIBIS III),576 patients with HFrEF who had not yet 
received ACE inhibitors or β -blockers were randomly 
assigned to either an ACE inhibitor-first group or a 
β-blocker-first group. There was no significant difference 
between the 2 groups in the primary endpoint (all-cause 
death plus hospitalization for any cause).576 Consequently, 
there is no evidence to recommend prioritizing ACE inhib-
itors or β -blockers in the initial treatment strategy. 
Although some studies suggest that β-blockers do not 
improve survival in patients with atrial fibrillation,577 other 
studies indicate that they do reduce mortality. 578 Con-
versely, some studies have suggested that heart rate reduc-
tion in patients with atrial fibrillation is not associated with 
reverse remodeling or a reduction in subsequent 
events.
574,579 This could be because patients with atrial 
fibrillation may require a higher heart rate than those with 
sinus rhythm,580 and a single measurement of resting heart 
rate in patients with atrial fibrillation may not accurately 
reflect total daily heart rate.
581 Based on these findings, the 
target heart rate remains unclear in patients with atrial 
fibrillation, although β-blockers are still recommended for 
those with atrial fibrillation.
Although concerns have been raised regarding potential 
side effects and adverse events associated with β -blocker 
use in patients with renal dysfunction,
582 diabetes,583,584 and 
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease,585 these meta-anal-
yses have demonstrated that β -blockers are beneficial in 
improving survival across all these conditions, 582–585 and 
the administration of β-blockers should be carefully con-
sidered in these patient populations.
In an RCT, patients hospitalized for acute HF exacerba-
tion while on β -blockers were randomized to either 
β-blocker continuation or discontinuation. Post-hospital-
ization analysis demonstrated no statistically significant 
differences in symptom improvement or BNP reduction 
between the 2 treatment arms. 586 In fact, it was reported 
that the β-blocker administration rate 3 months after hos-
pitalization was lower in the discontinuation group. 586 
Based on these findings, it is recommended that β-blockers 
are continued as much as possible, even during acute HF 
exacerbation.
  ▋ 2.1.5 Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists
Studies have shown that the MRAs spironolactone and 
eplerenone are effective in patients with HFrEF, ranging 
from mild HF (Eplerenone in Mild Patients Hospitaliza-
tion and Survival Study in Heart Failure: EMPHASIS-
HF) to severe HF (Randomized Aldactone Evaluation 
Study [RALES], the Eplerenone Post–Acute Myocardial 
Infarction Heart Failure Efficacy and Survival Study 
[EPHESUS]).
500,515,516,587 It has been shown that these 
MRAs reduce not only HF death, but also sudden 
death.
500,515,516 Careful monitoring is required when initiat-
ing MRAs in patients with an estimated glomerular filtra-
tion rate <30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or a serum potassium level 
≥5.0 mEq/L. However, a subanalysis of RALES demon-
strated that spironolactone maintains its therapeutic ben-
efit in patients with HFrEF with serum potassium levels up 
to 5.5 mEq/L.
588
  ▋ 2.1.6 SGLT2 Inhibitors
Two large RCTs demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors 
improved clinical outcomes in patients with HFrEF, 
regardless of diabetes status. In the Dapagliflozin and Pre-
vention of Adverse Outcomes in Heart Failure(DAPA-
HF) trial,
517 dapagliflozin significantly improved the 
primary endpoint, a composite of HF exacerbation and 
cardiovascular death, significantly reduced cardiovascular 
death, and improved subjective symptoms as assessed by 
the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ).
589 
Further subgroup analysis demonstrated that these benefi-
cial effects were consistent across almost all patient sub-
groups examined, regardless of diabetes status. 517 In the 
Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients With Chronic 
Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction (EMPEROR-
Reduced), empagliflozin significantly improved the pri-
mary endpoint of a composite of HF hospitalization or 
cardiovascular death and the secondary endpoint of HF 
hospitalization, but did not reduce cardiovascular death, 
in patients with LVEF <40%.
518 Similar to dapagliflozin, 
the effect of empagliflozin on the primary endpoint was 
consistent regardless of diabetes status. A meta-analysis of 
DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced demonstrated that 
SGLT2 inhibitors reduced all-cause death by 13%,
590 car-
diovascular death by 14%, the composite of HF rehospi-
talization and cardiovascular death by 25%, and renal 
composite events by 38%. Although some interaction was 
observed with HF severity and race, the beneficial effect 
was consistent across a wide range of patient characteris-
tics, including age, sex, and diabetes status.
590 A subanaly-
sis of the DAPA-HF study investigating the effect of 
dapagliflozin on sudden death demonstrated that patients 
with dapagliflozin had significantly lower rates of fatal 
arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, and sudden death, suggesting 
a preventive effect against sudden death.
591 Based on these 
findings, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin are recommended 
in patients with symptomatic HFrEF regardless of diabe-
tes status to reduce HF hospitalization and cardiovascular 
death.
Regarding effects in the subacute phase of HF, the 
Empagliflozin in Patients Hospitalized With Acute Heart 
Failure Who Have Been Stabilized (EMPULSE) trial dem-
onstrated that early administration of empagliflozin after 
stabilization of patients hospitalized for acute HF resulted 
in significantly better clinical benefit at 90 days after initia-
tion compared with placebo.
592 In addition, no particular 
safety concerns were observed with administration starting 
from the subacute phase. 592 These results suggest that 
administration of SGLT2 inhibitors starting from the 
acute phase of HF may improve prognosis; however, there 
are currently no data on their effects on reducing events, 
and further studies are needed.
In patients with frailty, studies have demonstrated com-
parable or superior therapeutic effects of SGLT2 inhibitors 
in both HFrEF and HFpEF patients compared to those 
without frailty.
593,594 However, given the substantial differ-
ences in frailty phenotypes between Japanese and Western 
populations, careful administration may be warranted in 
Japanese patients with frailty. With respect to the efficacy 
[[p37]]

1311

in underweight patients, who are more common in the 
Japanese population, previous studies in patients with 
HFpEF have shown that SGLT2 inhibitors are effective in 
a wide range of body mass index (BMI) among patients 
with a BMI ≥ 20 kg/m
2.595 However, data on Japanese 
patients with HFrEF, particularly those with a BMI 
<20 kg/m2, are lacking, and further research is warranted.
  ▋ 2.1.7 HCN Channel Blockers
Multiple observational studies have shown that heart rate 
is a significant prognostic factor in patients with 
HFrEF.
575,596 The SHIFT trial, an RCT of ivabradine in 
patients with HFrEF, demonstrated a significant reduction 
in heart rate and subsequent clinical adverse events (car-
diovascular death plus HF hospitalization) in the 
ivabradine compared with placebo group.
597 In a post hoc

Based on these findings, ivabradine is recommended for 
patients with symptomatic HFrEF (NYHA Class ≥ II, 
LVEF ≤35%) who are in sinus rhythm with a heart rate 
>75 beats/min despite receiving optimal GDMT, including 
maximally tolerated β-blockers, to reduce the risk of HF 
hospitalization and cardiovascular death.
In the SHIFT trial, ivabradine was uptitrated according 
to a gradual dose titration protocol targeting a heart rate 
between 50 and 60 beats/min. Patients who achieved a 
heart rate <60 beats/min by Day 28 had the lowest event 
rate of cardiac death and HF hospitalization.
575 Unlike 
β-blockers, ivabradine exhibits minimal blood pressure-
lowering and negative inotropic effects, and has been 
shown to produce superior improvements in exercise 
capacity compared with β -blockers.
74 However, patients 
should be monitored carefully for potential side effects, 
particularly phosphenes and atrial fibrillation.597,599
  ▋ 2.1.8 Vericiguat
The Vericiguat Global Study in Subjects with Heart Fail-
ure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (VICTORIA) trial, 
which included study sites in Japan, was an RCT designed 
to evaluate the efficacy of vericiguat, a soluble guanylate 
cyclase stimulator. In that trial, vericiguat demonstrated a 
significant reduction in the primary endpoint, a composite 
of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, compared 
with placebo.
600 The efficacy of vericiguat was primarily 
attributed to a reduction in HF hospitalizations. There-
fore, in patients with HFrEF (NYHA Class II–IV) who 
have experienced worsening HF despite GDMT, the 
administration of vericiguat can be considered to reduce 
the risk of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization. 
However, the VICTORIA trial did not demonstrate the 
efficacy of vericiguat in patients with HFrEF and NT-
proBNP levels >5,314pg/mL, suggesting that careful con-
sideration is needed when prescribing vericiguat to patients 
with similarly elevated NT-proBNP levels.
  ▋ 2.1.9 Digoxin
The Digitalis Investigation Group (DIG) trial demon-
strated that, in HF patients with sinus rhythm and NYHA 
Class II–III symptoms with LVEF ≤45%, digoxin did not 
reduce all-cause mortality but showed a trend towards 
fewer deaths from worsening HF and significantly reduced 
hospitalizations for worsening HF.601 Therefore, in symp-
tomatic patients with sinus rhythm and HFrEF, the use of 
digoxin to prevent death or hospitalization due to worsen-
ing HF may be considered.
There are no large-scale clinical trials specifically for HF 
patients with atrial fibrillation. A meta-analysis of obser-
vational studies did not demonstrate a definitive effect of 
digoxin on all-cause mortality.
602 The Rate Control Ther-
apy Evaluation in Permanent Atrial Fibrillation (RATE-
AF) trial showed that, in patients with atrial fibrillation 
and HF symptoms, QOL after the initiation of treatment 
was similar between the digoxin and bisoprolol groups.
603 
Therefore, although the efficacy of digoxin in HFrEF 
patients with atrial fibrillation remains uncertain, it may be 
considered as an equally viable option as β-blockers.
Notably, the DIG trial was conducted in an era mark-
edly different from contemporary HF treatment. To 
address this temporal gap, the efficacy of digitalis in 
patients with HFrEF is being re-evaluated through clinical 
trials such as the Digitoxin to Improve Outcomes in 
Patients With Advanced Chronic Heart Failure (DIGIT-
HF)
604 and Digoxin Evaluation in Chronic Heart Failure: 
Investigational Study In Outpatients in the Netherlands 
(DECISION; NCT03783429) trials, which are evaluating 
outcomes in patients with both sinus rhythm and atrial 
fibrillation.
  ▋ 2.1.10 Oral Inotropic Agents
Oral inotropic agents such as milrinone and vesnarinone 
are not recommended for chronic HF in Western countries 
because they did not improve survival rates in previous 
RCTs.
605,606 However, considering that vesnarinone sig-
nificantly improved QOL, that the goals of HF treatment 
include both survival and symptom relief, and that the lack 
of mortality benefit was due primarily to increased fatal 
arrhythmias in an era when β-blockers were not standard 
therapy, future studies are warranted on the use of oral 
inotropic agents aimed at improving subjective symptoms 
while taking precautions against arrhythmias.
In Japan, pimobendan, denopamine, and docarpamine 
are currently approved oral inotropic agents. Pimobendan, 
an oral inotropic agent with phosphodiesterase 3 inhibi-
tory action, has been shown to improve exercise capacity 
in HF patients
607,608 and significantly reduce HF-related 
events.608 In addition, there was a trend towards fewer 
patients discontinuing β -blocker therapy with pimoben-
dan.609
Based on current evidence, pimobendan may have ther-
apeutic utility in improving QOL, facilitating the discon-
tinuation of intravenous inotropic agents, and assisting 
with the introduction of β -blocker therapy, although 
extended administration is not recommended in asymp-
tomatic patients. There is insufficient evidence regarding 
denopamine and docarpamine to make any recommenda-
tions.
  ▋ 2.1.11 Other Drugs
a. Antiarrhythmic Drugs (Amiodarone and Others)
The reported effects of amiodarone on preventing sudden 
[[p38]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1312
KITAI T et al.
death and improving clinical outcomes in patients with 
HFrEF vary considerably across studies. Although the 
Sudden Cardiac Death in Heart Failure Trial (SCD-
HeFT), an RCT, showed no significant reduction in events 
in patients with amiodarone compared with placebo,
610 a 
meta-analysis reported reductions in sudden death and 
cardiovascular death in patients treated with amioda-
rone.611 Based on these findings, oral amiodarone can be 
considered for patients with a history of severe ventricular 
arrhythmia and cardiac arrest, but it is important to con-
sider ICD implantation to prevent sudden death.
The Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial (CAST) 
showed an increase in mortality with the use of Class Ic 
antiarrhythmic drugs for the reduction of ventricular 
ectopy after myocardial infarction.
612 Although the effects 
of Class Ic antiarrhythmic drugs on patients with the other 
etiologies are not clear, given their negative inotropic 
effects, their use in patients with HFrEF should be avoided. 
The effects of Class Ia and Ib drugs have not been well 
studied, but concerns remain regarding their negative ino-
tropic and proarrhythmic effects.
b. ω-3 Fatty Acids
The Gruppo Italiano per lo Studio della Sopravvivenza 
nell’Insufficienza cardiaca -heart failure(GISSI-HF) trial 
demonstrated that ω -3 fatty acid supplementation in 
patients predominantly with HFrEF reduced mortality 
after statistical adjustment, although the results for crude 
mortality were of borderline significance.
613 In addition, a 
subanalysis of the Reduction of Cardiovascular Events 
with Icosapent Ethyl–Intervention Trial (REDUCE-IT) 
trial,614 which investigated the efficacy of ω -3 fatty acid 
supplementation in patients with atherosclerotic cardio-
vascular disease or diabetes and other additional risk fac-
tors, showed a borderline effect of ω -3 fatty acid 
supplementation on the primary endpoint (a composite of 
cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, coro-
nary revascularization, and unstable angina) in patients 
with HF, similar to the overall analysis.
615
c. Anticoagulants
RCTs (Heart Failure Long-term Antithrombotic Study 
[HELAS],
616 Warfarin/Aspirin Study in Heart Failure 
[WASH]617) investigating the effects of warfarin in patients 
with sinus rhythm and HFrEF did not show any signifi-
cant benefit of warfarin. In the Warfarin Versus Aspirin in 
Reduced Cardiac Ejection Fraction (WARCEF) trial, war-
farin significantly reduced the incidence of ischemic stroke 
compared with aspirin, but also increased the incidence of 
major bleeding.
618 As a result, no significant difference was 
observed in the primary composite endpoint of all-cause 
mortality, ischemic stroke, and hemorrhagic stroke. A 
meta-analysis demonstrated that although warfarin did 
not significantly reduce all-cause mortality, it was associ-
ated with an increased risk of major bleeding.
619 In addi-
tion, the Study to Assess the Effectiveness and Safety of 
Rivaroxaban in Reducing the Risk of Death, Myocardial 
Infarction, or Stroke in Participants with Heart Failure 
and Coronary Artery Disease Following an Episode of 
Decompensated Heart Failure (COMMANDER HF) 
trial, which randomized patients with HFrEF and ischemic 
heart disease to a rivaroxaban or placebo group, did not 
show a significant difference in the primary composite 
endpoint of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, or 
stroke, whereas bleeding events were more frequent in the 
rivaroxaban group.
620 Therefore, current evidence does not 
support routine anticoagulation therapy in patients with 
HF with HFrEF who maintain sinus rhythm. Anticoagula-
tion therapy may be considered in patients with the 
reported risk factors for LV thrombus.
621
d. Calcium Channel Blockers
The dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker amlodipine 
reduced all-cause mortality in patients with non-ischemic 
cardiomyopathy in a subgroup analysis of Prospective 
Randomized Amlodipine Survival Evaluation (PRAISE)-1,
622 
but did not reduce mortality in PRAISE-2,623 which exclu-
sively enrolled patients with non-ischemic cardiomyopa-
thy. Thus, the use of dihydropyridine calcium channel 
blockers should only be considered in patients with HFrEF 
for the treatment of comorbid angina or hypertension. 
Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are contra-
indicated in patients with HFrEF due to their negative 
inotropic effects and potential of worsening cardiac func-
tion.
624
 ▋ 2.2 HF With Preserved Ejection Fraction
The Empagliflozin Outcome Trial in Patients With 
Chronic Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction 
(EMPEROR-Preserved) trial in 2021 626 and the Dapa-
gliflozin Evaluation to Improve the Lives of Patients With 
Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure (DELIVER) 
trial in 2022
627 demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors can 
improve the outcomes of patients with HFpEF, establish-
ing these agents as the cornerstone of contemporary 
HFpEF management. Concurrently, traditional approaches 
such as diuretics for managing congestion and treatment 
targeting comorbidities remain essential for alleviating 
symptoms and disease modification, and thus continue to 
be recommended as fundamental components of basic 
treatment strategies.
  ▋ 2.2.1 Evaluation and Treatment of Comorbidities
HFpEF frequently presents with multiple comorbidities, 
including hypertension, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery 
disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, anemia, and 
obstructive sleep apnea. These conditions often coexist in 
individual patients and play crucial roles in both the patho-
genesis and progression of HFpEF, while also serving as 
disease-modifying factors.
61 Given their significant impact 
on disease outcomes, systematic evaluation and manage-
ment of these comorbidities is strongly recommended for 
optimizing both symptomatic relief and long-term progno-
sis in patients with HFpEF.
61,471,628,629
  ▋ 2.2.2 SGLT2 Inhibitors
The EMPEROR-Preserved trial enrolled patients with 
chronic HF and LVEF >40%, NYHA Class II–IV, and 
elevated NT-proBNP (>300 pg/mL for those in sinus 
rhythm or >900 pg/mL for those in atrial fibrillation), 
regardless of diabetes status.626 Patients were randomized 
to receive either empagliflozin 10 mg or placebo. Treat-
ment with empagliflozin demonstrated a significant 21% 
risk reduction in the primary composite endpoint of car-
diovascular death or hospitalization for HF compared 
with placebo. This benefit was driven primarily by a reduc-
tion in HF hospitalizations, with empagliflozin having no 
significant effect on cardiovascular deaths.
626
Similarly, the DELIVER trial demonstrated that dapa-
[[p39]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1313
JCS/JHFS 2025 Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Heart Failure
gliflozin significantly reduced the primary composite end-
point of cardiovascular death or worsening HF in patients 
with chronic HF and LVEF >40%.627
A pooled analysis of the EMPEROR-Preserved and 
DELIVER trials showed that SGLT2 inhibitors (empa-
gliflozin and dapagliflozin) significantly reduced the com-
posite endpoint of cardiovascular death or hospitalization 
for HF.
631 Although this pooled analysis showed a signifi-
cant 26% risk reduction in HF hospitalization, it did not 
demonstrate a significant reduction in cardiovascular 
death. A separate pooled analysis that included the DAPA-
HF trial, in patients with HFrEF, demonstrated that the 
effectiveness of dapagliflozin spanned across patients with 
LVEF ranging from <40% to >60%.
632 In addition, dapa-
gliflozin resulted in significant improvements in QOL, as 
assessed by the KCCQ, compared with placebo.633
Based on these findings, empagliflozin or dapagliflozin 
is recommended for all symptomatic HFpEF patients 
without contraindications, aiming to reduce the risk of HF 
hospitalization or cardiovascular death. These agents can 
be initiated at various clinical time points, from the post-
stabilization phase of acute HF hospitalization to routine 
outpatient visits. The timing flexibility is supported by 
complementary evidence from multiple trials: the 
EMPEROR-Preserved trial enrolled stable outpatients, 
DELIVER included both outpatients and hospitalized 
patients, and the EMPULSE-HF trial (in which 32% of 
patients had LVEF >40%) demonstrated the effectiveness 
of early initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin and 
dapagliflozin) after stabilization of acute HF.
592
  ▋ 2.2.3 ACE Inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI (Sacubitril/Valsartan)
The Perindopril for Elderly People With Chronic Heart 
Failure (PEP-CHF) trial, which evaluated perindopril in 
HF patients with LVEF >40%, did not find a significant 
reduction in the composite endpoint of all-cause mortality 
or HF hospitalization.
634 Similarly, neither the Irbesartan 
in Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction 
(I-PRESERVE) trial
527 nor the Candesartan in Heart fail-
ure: Assessment of Reduction in Mortality and morbid-
ity–Preserved (CHARM-Preserved) trial
636 found 
improvements in their respective primary endpoints with 
ARBs. However, in the CHARM-Preserved trial, ARBs 
did reduce HF rehospitalization as a secondary endpoint.
636
Evidence for ARNI in HFpEF is more nuanced. 
Although the Prospective Comparison of Angiotensin 
Receptor Neprilysin Inhibitor With Angiotensin Receptor 
Blocker Global Outcomes in Heart Failure and Preserved 
Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (PARAGON-HF) trial 
did not meet its primary endpoint in patients with LVEF 
≥40% compared with valsartan,
637 both the Prospective 
comparison of ARNI with ARB Given following stabiLi-
zation In DEcompensated HFpEF (PARAGLIDE-HF) 
trial and the Prospective Comparison of ARNI vs Comor-
bidity-Associated Conventional Therapy on Quality of 
Life and Exercise Capacity (PARALLAX) trial demon-
strated significant reductions in NT-proBNP with S/V in 
patients with LVEF ≥40% compared with valsartan.
638,639 
In addition, the effect of ARNI appears to vary with 
LVEF. A pooled analysis of the PARAGON-HF and 
PARADIGM-HF trials showed that ARNI significantly 
improved the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death 
or HF hospitalization in patients with LVEF ≤57%.
640
Reflecting these findings, the US Food and Drug 
Administration has approved the use of ARNI in HFpEF 
patients with LVEF below the normal range. Furthermore, 
treatment response appears to be sex-dependent, with 
women showing significant reductions in cardiovascular 
death and HF hospitalization, whereas men demonstrated 
no significant benefit.
641 Based on the available evidence, 
ARNI may be considered for HFpEF patients with LVEF 
below the normal range.
  ▋ 2.2.4 Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists
In the Treatment of Preserved Cardiac Function Heart 
Failure with an Aldosterone Antagonist Treatment of Pre-
served Cardiac Function Heart Failure with an Aldoste-
rone Antagonist (TOPCAT) trial did not significantly 
reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular 
death, HF hospitalization, or resuscitation from cardiac 
arrest in patients with LVEF ≥ 45%.
528,642 However, it did 
significantly reduce the secondary endpoint of HF hospi-
talization. Furthermore, post hoc analyses have suggested 
potential benefits in patients with LVEF below the normal 
range and in women.
567,643 More recently, the non-steroidal 
MRA finerenone was shown to significantly reduce the 
primary endpoint of cardiovascular death or worsening 
HF events (HF hospitalization and urgent visits) in symp-
tomatic HF patients with LVEF ≥40%.
644 A simultane-
ously published pooled analysis of 4 trials examining the 
effects of steroidal and non-steroidal MRAs in patients 
with HFrEF, HFmrEF and HFpEF showed a significant 
risk reduction with MRAs in patients with HFpEF.
645 
Several ongoing trials are seeking to further clarify the role

  ▋ 2.2.5 Beta-Blockers
The role of β -blockers in HFpEF remains controversial, 
with inconsistent study results. The Japanese Diastolic 
Heart Failure Study (J-DHF), an RCT of carvedilol in 
patients with LVEF >40% conducted in Japan, found no 
improvement in prognosis.
646 This finding was reinforced 
by a TOPCAT trial subanalysis, which demonstrated that 
β-blocker use was associated with a significant increase in 
HF hospitalization in patients with LVEF ≥50%.
647 Simi-
larly, the Organized Program to Initiate Lifesaving Treat-
ment in Hospitalized Patients With Heart Failure 
(OPTIMIZE-HF) registry, examining 9,712 patients with 
LVEF >40%, showed no prognostic benefit from β-blocker 
therapy.
648 In contrast, a report from a Swedish registry 
showed that β-blockers were associated with a lower risk 
of all-cause mortality in patients with LVEF ≥40%, but not 
with a reduction in the composite endpoint of all-cause 
mortality or HF hospitalization.
649 Furthermore, a report 
from the Korean Strain for Risk Assessment and Thera-
peutic Strategies in Patients With Acute Heart Failure 
(STRATS-AHF) Registry showed that β -blockers were 
associated with a lower risk of all-cause mortality in 
patients with global longitudinal strain <14% among 1,969 
patients with LVEF ≥ 40%, but not in those with global 
longitudinal strain ≥ 14%.650 Despite these inconsistent 
findings on HFpEF, β-blockers remain essential for man-
aging comorbidities in these patients, particularly for rate 
control in atrial fibrillation and the treatment of ischemic 
heart disease.
Notably, a high proportion of HFpEF patients (40–
80%) have chronotropic incompetence, a condition char-
acterized by a reduced heart rate response to exercise.
651,652 
Studies have shown that discontinuing β-blockers in these 
patients can improve peak oxygen uptake during exer -
cise.653 However, the Rate-Adaptive Atrial Pacing in Dia-
stolic Heart Failure (RAPID-HF) trial, which investigated 
the effect of increasing heart rate during exercise with a 
newly implanted rate-responsive pacemaker (right atrial 
pacing) in HFpEF patients with chronotropic incompe-
tence, did not show an improvement in exercise capacity.
653a 
In contrast, the myPACE trial demonstrated that, in 
HFpEF patients who already had pacemakers implanted 
for sick sinus syndrome,653b accelerated physiological pac-
ing improved QOL, NT-proBNP levels, and physical activ-
ity compared with standard pacing settings. Building on 
these findings, the ongoing Physiologic Accelerated Pacing 
as Treatment for Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection 
Fraction (PACE-HFpEF) trial is investigating the safety 
and efficacy of this pacing therapy in HFpEF patients 
(LVEF ≥55%) who do not have conventional indications 
for pacemaker implantation.
653c These varied results high-
light the need for continued research to identify optimal 
treatment strategies for HFpEF patients with chronotropic 
incompetence.
  ▋ 2.2.6  Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) and 
Glucose-Dependent Insulinotropic Polypeptide/
GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (Incretin-Based 
Therapies)
The efficacy of semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, in 
patients with HFpEF and obesity was investigated in the 
Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with obesity and 
HFpEF (STEP-HFpEF) trial, which demonstrated sig-
nificant improvements in QOL and significant weight 
reduction in symptomatic HFpEF patients with LVEF 
≥45% and BMI ≥30 kg/m
2.654 Similar results were observed 
in the Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with obesity 
and HFpEF and type 2 diabetes (STEP-HFpEF DM) trial, 
which focused on HFpEF patients with type 2 diabetes and 
obesity.
655 These findings suggest the usefulness of sema-
glutide for a specific phenotype of patients with HFpEF 
and obesity. For details regarding obesity, see Chapter X, 
Section 2.5.
 ▋ 2.3 HF With Mildly Reduced Ejection Fraction
At present, clinical evidence for treating HFmrEF (LVEF 
40–49%) comes exclusively from subgroup analyses 
within broader HF trials. No randomized controlled trials 
have specifically targeted this population. Although these 
analyses suggest that medications effective for HFrEF may 
benefit patients with HFmrEF, treatment decisions should 
consider the patient’s clinical trajectory, including whether 
the current HFmrEF status evolved from previous HFrEF 
or HFpEF, and potential changes in LVEF over time. This 
dynamic nature of HFmrEF necessitates regular reassess-
ment of LVEF to optimize treatment strategies.
  ▋ 2.3.1 SGLT2 Inhibitors
In a subgroup analysis of the EMPEROR-Preserved trial, 
empagliflozin reduced the composite endpoint of HF hos-
pitalization or cardiovascular death by 29% compared 
with placebo in HFmrEF patients, with a tendency 
towards a lower rate of in first and total HF hospitaliza-
tions compared with HFpEF.
656 Similarly, a prespecified 
pooled analysis of the DAPA-HF and DELIVER trials 
showed that dapagliflozin reduced the risk of cardiovascu-
lar death and HF hospitalization risks across the LVEF 
spectrum, including in HFmrEF patients.
632 Based on 
these findings, empagliflozin or dapagliflozin is recom-
mended for all symptomatic patients with HFmrEF 
without contraindications to reduce the risk of HF hospi-
talization and cardiovascular death.
  ▋ 2.3.2 ARNI
In prespecified subgroup analyses of the PARAGON-HF 
trial, ARNI significantly reduced the primary composite 
endpoint of cardiovascular death or total HF hospitaliza-
tions compared with valsartan alone in patients with 
LVEF ≤57%, including those with HFmrEF (LVEF 
41–49%).
637 Subsequent prespecified pooled and virtual 
placebo analyses of the PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-
HF trials showed that the magnitude of risk reduction with 
ARNI was inversely related to LVEF.
640,657 Furthermore, 
a prespecified analysis combining patients from the 
PARAGLIDE-HF trial and those from the PARAGON-
HF trial with recent worsening HF hospitalization (within 
30 days) showed that S/V significantly improved the pri-
mary endpoint of cardiovascular death or total worsening 
HF events compared with valsartan, with greater treat-
[[p41]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1315
JCS/JHFS 2025 Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Heart Failure
ment effect observed in patients with LVEF ≤60%.658 The 
favorable reduction in NT-proBNP observed in the 
PARALLAX trial was also consistent in HFmrEF sub-
group.639 Collectively, these findings support considering 
ARNI for all patients with symptomatic HFmrEF without 
contraindications to reduce the risk of HF hospitalization 
and cardiovascular death.
  ▋ 2.3.3  Other Therapies (ACE Inhibitors, ARBs, MRAs, 
Beta-Blockers, Diuretics, and Intervention for 
Comorbidities)
No specific subgroup analysis of the PEP-CHF trial focus-
ing on HFmrEF is available.
634 However, in a subgroup 
analysis using data from the overall CHARM trial, which 
included HFmrEF, candesartan significantly reduced the 
primary endpoint of cardiovascular death or hospitaliza-
tion for HF compared with placebo, similar to findings in 
HFrEF.
659 Regarding MRAs, subgroup analysis of the 
TOPCAT trial included only 250 patients with LVEF 
<50% out of 3,444, providing insufficient power for con-
clusive results in HFmrEF. Nonetheless, the data sug-
gested that spironolactone’s potential benefits increased as 
LVEF declined, possibly mirroring its effects in HFrEF.
567 
More recently, finerenone was shown to significantly 
reduce cardiovascular death or total HF worsening events 
in symptomatic HF with LVEF ≥ 40%, including HFm-
rEF.
644 Concurrent with these findings, the Kyoto Conges-
tive Heart Failure (KCHF) Registry, a Japanese 
prospective observational study, found that MRA admin-
istration in acute HF patients, including those with 
HFmrEF, was associated with a lower risk of HF hospital-
ization.
660 Regarding β-blockers, a pooled meta-analysis of 
11 HF clinical trials demonstrated a reduction in the risk 
of the primary endpoint of all-cause and cardiovascular 
death in patients with sinus rhythm and LVEF ranging 
from 40% to 49%.
661 The management of HFmrEF, similar 
to HFrEF and HFpEF, requires interventions for comor-
bidities, including diuretics for alleviating symptoms and 
congestion management, 556 the treatment of iron defi-
ciency,662–664 blood pressure control,665 the management of 
chronic kidney disease, 471,629 and addressing sleep apnea 
syndrome.628
 ▋ 2.4 HF With Improved Ejection Fraction
According to the international definition and classification 
of HF proposed by the Heart Failure Society of America/
European Heart Failure Association/Japanese Heart Fail-
ure Society, HFimpEF is defined as HF where baseline 
LVEF ≤40% shows an improvement of ≥10%, resulting in 
an LVEF of >40%.
1 HFimpEF is commonly observed in 
patients who have achieved optimal GDMT 666–668 and is 
associated with a better prognosis than in patients whose 
LVEF does not improve.56,57,669,670 Nevertheless, even after 
LVEF improvement, structural abnormalities may per-
sist.
669,670 Predictors of HFimpEF include younger age, 
female sex, non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, a shorter dura-
tion of congestion, and fewer comorbidities.
671,672
Because the “improvement” of cardiac function in 
HFimpEF is not equivalent to “cure”, international guide-
lines recommend continuing GDMT without reduction or 
discontinuation.
2,4 This recommendation is primarily 
based on the Therapy Withdrawal in Recovered Dilated 
Cardiomyopathy – Heart Failure (TRED-HF) trial, a non-
blinded randomized trial. In the TRED-HF trial, among 
patients with dilated cardiomyopathy who had become 
asymptomatic and whose LVEF had improved from <40% 
to >50%, discontinuation of GDMT led to worsening of 
HF indicators in 44%.
526 However, several limitations of 
TRED-HF should be noted. The protocol required the 
sequential tapering or discontinuation of loop diuretics, 
MRAs, β-blockers, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs over 6 
months, ending in the complete cessation of all cardiopro-
tective medications. Thus, the safety of more gradual 
tapering approaches or discontinuation of individual med-
ications remains uncertain. It is also important to recog-
nize that recommended GDMT dosages in Japan differ 
from international guidelines, potentially limiting the tri-
al’s applicability to Japanese clinical practice. Further-
more, although the TRED-HF trial focused specifically on 
dilated cardiomyopathy, the optimal approach for HFim-
pEF with different underlying conditions remains unclear. 
For example, studies of postpartum cardiomyopathy have 
shown that discontinuing cardioprotective medications 
does not lead to HF hospitalization or LVEF decline.
674

3. Non-Pharmacological Therapy
 ▋ 3.1 Exercise Therapy
This chapter discusses non-pharmacological interventions, 
with a focus on exercise therapy. For details regarding 
comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation, see Chapter XI, 
Section 4.
 ▋ 3.2 Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device Therapy
  ▋ 3.2.1 Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator
a.  Risk of SCD and Primary and Secondary Prevention in 
HF Patients
For secondary prevention of SCD in HF patients, ICDs 
have been shown to reduce the risk of arrhythmia recur-
rence.676–678 Therefore, ICD implantation is recommended 
for patients with sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) 
leading to hemodynamic instability or ventricular fibrilla-
tion (VF), and those resuscitated from cardiac arrest, pro-
vided these events were not caused by reversible factors 
such as electrolyte abnormalities or treatable myocardial 
ischemia. However, the decision to proceed with ICD 
implantation should involve a comprehensive assessment 
of a patient’s overall prognosis, incorporating consider-
ations of functional impairment due to chronic comor-
bidities and the potential impact on life expectancy.
679–681
In primary prevention, the indication for ICD implanta-
tion in patients with HF and LVEF ≤35% has been evalu-
ated in multiple prospective interventional studies (Second 
Multicenter Automated Defibrillator Implantation Trial 
[MADIT II], SCD-HeFT), which have demonstrated its 
effectiveness, particularly in those with ischemic cardiomy-
opathy.
610,682 However, the Defibrillator in Acute Myocar-
dial Infarction Trial (DINAMIT) trial showed that 
although ICD implantation prevented arrhythmic death 
within 40 days following AMI, ICDs did not reduce over-
all mortality.683 Consequently, ICD implantation should 
be considered at least 40 days after the onset of acute myo-
cardial infarction (AMI). Conversely, with recent advances 
in GDMT for HF, the indications for ICD implantation in 
primary prevention have become increasingly complex. 
Specifically, the incidence of sudden death in HF patients 
has steadily declined, and the frequency of appropriate 
ICD activations has also shown a downward trend.
684,685 
The Danish Study to Assess the Efficacy of ICDs in 
Patients With Non-ischemic Systolic Heart Failure on 
Mortality (DANISH) trial, published in 2016, evaluated 
the efficacy of ICDs for primary prevention in patients 
with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy.
686 Although the study 
demonstrated significant reductions in both cardiovascular 
death and sudden death, ICD implantation did not reduce 
the primary endpoint of all-cause mortality.
686 Based on 
these findings, the current guideline provides a Class I 
recommendation for ICD implantation as primary preven-
tion in ischemic HF patients with NYHA Class II or 
higher, LVEF ≤35%, and at least 3 months of appropriate 
GDMT. For non-ischemic HF patients meeting the same 
criteria, a Class IIa recommendation is given.
However, in clinical practice, only a subset of HF 
patients receive comprehensive GDMT, and the risk of 
sudden death remains elevated in a significant proportions 
of patients.
591,687 In light of this, determining the indication 
for ICDs in primary prevention requires a thorough risk 
assessment of sudden death due to fatal arrhythmias, as 
well as non-arrhythmic death, in individual patients to 
identify patient populations who are most likely to benefit 
from ICD therapy. When determining ICD eligibility, it is 
essential to quantitatively assess the risk of life-threatening 
arrhythmia using scoring systems and imaging results. 
Subsequently, the benefits and risks of ICD implantation 
should be comprehensively assessed to evaluate its net 
benefit. In addition, it is crucial to provide patients with 
sufficient information to facilitate patient-centered deci-
sion making.

b.  Wearable Cardioverter Defibrillators and Subcutaneous 
Implantable Defibrillators
i. Wearable Cardioverter Defibrillators
Although patients with reduced cardiac function are at 
high risk of SCD, ICD implantation has been shown to 
adversely affect prognosis, especially in the acute phase of 
myocardial ischemia or the early stages of HF.
683,688 There-
fore, wearable cardioverter defibrillators (WCDs) serve as 
a bridge until the criteria for primary prevention ICD 
implantation are met. In Japan, a statement has been 
issued outlining the “conditions under which the use of 
WCD should be considered.”
689 With the development and 
widespread use of GDMT, the risk of SCD following AMI 
has declined in patients with ischemic heart disease. The 
Vest Prevention of Early Sudden Death Trial and VEST 
Registry (VEST) did not demonstrate a significant reduc-
tion in all-cause mortality with WCD therapy and GDMT 
in patients with AMI and LVEF ≤35%. However, the 
study highlighted the low adherence to WCD wear time, 
emphasizing the need for enhanced patient education to 
improve compliance with WCD usage.
738 WCD use may 
be considered in conditions where the risk of SCD is 
deemed high within 90 days of GDMT initiation after 
acute HF due to non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. In addi-
tion, because Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, peripartum car-
diomyopathy, and acute myocarditis often involve 
transiently reduced cardiac function, the potential benefit 
of WCDs for preventing SCD during the recovery phase 
has been reported. Similarly, WCD use may be considered 
for patients with other pathologies with elevated risk of 
SCD.
690–695
ii. Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator
Subcutaneous ICDs (S-ICDs) have demonstrated non-
inferiority to transvenous ICDs in device-related complica-
tions and inappropriate shocks in patients without pacing 
indications.
696 Another advantage of S-ICDs is the lower 
incidence of lead-related complications. 697 However, 
S-ICDs are often not suitable for patients with HF due to 
the lack of pacing capabilities for bradycardia and antit-
achycardia pacing function for VT. Therefore, an S-ICD 
is typically considered in specific situations, such as diffi-
cult vascular access for transvenous ICD placement, young 
age, high infection risk, or following the extraction of a 
transvenous ICD.
c.  Shared Decision Making for ICD Device Replacement in 
End-of-Life Care
Shared decision making is a crucial step when considering 
ICD device replacement in the end-of-life setting. Specifi-
cally, it is essential for healthcare professionals, patients, 
and their families to engage in discussions the medical 
rationale (outlining the risks and benefits of each treatment 
option) and the patient’s and family’s values, including the 
goals of care expected for the ICD, concerns, and anxieties, 
as well as acceptable levels of suffering, to facilitate 
informed decision making. It is crucial to recognize that 
palliative care during the end-of-life period is a therapeutic 
approach aimed at improving QOL. Therefore, it is recom-
mended advance care planning is initiated prior to ICD 
replacement, including the establishment of goals of care, 
the creation of advance directives in the event of serious 
deterioration, and the designation of a surrogate decision 
maker.
  ▋ 3.2.2 Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy
a. CRT for HFrEF
The efficacy of CRT in patients with HF was reported in 
the Multicenter InSync Randomized Clinical Evaluation 
(MIRACLE) trial, which demonstrated a reduction in 
mortality among HF patients with an LVEF of ≤35% and 
a QRS duration of ≥ 130 ms.
698 A meta-analysis of CRT 
clinical trials has demonstrated the efficacy of CRT in 
patients with complete left bundle branch block (LBBB) 
and a QRS duration ≥150 ms.
699 Conversely, the efficacy of 
CRT has been determined to be limited in patients with

non-LBBB, such as right bundle branch block, leading to 
a Class IIa recommendation for its use in this population 
(Figure 9).700–702 Among patients with a QRS duration of 
120–149 ms, the proportion of non-responders to CRT is 
high. The Echocardiography Guided Cardiac Resynchro-
nization Therapy (EchoCRT) trial compared CRT-on and 
CRT-off groups in patients with an LVEF ≤35%, a QRS 
duration ≤130 ms, and echocardiographic evidence of LV 
dyssynchrony, with all patients receiving CRT device 
implantation.
703 The results showed no significant differ-
ence in the primary endpoint of HF hospitalization and 
death between the 2 groups; however, mortality was sig-
nificantly higher in the CRT-on group. 703 In contrast, a 
Japanese multicenter database study demonstrated favor-
able responses to CRT in more than half of patients with a 
QRS duration between ≥120 and <150 ms.704 The Advance 
Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (ADVANCE CRT) 
study, a registry study of Asian vs. non-Asian HF patients, 
demonstrated the utility of CRT in the mid-range QRS 
group, showing a strong correlation between height-
adjusted QRS duration and CRT efficacy.
705 Meta-analyses 
of the Resynchronization–Defibrillation for Ambulatory 
Heart Failure Trial (RAFT), Multicenter Automatic Defi-
brillator Implantation With Cardiac Resynchronization 
Therapy (MADIT-CRT), and Resynchronization Reverses 
Remodeling in Systolic Left Ventricular Dysfunction 
(REVERSE) were stratified by QRS duration and investi-
gated the impact of sex on the benefits of CRT for HF 
hospitalization or death in LBBB patients, and found sig-
nificantly higher benefits of CRT in women with a QRS 
duration between ≥ 130 and <150 ms.
706 Septal flash, an 
echocardiographic indicator of CRT efficacy, was observed 
in more than 60% of women with a QRS duration of 
120–130 ms. CRT is considered effectiveeven in mid-range 
QRS in Asian HF patients (especially women), including 
Japanese patients, who tend to have smaller physiques 
than Western patients. Therefore, the lower limit of QRS 
duration for LBBB type is set at 120 ms, with a Class I 
recommendation for women. Conversely, there is insuffi-
cient evidence for non-LBBB type in the mid-range QRS, 
resulting in a Class IIb recommendation for patients with 
NYHA Class III or higher. In contrast, there is insufficient

evidence for non-LBBB patients with a mid-range QRS, 
resulting in a Class IIb recommendation for those with
