b. CRT in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation
Although it has been reported that 27% of patients with 
HFrEF who are indicated for CRT have atrial fibrilla-
tion,707 there is insufficient evidence to support the use of 
CRT in HF patients with coexisting atrial fibrillation. In a 
subanalysis of the MADIT-CRT trial, patients with a his-
tory of atrial tachyarrhythmia who had LBBB, a QRS 
duration ≥130 ms, and LVEF ≤ 30% were stratified into 
ICD and CRT-D groups, with the CRT-D group showing 
a significant reduction in HF events and mortality.
708 Con-
versely, subgroup analysis of RAFT showed no difference 
in HF hospitalization between the CRT-D and ICD 
groups in patients with permanent atrial fibrillation. 709 
Similarly, subgroup analysis of the Comparison of Medical 
Therapy, Pacing, and Defibrillation in Heart Failure 
(COMPANION) did not demonstrate the usefulness of 
CRT in patients with coexisting atrial fibrillation or atrial 
flutter.
710 In the Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy in 
Atrial Fibrillation Patients Multinational Registry 
(CERTIFY) trial, which included CRT patients with atrial 
fibrillation, the group undergoing atrioventricular node 
ablation had better outcomes than the pharmacological 
therapy group, achieving a survival outcome comparable 
to that of patients with sinus rhythm.
711 Therefore, achiev-
ing 100% biventricular pacing is crucial. In patients with a 
CRT indication, atrioventricular node ablation may be 
considered when there is a low biventricular pacing rate 
due to preserved atrioventricular conduction despite phar-
macological therapy. Furthermore, in CRT patients with 
concurrent atrial fibrillation, catheter ablation therapy is a 
potential therapeutic option when the probability of main-
taining sinus rhythm maintenance is favorable, based on 
clinical parameters such as age, atrial enlargement, and the 
duration of the condition.
712,713
c. CRT With a Defibrillator
CRTs are known to reduce HF mortality but do not pre-
vent SCD.714 Conversely, CRT with a defibrillator (CRT-
D) has demonstrated significant reductions in SCD among 
CRT-eligible populations.
715 Nevertheless, clinical trials 
have not shown reductions in all-cause mortality with 
CRT-D.
715,716 In particular, in the elderly cohort with LV 
dysfunction, regardless of ischemic or non-ischemic etiol-
ogy, non-arrhythmic death occurs more frequently than 
arrhythmia-related SCD, thereby attenuating the prognos-
tic efficacy of ICD for primary prevention.
717,718 Similar to 
ICD implantation, risk scoring tools such as the MADIT-
ICD Benefit Score and the Seattle Proportional Risk 
Model, which assess the risk of both arrhythmic and non-
arrhythmic death, can help determine the need for the 
addition of defibrillation capability in CRT patients. 
CRT-D implantation should be considered in accordance 
with ICD indications alongside CRT criteria, with treat-
ment decisions based on a comprehensive evaluation of 
individual patient’s clinical risk, life expectancy, and poten-
tial complications, as well as patient preferences and QOL 
considerations, through a shared decision-making process.

d.  CRT Upgrade in Patients With Existing Pacemakers or 
ICDs
The JCS/JHRS 2019 Guidelines on non-pharmacotherapy 
of cardiac arrhythmias recommend considering CRT 
implantation (Class IIa) in patients undergoing de novo 
pacemaker implantation who have an LVEF of ≤50% and 
are anticipated to require a high degree of ventricular pac-
ing.
719 However, for patients with existing pacemakers or 
ICDs, CRT upgrade (Class IIa) is recommended only if all 
3 of the following criteria are met: (1) right ventricular 
(RV) pacing dependence; (2) LVEF ≤35%; and (3) worsen-
ing HF. The Budapest Upgrade CRT Study (BUDAPEST-
CRT) randomized 360 patients with HFrEF (LVEF 
<35%), paced QRS duration >150 ms, and RV pacing 
>20% to either an CRT-D upgrade group or an ICD 
upgrade group. The trial’s primary endpoint was a com-
posite of all-cause mortality, HF hospitalization, and 
reduction in LV end-systolic volume (to <15%) at 1 year. 
The CRT-D upgrade group demonstrated a significantly 
lower event rate, with a hazard ratio of 0.11.
720 Neverthe-
less, most clinical trials investigating CRT upgrades have 
primarily included patients with LVEF ≤ 35%, leaving 
insufficient evidence of benefits in patients with moderately 
reduced LVEF. Studies have shown that CRT upgrade 
carries a significantly higher risk of mortality and compli-
cations associated with device replacement compared with 
de novo CRT implantation.
721,722 Given these increased 
procedural risks and the potential for infection, CRT 
upgrade in patients with moderately reduced LVEF may 
be considered during battery replacement procedures 
rather than as a routine upgrade.
e. Conduction System Pacing
RV apical pacing can induce cardiomyopathy and lead to 
HF.
723 His bundle pacing enables physiological ventricular 
activation,724 and has been shown to improve LVEF, pre-
vent HF hospitalization, and improve QOL;725 however, its 
procedural success rate remains a concern.726 Recently, an 
alternative approach involving direct capture of the left 
bundle branch area, in addition to His bundle pacing, has 
been reported to achieve physiological ventricular activa-
tion.
1353 This technique, known as conduction system pac-
ing (CSP), includes pacing of the right bundle branch, as 
well as the left bundle branch and its fascicles and has 
demonstrated improving procedural success rates. CSP 
should be considered for patients with atrioventricular 
block who are candidates for pacemaker implantation, 
have an LVEF between 36% and 50%, and are expected to 
require a high degree of ventricular pacing. In patients with 
an LVEF >50%, CSP may also be considered if high-fre-
quency pacing is anticipated to impair LV systolic func-
tion.
However, an observational study comparing CSP and 
CRT in patients with HF eligible for CRT showed that 
although CSP reduced HF hospitalization, it was associ-
ated with a low procedural success rate.
727 In general, CSP 
is not recommended for patients eligible for CRT. How-
ever, in cases where rate control with medication is chal-
lenging in patients with tachyarrhythmia atrial fibrillation, 
catheter ablation of the atrioventricular node may be per-
formed. Compared with conventional RV pacing, CRT 
has been shown to preserve LVEF after atrioventricular 
node ablation.
728,729 Similar effects to CRT have been 
observed with CSP,730 suggesting that CSP may be consid-
ered for patients requiring atrioventricular node ablation.
f.  Remote Monitoring of Cardiac Implantable Electronic 
Device Therapy
Patients undergoing therapy with implantable implantable 
electronic devices (CIEDs) require regular assessment of 
battery status, lead integrity, pacing parameters, intracar-
diac electrograms, and thresholds. In many CIEDs, these 
data is available through remote monitoring. Patient man-
agement with remote monitoring is as safe as conventional 
in-person visits, while also reducing healthcare costs asso-
ciated with device checks. Moreover, remote monitoring 
allows for the earlier detection of arrhythmias or malfunc-
tions in the lead or the device.
731–734 Particularly in patients 
with HF, remote monitoring can detect signs of HF exac-
erbation by tracking heart rate, physical activity levels, and 
fluid status, as measured by thoracic impedance. Studies of 
patients with HF have reported that remote monitoring is 
associated with lower mortality rates than conventional 
management.
735–737 Therefore, remote monitoring is recom-
mended as a standard management strategy for patients 
with implanted CIEDs.
 ▋ 3.3 Intervention for Ischemic Heart Disease
  ▋ 3.3.1 Intervention for Persistent Angina Symptoms
Ischemic heart disease frequently coexists with HF, requir-
ing a comprehensive treatment approach that includes 
both pharmacological and non-pharmacological treat-
ments, particularly revascularization. For patients with 
ischemic heart disease complicated by HF who continue to 
experience persistent symptoms despite optimal medical 
therapy, coronary revascularization should be considered 
when the coronary anatomy is suitable for interven -
tion.

  ▋ 3.3.2 Intervention for Improving HF Prognosis
A meta-analysis of 5 randomized controlled trials compar-
ing revascularization vs. medical therapy in patients with 
HF and ischemic heart disease demonstrated that revascu-
larization was associated with modest but significant 
reductions in both all-cause and cardiovascular mortality.
749
Data from the STICH trial showed that at the 10-year 
follow-up, coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) com-
bined with optimal medical therapy significantly reduced 
all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, and death from 
hospitalization for cardiovascular causes in patients with 
LVEF ≤35% and ischemic cardiomyopathy.
747,750
The REVIVED-BCIS2 trial, published in 2022, com-
pared percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) plus opti-
mal medical therapy with optimal medical therapy alone in 
a similar cohort.
751 This trial specifically included patients 
with LVEF ≤35%, severe coronary artery disease, and 
myocardial viability. The trial did not demonstrate a ben-
efit of PCI over pharmacological therapy for the primary 
composite endpoint of all-cause death or HF hospitaliza-
tion at 41 months.
751 Recent data have consistently dem-
onstrated the benefit of CABG over PCI in patients with 
diabetes and LV dysfunction, as well as in those with left 
main coronary artery disease and moderate to severe LV 
dysfunction.
752–754
Based on these results, in patients with HF and reduced 
LVEF (<35%) with concomitant coronary artery disease, 
CABG should be considered in addition to optimal medi-
cal therapy to improve symptoms, cardiovascular hospital-
ization, and long-term mortality, when anatomically and 
clinically suitable for CABG.
747,750,755,756 Furthermore, in 
patients with HF and reduced LVEF (<35%) with con-
comitant coronary artery disease, PCI may be consid-
ered as an alternative to CABG in addition to optimal 
medical therapy after an evaluation by the heart team 
considering coronary anatomy, comorbidities, and surgical 
risk.
749,752–754
 ▋ 3.4 Intervention for Valvular Heart Disease
This section describes the clinical indications for non-phar-
macological approaches in managing aortic stenosis (AS), 
mitral regurgitation (MR), and tricuspid regurgitation 
(TR) presenting with HF.
  ▋ 3.4.1 Aortic Stenosis
a.  Indications for Intervention (Surgery and Transcatheter 
Therapy) for AS
Severe AS cannot be effectively managed through medica-
tion alone, and no current pharmacological treatments 
improve its long-term outcomes. Therefore, when AS is 
identified as the underlying cause of HF, non-pharmaco-
logical intervention should be considered.
757–763 However, 
these interventions are typically not appropriate for 
patients with poor general condition in whom the proce-
dure is unlikely to improve activities of daily living and for 
those with a life expectancy of <1 year.
b.  Selection of Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement and 
Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation
The selection between surgical aortic valve replacement 
(SAVR) and transcatheter aortic valve implantation 
(TAVI) should be made collaboratively by the heart team, 
carefully considering multiple factors, including the 
patient’s background, prognosis, anatomical consider-
ations, and treatment-related risks. Furthermore, the 
decision-making process should involve a transparent dis-
cussion of their institution’s procedural outcomes, the 
advantages and disadvantages of both surgical and trans-
catheter treatments, and a thorough consideration of the 
patient’s preferences and values.
TAVI was originally indicated for patients considered 
inoperable or at high surgical risk (Society of Thoracic 
Surgeons [STS] score or EuroSCORE II > 8%).
757–760 How-
ever, recent studies have demonstrated the non-inferiority 
of TAVI vs. SAVR in moderate-risk 764–766 and even low-
risk767–769 patients. In Japan, TAVI has been approved for 
use in low-risk patients since 2021. In general, considering 
the average life expectancy in Japan, SAVR is typically 
?????VT?K??s`uh???
recommended for those aged over 80 years. However, the 
decision should ultimately be made based on the patient’s 
lifetime management, considering the size of the prosthetic 
valve and the potential need for future reintervention.
c. Indication for Percutaneous Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) is sometimes per-
formed as an emergency intervention prior to SAVR or 
TAVI in patients with hemodynamically unstable severe 
HF or infection-related complications. However, with the 
widespread use of TAVI, its indications have become lim-
ited.
In patients with symptomatic severe AS who are at high 
risk for SAVR or TAVI due to poor general condition or 
hemodynamic instability, or in cases where it is difficult to 
determine whether life expectancy is >1 year , BAV may be 
performed as a bridge to SAVR or TAVI or for the pur-
pose of re-evaluation after initial treatment.
770–775 BAV 
may also be performed in cases requiring urgent interven-
tion for AS due to hemodynamic instability where pros-
thetic valve implantation is not appropriate, such as in 
patients with uncontrolled infection.
770–775

  ▋ 3.4.2 Mitral Regurgitation
a. Primary MR
i.  Indication for Intervention (Surgery and Transcatheter 
Therapy) for Chronic Primary Severe MR
The prognosis for symptomatic severe MR managed con-
servatively is poor, and therapeutic intervention is war-
ranted.776–778 The long-term prognosis of valve repair is 
generally better than that of valve replacement,779–781 and 
valve repair should be selected in cases wherever it is fea-
sible. The EVEREST II trial, a randomized trial compar-
ing transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) with surgery, 
enrolled substantial number of patients with symptomatic 
primary severe MR. Although there was no difference in 
survival between the 2 groups, the rate of MR surgery 
within 1 year (due to recurrent/residual MR) was signifi-
cantly higher in the TEER group. Conversely, the rate of 
reoperation due to MR recurrence was low after 1 year, 
even in the TEER group.
784 TEER may be considered in 
patients at high surgical risk or in those who are inoperable 
if they have valve morphology suitable for TEER.782–785
ii. Acute MR
Acute MR is commonly precipitated by chordal rupture or 
infective endocarditis, and in these cases it is often difficult 
to control HF. The need for surgical intervention should 
be assessed without delay.
b. Secondary (Functional) MR
Secondary MR is classified into ventricular functional 
MR, primarily caused by mitral valve tethering due to 
reduced ejection fraction, and atrial functional MR, 
mainly resulting from atrial and annular dilatation associ-
ated with atrial fibrillation.

i.  Indication for Intervention (Mitral Valve Surgery,  
Other Surgical Treatments, and TEER) for  
Ventricular Functional MR
Because the primary pathology of ventricular functional 
MR originates in the LV, appropriate pharmacological 
therapy for HFrEF, together with CRT when indicated, is 
essential as a part of the initial management. Subsequently, 
a thorough discussion within the heart team regarding the 
potential benefits of intervention for MR is essential 
(Figure 10).
① 
 Importance of GDMT and Significance of Mitral Valve 
Intervention
The Cardiovascular Outcomes Assessment of the Mitra-
Clip Percutaneous Therapy for Heart Failure Patients 
With Functional Mitral Regurgitation (COAPT) trial and 
Randomized Investigation of the MitraClip Device in 
Heart Failure: 2nd Trial in Patients with Clinically Signifi-
cant Functional Mitral Regurgitation (RESHAPE-HF2) 
trials demonstrated the survival benefit of TEER for ven-
tricular functional MR.
786,786a In contrast, no significant 
benefit was observed in the Multicentre Study of Percuta-
neous Mitral Valve Repair MitraClip Device in Patients 
With Severe Secondary Mitral Regurgitation (MITRA-
FR) trial,787 with subsequent analyses suggesting that sub-
optimal implementation of GDMT and a higher prevalence 
of residual MR compared with the COAPT trial may have 
contributed to these findings. 788 In the COAPT trial, 
improvement in MR was observed with GDMT alone, but 
residual severe MR remained an adverse prognostic factor 
independent of mitral valve intervention.789 Similarly, with 
surgical treatment, residual or recurrent MR has been 
reported to negatively impact survival, HF improvement, 
and reverse remodeling.790,791 Therefore, mitral valve inter-
vention should be considered for symptomatic severe MR 
that persists despite optimal medical therapy. In addition, 
factors such as potential improvement in survival, reduc-
tion in HF rehospitalization, induction of reverse remodel-
ing, and suppression of recurrent/residual MR should be 
evaluated when considering intervention. The presence or 
absence of coronary artery lesions that may require con-
comitant revascularization should also be considered to 
determine the most appropriate interventional approach. 
Appropriate GDMT should be continued after the proce-
dure. Notably, as LV dilatation and RV dysfunction prog-
ress, the degree of MR ceases to affect prognosis,

② Selection of Mitral Valve Intervention Methods
Currently, the mitral valve intervention options available 
in Japan are TEER, surgical valve repair, and surgical 
valve replacement. A comparison of TEER with surgical 
valve repair using an annuloplasty ring showed no differ-
ence in survival rates, but TEER was shown to be less 
invasive than surgical valve repair with fewer adverse 
events, such as postoperative bleeding, although the MR 
recurrence rate was higher.
783,793 A comparison between 
surgical valve repair and valve replacement with complete 
subvalvular preservation showed no significant difference 
in survival, but surgical valve repair had a higher MR 
recurrence rate.
790 European and US guidelines suggest 
that TEER may be effective in cases of severe MR, an 
LVEF of 20–50%, and a LV end-systolic diameter <70 
mm.795,796 Risk factors for MR recurrence after TEER 
include preoperative severe MR, LV enlargement, and 
residual MR,789,797 whereas those after surgical valve repair 
include preoperative LV enlargement and severe tether-
ing.
798 Therefore, the treatment approach with the greatest 
therapeutic efficacy and durability should be selected after 
evaluating a patient’s overall condition, risk factors for 
recurrence, invasiveness of treatment, and potential risks.
③  
Cases With Coronary Artery Lesions Requiring 
Revascularization
TEER may be considered for severe ischemic MR that 
persists or worsens after CABG or PCI. In ischemic MR, 
reverse remodeling after TEER is less likely to occur than 
in non-ischemic MR,
799 and the amount of scar tissue 
affects prognosis;800 therefore, surgical intervention on the 
LV to exclude scar tissue may also be considered.
ii.  Indication for Intervention (Surgical Mitral Valve 
Surgery and TEER) for Atrial Functional MR
It has been reported that atrial functional MR improves 
when sinus rhythm is maintained following catheter abla-
tion for atrial fibrillation.
801–805 Conversely, surgical inter-
vention for the mitral valve has been reported to improve 
symptoms. In cases of severe atrial functional MR with 
HF symptoms even after optimal treatment for atrial fibril-
lation and HF, mitral valve surgery, with concomitant 
surgery for tricuspid valve or atrial fibrillation if needed, 
can be considered.
806–810 Evidence from Japanese studies 
demonstrates that mitral valve surgery in patients with 
moderate to severe MR leads to significant reductions in 
BNP and event rates. 811 In most cases, surgical interven-
tion is preferred because it allows for concomitant inter-
vention for secondary TR, maze procedure, and left atrial 
appendage closure. However, TEER may be considered 
for high-risk or inoperable patients with severe MR if 
anatomically feasible to improve MR and mitigate 
symptoms.
812,812a,812b
  ▋ 3.4.3 Tricuspid Regurgitation
Surgical outcomes of isolated tricuspid valve surgery for 
TR presenting with right HF symptoms are generally con-
sidered to be worse than those of left-sided valve sur-
gery.
813–816 Some retrospective observational studies 
suggest that surgical treatment for isolated TR does not 
improve prognosis compared with medical therapy, 
whereas others have pointed out that delayed surgical 
intervention contributes to poorer surgical outcomes, 
prompting a shift towards earlier consideration of mechan-
ical interventions before irreversible RV dysfunction 
occurs.
817,818 Currently, there are no established criteria for 
RV function to guide precise indication of surgical inter-
vention.
a. Primary TR
Tricuspid valve surgery should be considered for severe 
primary TR accompanied by right HF symptoms.819–821
b. Secondary TR
Secondary TR caused by elevated pulmonary artery pres-
sure associated with left HF or pulmonary arterial hyper-
tension is primarily treated by treating the underlying 
disease and is often not an indication for isolated tricuspid 
valve surgery. Patients who have undergone surgery for 
cardiac diseases, such as mitral valve disease, and elderly 
patients with atrial fibrillation are candidates for surgical 
treatment for secondary TR. In a Japanese observational 
study on secondary TR due to atrial fibrillation, the mean 
patient age was in the late 70s.
822,822a
Severe secondary TR with recurrent right HF carries a 
poor prognosis even under medical therapy based on 
diuretics.820,823–825 Moreover, severe secondary TR after 
cardiac surgery often involves reoperation and is fre-
quently accompanied by pulmonary hypertension, result-
ing in a higher perioperative risk than severe secondary TR 
associated with atrial fibrillation. As mentioned earlier, 
there is still insufficient evidence regarding the appropriate 
timing of surgery for secondary TR.
826,827
c. Future Perspectives for Transcatheter Therapy
Multiple ongoing clinical trials are evaluating transcathe-
ter tricuspid valve interventions, including percutaneous 
tricuspid valve repair using clips and percutaneous tricus-
pid valve replacement. These therapies may provide thera-
peutic alternatives for patients with TR who are deemed 
high-risk candidates for conventional open surgery.
828,829

  ▋ 3.5.2  Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation Coexisting With HF 
(Figure 11)
a. Drug Therapy
i. Rate Control and Rhythm Control
In patients presenting with acute HF with concomitant 
tachycardiac atrial fibrillation, rate control is preferred if 
anticoagulation therapy has not been initiated. 833 
Symptom-focused treatments are deferred until the acute 
HF has resolved. Advances in pharmacological therapies 
and catheter ablation have expanded treatment options for 
atrial fibrillation in HF. The decision between rhythm 
control and rate control strategies is made with consider-
ation of the likelihood of maintaining sinus rhythm. 
Rhythm control is typically attempted when rate control 
with medication is difficult or when maintaining sinus 
rhythm is deemed beneficial from the perspective of hemo-
dynamics and HF management.
For rate control in HFrEF patients, β-blockers are one 
option that can be considered. If used, β -blockers should 
be initiated at a low dose and titrated gradually to mini-
mize the risk of HF exacerbation. Although long-term oral 
digoxin has historically been viewed as harmful, the 
RATE-AF trial demonstrated comparable outcomes 
between digoxin and bisoprolol in terms of resting heart 
rate reduction after 6 months and QOL.
603 In addition, 
NT-proBNP levels and NYHA functional classification at 
12 months were significantly lower in the digoxin group, 
with fewer adverse events. 603 Based on these findings, 
digoxin may serve as an effective alternative for heart rate 
control when β-blockers are contraindicated, poorly toler-
ated, or fail to achieve adequate rate control.602,603
ii. Anticoagulation Therapy
Warfarin has long been used as an anticoagulant. How-
ever, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) offer several 
advantages over warfarin because they have a fixed dosage 
based on age, weight, and renal function. In addition, 
although their efficacy is comparable to that of warfa-
rin,
835–838 DOACs are associated with fewer bleeding com-
plications, including a lower risk of intracranial hemorrhage, 
and offer superior safety overall. 839,840 DOACs should be 
considered as the first choice over warfarin for cases of 
non-valvular atrial fibrillation coexisting with HF. It is 
important to note that the insurance coverage in Japan is 
only for cases of non-valvular atrial fibrillation, and is not 
applicable to patients with severe mitral stenosis or pros-
thetic mechanical valves.
841
b. Electrical Cardioversion
Electrical cardioversion is an important treatment for

In patients with HF, it has been reported that atrial

6 months after electrical cardioversion.
842,843 Therefore, it

c. Catheter Ablation
In patients with HFrEF, atrial fibrillation often exacer-
bates HF symptoms, such as dyspnea and edema. There-
fore, a treatment strategy requires a comprehensive mid- to 
long-term strategy aimed at improving life expectancy and 
QOL. Treatment options range from pharmacological 
therapy to non-pharmacological therapy. The benefits and 
risks of each treatment should be explained to the patient, 
and the treatment plan should be decided through shared 
decision making with the patient.
845 If maintaining sinus 
rhythm is difficult or the patient refuses non-pharmacolog-
ical therapy, rate control is chosen, and pharmacological 
therapy with β -blockers, digitalis preparations, or other 
medications is administered. For patients who prefer to 
maintain sinus rhythm and have no contraindications, 
treatment options include antiarrhythmic medications, 
planned electrical cardioversion, or catheter ablation. If

i.  Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation Coexisting 
With HFrEF
After the publication of the Catheter Ablation vs. Stan-
dard Conventional Treatment in Patients With LV Dys-
function and AF (CASTLE-AF) trial,
712 numerous studies 
reported the superior efficacy of catheter ablation over 
pharmacological therapy for atrial fibrillation in patients 
with reduced ejection fraction; the results of several meta-
analyses have shown improvements in all-cause mortality, 
LVEF, and QOL.
846,847 However, in the RAFT-AF trial, 
although improvements in LVEF and QOL and a decrease 
in NT-proBNP levels were observed, no statistically sig-
nificant difference was found in the composite endpoint of 
all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization between cath-
eter ablation and pharmacological therapy group.
848 Fur-
thermore, in the Atrial Fibrillation Management in 
Congestive Heart Failure With Ablation (AMICA) trial,
849 
which investigated the effectiveness of catheter ablation in 
improving cardiac function in patients with persistent 
atrial fibrillation and HF with an LVEF of <35%, the sinus 
rhythm maintenance rate was significantly higher in the 
catheter ablation than drug therapy group. However, there 
was no difference between the 2 groups in the improvement 
of LVEF, which was 8.8% in the ablation group and 7.3% 
in the drug therapy group.
849 The median LVEF of the 
enrolled cases was 26.1%, suggesting that the therapeutic 
effect of ablation may be limited in patients with advanced 
HF.
The Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation in Patients 
With End-Stage Heart Failure and Eligibility for Heart 
Transplantation (CASTLE-HTx) trial targeted patients 
with treatment-resistant HF and symptomatic atrial fibril-
lation who were candidates for heart transplantation or 
left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation.
713 
However, the trial was discontinued early due to the dem-
onstrated effectiveness of catheter ablation at 1 year after 
randomization. At 18 months of observation, the addi-
tional catheter ablation group achieved a 76% reduction in 
the composite endpoint of all-cause death, LVAD implan-
tation, and urgent heart transplantation compared with 
the medical therapy group.
713 Therefore, catheter ablation 
may be considered in patients with atrial fibrillation and 
HFrEF to reduce mortality and hospitalization rates. 
However, the effect of catheter ablation has not been con-
firmed in patients with an LVEF <25%, and further inves-
tigation is needed because the CASTLE-HTx trial was a 
single-center study.
There is a condition known as tachycardia-induced or 
arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy, which can be caused 
by tachycardic atrial fibrillation.
850,851 In cases without 
obvious delayed enhancement on cardiac magnetic reso-
nance imaging, it has been reported that restoration of 
sinus rhythm by catheter ablation improves cardiac func-
tion. A subgroup analysis of the Catheter Ablation Versus 
Medical Rate Control in Atrial Fibrillation and Systolic 
Dysfunction (CAMERA-MRI) trial revealed that atrial 
fibrillation ablation significantly shortened T
1 values on T1 
mapping, which was shown to be correlated with improved 
LV function, suggesting that atrial fibrillation itself affects 
the deterioration of cardiac function.852 The absence of LV 
end-diastolic diameter enlargement on echocardiogra-
phy
853 or reduced RV systolic function on cardiac magnetic 
resonance imaging 854 were predictors of tachycardia-
induced cardiomyopathy. Based on these findings, catheter 
ablation for the purpose of improving cardiac function is 
recommended in patients who have no obvious underlying 
heart disease on examination and no other pathophysio-
logical condition causing LV dysfunction other than atrial 
fibrillation.
855

With HFpEF
Although clinical trials of catheter ablation for HFpEF are 
limited compared with HFrEF, a combined analysis of the 
Atrial Fibrillation registry to Follow the long-teRm Out

Frontier Ablation Registry) in Japan reported that cathe-
ter ablation for atrial fibrillation coexisting with HFmrEF 
or HFpEF was associated with a reduction in the incidence 
of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization compared 
with pharmacological therapy.
856 A small RCT examining 
the effect of catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation coexist-
ing with HFpEF showed that the catheter ablation group 
had significantly improved hemodynamics, exercise toler-
ance, and QOL at 6 months compared with the drug ther-
apy group.
857 According to ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS 
guideline, catheter ablation of symptomatic atrial fibrilla-
tion attributable to the presence of HFpEF, with the goal 
of improving related symptoms and patients’ QOL, is a 
Class IIa recommendation.
858 Although meta-analyses of 
observational studies reported benefits of catheter ablation 
for maintaining sinus rhythm and reducing HF rehospital-
ization,859,860 a meta-analysis of RCTs found no effect on 
overall mortality or HF events,861 highlighting the lack of 
consensus to date. Based on these findings, catheter abla-
tion therapy as a rhythm control strategy aimed at reduc-
ing symptoms and improving QOL in patients with atrial 
fibrillation and HFpEF is classified as a Class IIa recom-
mendation. Given the heterogeneous pathophysiology of 
HFpEF and the importance of risk factor management in

 ▋ 3.6  Other Surgical Treatments and Regenerative 
Medicine
  ▋ 3.6.1 LV Reconstruction Surgery
The STICH trial, an RCT conducted in the US, compared 
CABG alone to CABG plus surgical ventricular recon-
struction (SVR) in patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy 
(LVEF <35%) and concluded that the addition of SVR to 
CABG did not improve survival.
873 In contrast, a multi-
center study and single-center studies in Japan suggested a 
survival benefit of SVR in highly selected patients by 
improving LVEF and promoting LV reverse remodel-
ing.
874–878
  ▋ 3.6.2 Regenerative Medicine
Research on cell transplantation therapies using autolo-
gous myoblasts, 879 bone marrow-derived mesenchymal 
stem cells,880 and embryonic stem cell-derived cardiomyo-
cytes881 has not demonstrated convincing clinical benefits. 
In contrast, newer approaches using induced pluripotent 
stem cell-derived therapies, such as cardiomyocyte sheet 
transplantation and transplantation of “myocardial spher-
oids” (clusters of approximately 1,000 cardiomyocytes, 
developed in Japan), have shown promising results in large 
animal models of HF.
882,883 These advances have led to 
investigator-initiated clinical trials in Japan for ischemic 
cardiomyopathy, with cardiomyocyte sheet trials and myo-
cardial spheroid trials having started in 2019 and 2022, 
respectively. Although challenges remain, including the 
need for immunosuppression and concerns about the 
potential risk of post-transplant ventricular arrhythmias, 
ongoing research continues to evaluate the safety and ther-
apeutic potential of these innovative approaches for the 
treatment of failing hearts.
VII. Acute Decompensated Heart Failure
PM?c
 ▋ 1.1 Definition and Assessment of ADHF
Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) is defined as 
a subset of decompensated heart failure (HF) requiring 
urgent intensified treatment, particularly therapy aimed at 
avoiding a life-threatening crisis (i.e., life-saving treat -
ment). ADHF typically refers to cases that cannot be suf-
ficiently managed through outpatient therapy alone, 
necessitating emergency department care, intravenous 
diuretic therapy, or hospitalization.
884,885
 ▋ 1.2  Assessment of Congestion and Tissue 
Hypoperfusion in ADHF
In ADHF, congestion should be assessed by evaluating 
both pulmonary and systemic congestion. Because organ 
congestion and hypoperfusion can lead to acute damage in 
various organs throughout the body (e.g., in the kidneys, 
lungs, or liver), vigilant monitoring and management are 
critical.
2. Epidemiology and Prognosis
For details, please see Chapter III.
3. Treatment
 ▋ 3.1 Principles of Initial Management
ADHF is one of the life-threatening cardiovascular emer-
gencies that require rapid and appropriate therapeutic 
intervention tailored to specific pathophysiology.
In critical conditions, such as cardiogenic shock or respi-
ratory failure, it is essential to initiate treatment promptly 
with careful attention to timing (Figure 12), aiming to sta-
bilize hemodynamics and respiratory status as early as 
possible. Simultaneously, an accurate diagnosis of ADHF 
must be made. It is crucial to collect patient background 
information (e.g., history of prior HF hospitalizations, 
treatment history, and comorbidities) at the earliest oppor-
tunity, assess current symptoms and physical findings, and 
obtain a 12-lead electrocardiogram. Measuring natriuretic 
peptides (B-type natriuretic peptide [BNP]/N-terminal pro 
B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP])
110,886 and per-
forming echocardiography may further refine the diagnosis 
and clarify the clinical status. In addition, chest X-ray and 
lung ultrasound are invaluable for differentiating pulmo-
nary edema and understanding the pathophysiology. Clini-
cians should assess the patient’s condition, specifically 
pulmonary congestion, systemic congestion, and low car-
diac output/tissue hypoperfusion, to guide treatment 
(Figure 12). In addition, identifying the causes and triggers 
of ADHF is critical. Improving the prognosis of ADHF 
hinges on simultaneously managing the underlying pathol-
ogy and any exacerbating factors.
887–891

 ▋ 3.2 Pathophysiology and Management of ADHF
  ▋ 3.2.1 Assessment and Management of Congestion
a. Congestion
Most of patients with ADHF present primarily with signs 
and symptoms of congestion, making its management a 
principal goal. Subanalyses of large-scale studies and 
observational research have revealed that both the severity 
of congestive findings at admission and any residual con-
gestion at discharge correlate with worse outcomes. These 
findings underscore the importance of alleviating conges-
tion during hospitalization.
80,81,545,892–897
i. Systemic and Pulmonary Congestion
In HF, congestion results from elevated left- and right-
sided filling pressures (i.e., raised left atrial pressure [pul-
monary capillary wedge pressure] and right atrial [RA] 
pressure), leading to both pulmonary and systemic conges-
tion. As central venous pressure rises, renal venous pres-
sure also increases, causing renal congestion, which lowers 
the glomerular filtration rate via increased renal interstitial 
pressure and decreased renal blood flow. Renal congestion 
is a key contributor to worsened renal function over the 
course of HF.
898 Congestion of the liver causes compres-
sion of the liver parenchyma, reduced bile excretion, and 
elevated hepatobiliary enzymes, all of which correlate with 
HF outcomes.899,900 When elevated left ventricular (LV) 
filling pressure also affects the pulmonary circulation and 
right heart, right-sided filling pressures increase, leading to 
both pulmonary and systemic congestion. However, 
20–30% of patients with HF may exhibit an isolated eleva-
tion of either right- or left-sided filling pressures.
900a–900c
ii. Fluid Redistribution and Fluid Retention Types
Congestion can be classified into fluid redistribution and 
fluid retention types. The venous network of the abdomi-
nal visceral organs holds 20–50% of total blood volume.
901 
Normally, this “reservoir” blood (unstressed volume) does 
not increase central venous pressure. However, if sympa-
thetic overactivation triggers abrupt vasoconstriction in 
the abdominal visceral veins, reservoir blood swiftly shifts

into the circulating vein compartment (transition to 
stressed volume). Such fluid redistribution leads to sudden 
intravascular congestion and can precipitate acute pulmo-
nary edema.902 Alternatively, persistently elevated sympa-
thetic activity and neurohormonal factors reduce 
glomerular filtration via afferent arteriolar constriction 
and promote sodium and water retention, culminating in 
systemic fluid overload. Sustained elevation of venous and 
capillary pressures causes fluid transudation into the inter-
stitium, producing interstitial and tissue congestion. This 
fluid retention type of congestion evolves more gradually 
and often manifests as pleural effusion, ascites, and periph-
eral edema.
903,904
b. Assessment of Congestion (Figure 13)
Recognizing the degree of congestion and tracking its 
improvement are both essential in managing ADHF. In 
refractory cases or when it is unclear that whether the 
cause of respiratory failure is cardiogenic or not, right 
heart catheterization (RHC) may be performed to measure 
RA pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
i.  Symptoms and Physical Findings (See Chapter IV, 
r?PH
Orthopnea is one of the most sensitive symptoms indicat-
ing pulmonary congestion in ADHF. Jugular venous dis-
tension is a useful physical finding for assessing systemic 
congestion.
ii. Blood Tests (See Chapter IV, Section 2)
Natriuretic peptide levels reflect ventricular pressure over-
load and are correlated with signs of congestion. However, 
these levels may be chronically elevated in HF and can also 
be affected by non-congestive factors, including renal dys-
function and systemic inflammation. Improvement in con-
gestion often coincides with a rise in hemoglobin and 
hematocrit, which has been associated with favorable post-
discharge outcomes.
895,905 Other biomarkers have been pro-
posed (e.g., carbohydrate antigen-125, soluble CD146, 
biologically active adrenomedullin),903 although their clin-

ical application remains limited.
iii. Echocardiography (See Chapter IV, Section 3)
Echocardiographic evaluation of RA pressure and LV fill-
ing pressure involves measuring inferior vena cava diam-
eter and respiratory variation, hepatic vein dilation or 
regurgitation, mitral inflow patterns, tricuspid regurgita-
tion velocity, and tissue Doppler imaging.
iv. Others (See Chapter IV, Section 3)
Pulmonary ultrasound, renal venous Doppler, and liver 
stiffness measurements have been reported to estimate pul-
monary congestion, renal congestion, and RA pressure, 
respectively.
248,906,907
c. Management of Congestion (Figure 13)
Relieving dyspnea due to pulmonary congestion is a cen-
tral objective in the early management of ADHF. Diuret-
ics, particularly intravenous loop diuretics, are the 
mainstay of therapy and should be started promptly if 
there is evidence of fluid overload. Urine output should be 
checked several hours after administration, and the 
diuretic dose should be adjusted accordingly. Urinary 
sodium concentration, in addition to urine volume, has 
been reported as a useful early indicator of loop diuretic 
responsiveness.
908,909 Ongoing assessment of congestion 
should involve the monitoring of respiratory status, jugu-
lar venous distension, weight reduction, chest X-ray find-
ings, and echocardiography.
Among HF patients presenting with pulmonary conges-
tion, those whose primary mechanism is fluid redistribu-
tion may develop acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema with 
marked hypoxemia; non-invasive positive pressure ventila-
tion (NPPV) is beneficial in these scenarios. These patients 
frequently have hypertension, and cautiously administered 
vasodilators may be considered, although care should be 
taken to avoid precipitous hypotension. During deconges-
tion, a pronounced reduction in intravascular volume or 
preload can compromise cardiac output, leading to tissue 
hypoperfusion. In cases of significantly low cardiac output, 
renal perfusion may be insufficient to produce an adequate 
diuresis. If low cardiac output and tissue hypoperfusion 
persist, inotropes or mechanical circulatory support (MCS) 
may be required. In particular, patients with aortic stenosis 
or obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may rapidly 
decompensate into shock with the inappropriate use of 
diuretics or vasodilators.
Worsening of renal function is often observed during 
hospitalization in patients with HF. This is associated with 
many factors, including renal congestion, decreased renal 
blood flow due to low cardiac output and hypotension, 
drug effects, infection, and post-renal factors. Therefore, 
whenever renal function deteriorates, the clinical course, 
therapy modifications, and changes in signs and symptoms 
must all be meticulously reviewed, especially their interplay 
with diuresis and congestion. An increase in serum creati-
nine linked to improved congestion or the initiation/upti-
tration of renin–angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors is not 
necessarily associated with poor prognosis.
910 Conse-
quently, clinicians should avoid arbitrarily reducing or 
discontinuing HF therapies solely based on mild renal 
function deterioration. Because electrolytes (particularly 
potassium and sodium) may also change due to diuresis, 
altered renal function, or RAS inhibitor therapy, appropri-
ate monitoring and correction are vital.
Once euvolemia is achieved, therapy should shift 
towards maintaining this stable volume status. No univer-
sally accepted clinical indicator defines euvolemia, so reso-
lution of congestive findings typically serves as a practical 
guide. In patients presenting with weight gain due to fluid 
retention, their pre-exacerbation weight or discharge 
weight from a previous HF admission can be helpful. Eval-
uating relief of dyspnea during exertion (e.g., a 6-min walk 
test or cardiac rehabilitation) is as critical as assessing it at 
rest. If there is uncertainty, RHC may be considered.
  ▋ 3.2.2  Assessment and Management of Tissue 
Hypoperfusion and Cardiogenic Shock
a.  Assessment of Tissue Hypoperfusion and Cardiogenic 
Shock
Cardiogenic shock arises from reduced cardiac output 
leading to tissue hypoperfusion and organ dysfunction. A 
recent Japanese report indicated that in-hospital mortality 
is approximately 30% in patients with cardiogenic shock 
requiring MCS,
911 underscoring its dire prognosis. Early 
detection, risk stratification, targeted treatment of the 
underlying etiology, and hemodynamic stabilization are 
essential.

Cardiogenic shock is diagnosed by hypotension (systolic 
blood pressure [SBP] <90 mmHg, mean arterial pressure 
<60 mmHg, or a ≥ 30-mmHg drop of SBP from baseline) 
along with signs of tissue hypoperfusion (altered mental 
status, cold extremities, oliguria [<30 mL/h], and elevated 
lactate >2 mmol/L). However, the classic criteria for car-
diogenic shock proposed by the Society for Cardiovascular 
Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) are not absolute; 
for example, compensatory vasoconstriction may sustain 
blood pressure despite significant tissue hypoperfusion
912 
and the relationship between cardiac index, lactate levels, 
and clinical findings can vary depending on chronic HF or 
comorbidities such as infection. A comprehensive evalua-
tion of organ hypoperfusion is therefore crucial.
According to the SCAI shock classification, cardiogenic 
shock is categorized from Stage A through Stage E.
913 
Stage A (At risk) encompasses high-risk conditions such as 
severe myocardial infarction or myocarditis, yet blood 
pressure and tissue perfusion remain preserved. Stage B 
(Beginning) involves hypotension alongside intact tissue 
perfusion; despite an initially less concerning prognosis, 
meticulous monitoring is necessary because tissue hypo-
perfusion may still occur. Stage C (Classic), the “classic” 
form of cardiogenic shock, presents with hypotension and 
overt signs of tissue hypoperfusion, such as renal and 
hepatic dysfunction, cold, clammy extremities, poor skin 
coloration, livedo reticularis, rales, and elevated venous 
pressures. Stage D (Deteriorating/doom) arises when a 
patient fails to respond to treatment initiated for Stage C. 
Finally, Stage E, known as “Extremis,” involves cardiac 
arrest and necessitates cardiopulmonary resuscitation or 
extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Prognosis is dire 
at the higher stages (in-hospital mortality: Stage A, 3.0%; 
Stage B, 7.1%; Stage C, 12.4%; Stage D, 40.4%; Stage E, 
67.0%).
914
b.  Management of Tissue Hypoperfusion and Cardiogenic 
Shock
The causes of cardiogenic shock are diverse. Therefore, it 
is essential to identify the cause as soon as possible and 
initiate appropriate interventions while maintaining circu-
latory dynamics. If AMI is suspected, the patient should be 
transferred to a cardiac catheterization laboratory where 
emergency revascularization can be performed.
To maintain circulatory stability, intravenous inotropes 
may be required to augment cardiac output and improve 
tissue perfusion.
915 Dobutamine or phosphodiesterase 3 
(PDE3) inhibitors may be used alone or in combination for 
their inotropic effects, and norepinephrine can be adminis-
tered to maintain blood pressure. Rapid fluid loading with 
normal saline or Ringer’s solution can be considered for 
patients without fluid overload.
If initial medical therapy yields insufficient improve-
ment, MCS should be considered, taking into account the 
patient’s age, cognitive function, comorbidities, and social 
context. A multidisciplinary team approach is ideal in such 
cases. However, routine use of intra-aortic balloon pump-
ing (IABP) is not recommended in AMI with cardiogenic 
shock, as the Intraaortic Balloon Pump in Cardiogenic 
Shock II (IABP-SHOCK II) trial did not show clinical 
benefits of IABP.
916

  ▋ 3.3.2 Heart Rate and Blood Pressure Management
a. Heart Rate Control
The approach to heart rate control in tachycardia varies 
depending on the underlying rhythm.
In sinus rhythm, elevated heart rate may represent a 
compensatory mechanism for low cardiac output, and the 
significance of strict heart rate control during the acute 
phase remains unclear. In contrast, in atrial fibrillation, 
rapid ventricular rates can impair LV filling, making heart 
rate control beneficial. The Japanese Landiolol versus 
Digoxin (J-Land) study, a multicenter randomized trial 
conducted in Japan, compared landiolol to digoxin for rate 
control in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction 
(HFrEF) and rapid atrial fibrillation, targeting a heart rate 
below 110 beats/min.
926 Although landiolol significantly 
reduced heart rate at 2 h compared with digoxin, there 
were no significant differences in New York Heart Asso-
ciation functional class, renal function, or BNP levels 
between the 2 groups.
926 Although digoxin is physician-
friendly for heart rate control due to a lack of negative 
inotropic effects, it has been demonstrated that a serum 
digoxin concentration ≥1.2ng/mL is associated with 
increased mortality, with a positive correlation between 
serum digoxin concentrations and mortality risk.927
b. Blood Pressure Control
Prompt and appropriate blood pressure reduction is cru-
cial in acute HF precipitated by severe hypertension or 
hypertensive emergencies. A randomized trial comparing 
isosorbide dinitrate and furosemide in acute HF patients 
demonstrated that the isosorbide dinitrate group achieved 
more rapid improvement in oxygenation and experienced 
significantly lower rates of mechanical ventilation and 
AMI.
928 Although retrospective studies have noted a 
potential relationship between early blood pressure reduc-
tion and worsening renal function in acute HF,
929,930 pro-
spective data examining the relationship between lower 
blood pressure targets and clinical outcomes is lacking.

b.  Risk and Prevention of Venous Thromboembolism in 
ADHF
To prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE), early mobi-
lization and rehabilitation should be initiated in patients 
hospitalized with ADHF, while carefully monitoring for 
any deterioration in HF or respiratory status. Only a few 
studies have examined the effectiveness of elastic stockings 
and intermittent pneumatic compression in patients with 
acute medical conditions, and none have focused on their 
efficacy in ADHF. In Japan, low molecular weight heparin 
is not covered by universal insurance; therefore, the use of 
low-dose unfractionated heparin may be considered as an 
alternative.
934 The incidence of VTE in ADHF in Japan 
has not been reported, and the need for prophylactic anti-
coagulation, as practiced in Western countries, remains 
uncertain. Moreover, a Japanese observational study 
reported an increased risk of bleeding events with unfrac-
tionated heparin,
935 indicating the need for careful consid-
eration.
c. Risk and Prevention of Stroke in ADHF
In a Japanese registry of ADHF, the incidence of ischemic 
stroke during hospitalization was 1.6%; atrial fibrillation 
was present in 46.0% of these patients. 936 No significant 
difference in the incidence ischemic stroke was observed 
between patients who received heparin and those who did 
not; however, bleeding events were significantly more com-
mon in the heparin group.
For patients with ADHF complicated by atrial fibrilla-
tion, anticoagulation therapy is recommended because the 
presence of HF itself poses a significant risk for thrombus 
formation. Conversely, no RCTs have specifically evalu-
ated the use of anticoagulation to prevent ischemic stroke 
in ADHF patients with sinus rhythm.
d. Treatment of LV Thrombus in ADHF
Patients with HF and LV dysfunction are at risk of devel-
oping LV thrombus, and the frequency of LV thrombus is 
reported to be inversely correlated with LV ejection frac-
tion (LVEF).
937 The efficacy of anticoagulation therapy 
with warfarin for LV thrombus associated with AMI has 
been established, and it is also used in non-ischemic cardio-
myopathy.621,938 If there are no bleeding complications, 
anticoagulation therapy is continued for 3–6 months; in 
cases where the thrombus resolves or LVEF improves, 
discontinuation can be considered. A meta-analysis of 
observational studies suggests that direct oral anticoagu-
lants have comparable efficacy and safety to warfarin,
940 
although no RCTs have been performed to date.
 ▋ 3.4 Pharmacotherapy
  ▋ 3.4.1 Diuretics
a. Role of Diuretics in ADHF
Intravenous loop diuretics serve as first-line therapy for 
patients with ADHF because they rapidly ameliorate con-
gestion. In Japan, intravenous loop diuretics are adminis-
tered in over 80% of patients hospitalized for ADHF.
45,48 
Recent studies indicate that delays in initiating or appro-
priately titrating intravenous loop diuretics,
47,942,943 as well 
as poor early response (urine output, BNP reduction) to 
diuretic-centered acute-phase treatment,
944,945 are associ-
ated with worse outcomes. Therefore, it is important to 
rapidly and accurately assess a patient’s condition and to 
initiate and optimize therapy in a timely manner, being 
attentive to the “time axis.”
b. Diuretic Treatment Strategy for ADHF
Once signs of congestion are identified, the first dose of a 
loop diuretic should be administered promptly (within 1 h 
of arrival in the emergency department; Figure 14). Urine 
output should then be evaluated within 1–2 h if possible (or 
by 6 h at the latest) to assess the response to the initial loop 
diuretic dose. If the response is inadequate, the diuretic 
regimen should be intensified (e.g., doubling the loop 
diuretic dose or adding another diuretic with a different 
mechanism), while simultaneously investigating and 
appropriately treating any non-renal causes of diuretic 
resistance (e.g., low cardiac output/tissue hypoperfusion, 
hypotension, anemia, infection, hypoalbuminemia, or 
hyponatremia).
946 Recently, urinary sodium concentration 
has been proposed as an acute-phase indicator of loop 
diuretic responsiveness,
908,909 but its utility in Japan, where 
tolvaptan use is common, has not been fully validated.
c.  Intensification of Diuretics When the Initial Response to 
Loop Diuretics Is Insufficient
In patients with ADHF, the natriuretic threshold is 
increased due to activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldo-
sterone system (RAAS), requiring higher doses of loop 
diuretics.
948
i. Increasing the Dose of Loop Diuretics
In the Diuretic Optimization Strategies Evaluation(DOSE) 
trial,
949 which evaluated patients over 72 h in the acute 
phase of ADHF, those receiving high-dose intravenous 
furosemide had greater reductions in fluid volume and 
body weight than those in the low-dose group (secondary 
endpoints). However, the high-dose group had a higher 
incidence of serum creatinine elevation >0.3 mg/dL.
949 
Although there was a tendency for patient-reported symp-
toms to improve in the high-dose group, the difference did 
not reach statistical significance for the primary endpoint.
These findings suggest that dose escalation of loop 
diuretics can be effective; however, it has also been reported 
that once the natriuretic threshold is exceeded, additional 
increases in loop diuretics confer diminishing returns 
(approaching a “ceiling” effect).
948 Furthermore, patients 
requiring high-dose intravenous loop diuretics during hos-
pitalization tend to have poorer prognoses.
950 Conse-
quently, if increasing the initial loop diuretic dose by 2- to 
4-fold still fails to achieve sufficient urine output, the 
causes of diuretic resistance should be investigated and 
combination diuretic therapy or blood purification consid-
ered.
Notably, no significant difference in improvements in 
dyspnea or renal function was observed between bolus and 
continuous infusion regimens of loop diuretics.
949 Hence, 
the optimal administration method should be chosen 
according to individual patient characteristics and each 
facility’s protocols.
ii. Vasopressin V
2 Receptor Antagonists
Tolvaptan is an arginine vasopressin type 2 receptor antag-
onist that promotes diuresis by inhibiting water reabsorp-
tion in the renal collecting ducts. Multiple RCTs, such as 
the EVEREST trial and studies in Japan and other coun-
tries, have consistently shown short-term increases in 
[[p61]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1335
JCS/JHFS 2025 Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Heart Failure
urine output and reductions in body weight with tolvap-
tan.537,543,544,951
However, tolvaptan’s early effect on improving subjec-
tive symptoms varies among studies,537,543,544,951 and it has 
not been demonstrated to improve key clinical outcomes 
such as mortality.953 Tolvaptan is useful for fluid manage-
ment in patients who exhibit an inadequate response to 
loop diuretics, and its use in clinical practice in Japan is 
increasing.
547,954 After achieving euvolemia, the need to 
continue tolvaptan after discharge should be carefully con-
sidered.
From a safety perspective (monitoring SBP, renal func-
tion, and serum sodium), tolvaptan is generally considered 
safer than uptitration or combination of standard natri-

In the recently published CLOROTIC trial, adding hydro-

  ▋ 3.4.2 Vasodilators
From a pathophysiological perspective, vasodilators were 
thought to be more effective than diuretics in the initial 
management of patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary 
edema.
928 However, subsequent RCTs have shown that 
neither early intensive therapy with high-dose vasodila-
tors959,960 nor vasodilators with additional organ-protective 
effects961–963 improved outcomes compared with conven-
tional therapy in patients with ADHF. To date, there is no 
evidence supporting the routine use of vasodilators to 
improve the prognosis of patients with ADHF. Vasodila-
tors are used to alleviate symptoms of pulmonary conges-
tion, such as dyspnea, in ADHF patients without systemic 
hypotension or other contraindications.
a. Nitrates
In an RCT of patients with severe pulmonary edema, the 
combination of high-dose intravenous nitrates given as 
boluses plus low-dose furosemide was associated with a 
lower incidence of mechanical ventilation and AMI than 
high-dose furosemide plus low-dose continuous infusion of 
nitrates.
928 The efficacy of nitrates may decrease due to the 
development of tolerance when used for more than 24 h.
b. Nicorandil
Nicorandil exerts vasodilatory effects on both venous and 
arterial vessels and improves coronary microcirculation. 
Nicorandil is less likely to cause excessive hypotension and 
tolerance compared with nitrates.
c. Carperitide
Carperitide induces venous vasodilation, exhibits natri-
uretic properties, and ameliorates the activation of the 
RAAS. A small-scale RCT of Japanese patients with 
ADHF reported lower rates of death or rehospitalization 
in the carperitide group compared with conventional treat-
ment group over an 18-month follow-up period.
964 How-
ever, retrospective observational studies have shown that 
carperitide use was associated with increased in-hospital 
mortality.
965,966 Furthermore, an analysis using Diagnosis 
Procedure Combination data found no evidence of 
improved prognosis or reduced healthcare costs associated 
with the use of carperitide.967 In addition, the recently pub-
lished Low-dose Administration of Carperitide for Acute 
Heart Failure (LASCAR-AHF) trial, a randomized con-
trolled study of 247 Japanese patients with ADHF, dem-
onstrated that low-dose carperitide during the acute phase 
does not provide benefits regarding 2-year mortality, wors-
ening HF, subjective symptoms within 72 h, urine output, 
renal function, or changes in BNP levels.
968,969 Given its 
lack of impact on outcomes in ADHF, the routine use of 
carperitide is not recommended.
  ▋ 3.4.3 Inotropes
a. Overview of Inotropes and Vasopressors
Recent acute HF registries in Japan indicate that approxi-
mately 16–20% of patients receive inotropes. 47,445,972 
Among patients with SBP <90 mmHg or those presenting 
a “cold” profile (i.e., tissue hypoperfusion), the adjusted 
mortality risk did not differ between those receiving inotro-
pes/vasopressors and those who did not; however, among 
patients with SBP ≥90 mmHg and a “warm” profile, ino-
trope/vasopressor use was associated with a significant 
1.36-fold increase in mortality risk.
973 Similarly, the US 
Acute Decompensated Heart Failure National Registry 
(ADHERE) trial demonstrated that inotrope use was asso-
ciated with a higher in-hospital mortality rate.974 Because 
inotrope and vasopressor usage varies considerably among 
institutions,975 guidelines emphasize cautious use. The 
appropriate agent should be selected based on the patient’s 
condition, administered at the minimum effective dose, 
and used under careful monitoring. The routine use of 
inotropes or vasopressors in patients without low cardiac 
output, tissue hypoperfusion, or shock is strongly discour-
aged.

b.  Characteristics and Use of Catecholamines and 
Inotropes
i. Dobutamine
A multicenter randomized crossover trial conducted in 
Japan during the initial development of dopamine and 
dobutamine found that dobutamine was more effective 
than dopamine in reducing pulmonary artery diastolic 
pressure and alleviating pulmonary congestion in patients 
with pump failure due to AMI.
976 However, a subanalysis 
of the FIRST trial indicated that dobutamine administra-
tion may worsen long-term outcomes.
977 Consequently, 
dobutamine should be used at the minimum effective dose 
and for the shortest possible duration.
ii. Dopamine
Several randomized trials, including the Reevaluation of 
Systemic Early Neuromuscular Blockade (ROSE) trial, 
have failed to demonstrate the benefits of dopamine (e.g., 
increased urine output or renal protection).
978–980 A sub-
group analysis of the ROSE trial indicated that patients 
with an LVEF >50% may exhibit reduced diuretic respon-
siveness when treated with dopamine, highlighting the 
importance of careful patient selection.
iii. Norepinephrine
Norepinephrine is the first-line agent for patients requir-
ing rapid blood pressure elevation. For patients with 
cardiogenic shock who remain refractory to other inotro-
pes and volume correction, norepinephrine should be 
initiated as a continuous intravenous infusion at 0.03–
0.3 μg/kg/min. Norepinephrine is particularly beneficial 
for patients with septic shock. The Sepsis Occurrence in 
Acutely Ill Patients (SOAP) II trial, which compared nor-
epinephrine to dopamine in shock patients, found no 
difference in overall 28-day mortality.
981 However, in the 
subgroup with cardiogenic shock, those receiving norepi-
nephrine had significantly lower mortality rates and fewer 
arrhythmic events.981
iv. PDE3 Inhibitors
The advantages of PDE3 inhibitors include the following: 
(1) they are effective even in catecholamine-resistant states 
due to their β-adrenergic receptor-independent mechanism 
of action; (2) they provide both vasodilatory and inotropic 
effects, resulting in a smaller increase in myocardial oxygen 
consumption compared with catecholamines; and (3) 
patients are less likely to develop tolerance to them com-
pared with nitrates. Because PDE3 inhibitors are renally 
excreted, caution is required when they are used in patients 
with renal impairment.
In the Acute Decompensated Heart Failure National 
Registry (ADHERE), in-hospital outcomes were better in 
patients who received milrinone than in those who received 
dobutamine.
982 However, in the single-center small-scale 
randomized double-blind Dobutamine Compared with 
Milrinone (DOREMI) trial conducted in patients with 
cardiogenic shock, there was no significant difference in the 
primary composite outcome between milrinone and dobu-
tamine, indicating no clear difference in efficacy or safety 
between the 2 agents.
983 Furthermore, the Outcomes of a 
Prospective Trial of Intravenous Milrinone for Exacerba-
tions of Chronic Heart Failure (OPTIME-CHF) trial com-
paring milrinone to placebo showed no difference in the 
rate of cardiovascular readmission or death within 60 days 
and found higher rates of hypotension and new-onset 
atrial arrhythmias in patients receiving milrinone.
984
Overall, the prognostic benefit of PDE3 inhibitors in 
acute HF patients has not been established. Their use 
requires careful consideration of indications, dosage, and 
treatment duration, with a emphasis on using the mini-
mum effective dose for the shortest period necessary.
985–987
  ▋ 3.4.4 Other Medications
a. Sedatives (Morphine Hydrochloride)
Morphine can reduce pulmonary congestion by suppress-
ing sympathetic activity, thereby reducing both preload 
and afterload.
988 However, retrospective observational 
studies have linked morphine administration to increased 
rates of intubation and mortality. 989–992 Thus, routine 
administration is not recommended.
b. Kampo Medicine
To improve the symptoms of HF in patients with conges-
tive HF with edema, Kampo medicines indicated for 
edema, such as Mokuboito, Goreisan, and Goshajinkigan, 
may be useful.
993 In an RCT of patients hospitalized for 
ADHF, Mokuboito was reported to significantly improve 
HF symptoms compared with conventional treatment. 994 
In cases where congestion is difficult to control with exist-
ing diuretics, the administration of Kampo medicine indi-
cated for edema may be effective in improving congestion 
and HF symptoms. A multicenter RCT (Goreisan for HF 
[GOREISAN-HF]) is currently underway to evaluate the 
efficacy of adding Goreisan to loop diuretics during hospi-
talization for ADHF.
995
c.  Management of Inflammatory Response (Elevated 
C-Reactive Protein)
Recent evidence highlights the potential role of inflamma-
tion and oxidative stress, mediated by tumor necrosis 
factor-α, interleukin-6, and other factors, in the patho-
physiology of HF, particularly HFpEF, through myocar-
dial remodeling and endothelial dysfunction.
995a–995c Such 
inflammatory processes may also be involved in ADHF.996–998 
A report from Acute Study of Clinical Effectiveness of 
Nesiritide in Decompensated Heart Failure (ASCEND-
HF) indicated that high-sensitivity C-reactive protein 
(hs-CRP) levels in patients hospitalized with ADHF were 
comparable to those observed in acute exacerbations of 
asthma or COPD.
999 A Research Study to Look at How 
Ziltivekimab Works Compared to Placebo in People 
With Heart Failure and Inflammation (HERMES; 
NCT05636176) is currently investigating whether interleu-
kin-6 inhibition (with ziltivekimab) can benefit HF patients 
who have elevated hs-CRP.
 ▋ 3.5 Non-Pharmacological Therapy
  ▋ 3.5.1 Oxygen Therapy and Respiratory Management
a. Oxygen Therapy
Oxygen should be administered via a nasal cannula or face 
mask to patients with acute HF who exhibit poor oxygen-
ation.
b. Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation
If respiratory distress or inadequate oxygenation does not 
improve with standard oxygen therapy, NPPV should be 
promptly initiated. RCTs and meta-analyses have shown 
that NPPV alleviates dyspnea and reduces the need for 
intubation and mortality compared with conventional oxy-
[[p64]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1338
KITAI T et al.
gen therapy. 1000–1002 According to data from the Acute 
Decompensated Heart Failure Syndromes (ATTEND) 
registry and the Tokyo CCU Network, approximately 24% 
of patients hospitalized with acute HF were treated with 
NPPV.
44,1003
i. High-Flow Nasal Cannula Therapy
High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) therapy is a form of 
NPPV that delivers a heated and humidified high-flow 
mixture of oxygen and air through a dedicated nasal can-
nula without a face mask. A meta-analysis of small RCTs 
suggests that HFNC therapy improves dyspnea and oxy-
genation, as well as reducing the need for intubation.
1004 
Although NPPV is generally the primary option, HFNC 
therapy may be considered as an alternative in patients 
who cannot tolerate a face mask or have other contraindi-
cations to its use. HFNC therapy offers benefits such as 
improved patient comfort, better tolerance, and effective 
oxygen delivery, making it a viable option in specific clini-
cal scenarios.
c. Intubation and Mechanical Ventilation
If respiratory status fails to improve with oxygen therapy 
or NPPV, intubation and mechanical ventilation should be 
performed. In cases of cardiopulmonary or respiratory 
arrest, altered consciousness, the need to secure the airway, 
or persistent hemodynamic instability, mechanical ventila-
tion via endotracheal intubation should be initiated with-
out attempting NPPV.
  ▋ 3.5.2 Mechanical Circulatory Support
a. Definition of Cardiogenic Shock
Cardiogenic shock is defined as hypotension with signs of 
hypoperfusion and end-organ dysfunction due to impaired 
cardiac function.
913 Clinicians should appropriately recog-
nize the state of cardiogenic shock, consider hemodynamic 
evaluation by RHC, and optimize pharmacotherapy in the 
presence of hemodynamic instability even after the initia-
tion of intravenous inotropes. Clinicians should also con-
sider the use of temporary MCS as cardiogenic shock 
progresses.
b. Temporary MCS for Cardiogenic Shock
For cardiogenic shock in which end-organ dysfunction 
progresses despite the administration of intravenous ino-
tropes and other medications, temporary MCS can be 
considered.
2,9,1005 Temporary MCS includes IABP, veno-
arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and 
Impella (a transcatheter percutaneous left ventricular assist 
device). Although clinical trials comparing the prognostic 
impact of these devices have not been reported thus far, 
hemodynamic improvements have been shown with each 
device, and their use has increased rapidly in recent 
years.
916,1006–1010 In the Danish–German Cardiogenic Shock 
(DanGer Shock) trial, Impella CP plus standard care 
showed 6-month survival superiority over standard care 
alone in patients with AMI-related cardiogenic shock.1011 
However, vascular complications, bleeding, and neuro-
logical dysfunction are also common complications of such 
temporary MCS devices.1011–1014 Therefore, patients should 
be evaluated by a multidisciplinary team for their prefer-
ences, medical history, expected prognosis, and treatment-
related adverse events before initiation of MCS.1015–1019
