  ▋ 3.5.3 Renal Replacement Therapy
a. Indication
Acute blood purification therapy should be considered for 
patients who remain inadequately decongested despite 
optimal diuretic therapy and whose renal function deterio-
rates with further diuretic treatment.
1020
b. Evidence in Patients With ADHF
Clinical trials have investigated whether proactive acute 
blood purification therapy can relieve symptoms, reduce 
organ damage from congestion, and protect renal func-
tion. In the Ultrafiltration Versus Intravenous (IV) Diuret-
ics for Patients Hospitalized for Acute Decompensated 
Heart Failure (UNLOAD) trial, patients with ADHF and 
volume overload were randomized to ultrafiltration using 
an extracorporeal ultrafiltration method (ECUM) or intra-
venous diuretic therapy.
1021 In that trial, reductions in body 
weight and fluid volume were significantly greater in the 
ECUM group.1021 Although no significant differences were 
observed in symptoms or renal function, ECUM reduced 
90-day rehospitalization and unplanned visits.
1021
The Cardiorenal Rescue Study in Acute Decompensated 
Heart Failure (CARRESS-HF) trial randomized patients 
with ADHF who presented with volume overload and 
worsening renal function to either ECUM or intravenous 
diuretic therapy. Unlike the UNLOAD trial, the 
CARRESS-HF trial did not observe any significant differ-
ences in weight loss between the 2 groups.
1022 Moreover, 
the ECUM group had a greater increase in serum creati-
nine levels and a higher incidence of adverse events, such 
as catheter-related bleeding and infections.1022 Therefore, 
ECUM should only be considered for patients whose con-
gestion cannot be resolved with optimal doses of diuretics, 
and who have no contraindications for ECUM, such as 
hypotension or severe infection.
  ▋ 3.5.4 Acute Phase Rehabilitation
Exercise therapy is not recommended for ADHF patients 
with unstable hemodynamics or patients with dyspnea at 
rest due to pulmonary congestion or fever. 1023 However, 
even during mechanical ventilation, MCS, or continuous 
intravenous administration of vasoactive drugs, early-
phase rehabilitation can be initiated if the patient’s hemo-
dynamics are stable.
373 Early cardiac rehabilitation and 
early mobilization are essential, but it must be tailored to 
the patient’s condition with a structured and progressive 
approach.1024,1711–1713
4. Management During the Transition From  
the Decompensated to Compensated Phase
 ▋ 4.1  Importance of Comprehensive Management 
During the Vulnerable Phase
The period immediately after hospital discharge is consid-
ered a “vulnerable phase,” 60,1025,1026 during which HF is 
prone to worsen and requires careful management and 
support.1027–1029 Approximately 25% of patients hospital-
ized for HF exacerbation develop hospital-acquired dis-
ability, and these patients in particular are at higher risk of 
readmission and mortality after discharge.
1030
Several factors contribute to increased cardiac events 
shortly after discharge after hospitalization. Patients with 
HF may be unable to adapt to the transition from hospital 
to home because of incomplete cardiac and physical recov-
ery, suboptimal diagnosis or treatment of HF,1031,1032 and 
inadequate follow-up.142 A lack of self-management by 
patients and insufficient social support can also contribute 
to poor outcomes.1033–1038 It is therefore essential to ensure 
comprehensive HF management is provided seamlessly 
from hospitalization through discharge and beyond.
1039,1040 
A retrospective study in Japan reported that longer inter-
vals between outpatient visits after discharge were associ-
ated with an increased rate of HF readmission.
1041
 ▋ 4.2  Appropriate Diagnosis, Treatment, and 
Management of Exacerbating Factors
Several factors contribute to the worsening HF, including 
medical problems and poor self-management. When 
patients are repeatedly readmitted or are refractory to 
treatment, it is important to re-evaluate the underlying 
cause of HF and exacerbating factors while maintaining an 
objective attitude in assessment, rather than simply assum-
ing poor self-care adherence.
1039
 ▋ 4.3  Early Initiation and Optimization of Guideline-
Directed Medical Therapy
According to the CHAMP-HF registry, among patients 
with HFrEF who were eligible for angiotensin-converting 
enzyme (ACE) inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers 
(ARBs)/angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), 
β-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists 
(MRAs), prescription rates were only 73%, 66%, and 33%, 
respectively.
1042 Over the subsequent 12-month follow-up, 
many patients did not undergo dose titration, and few 
achieved the guideline-recommended doses. 1043 This dis-
crepancy highlights a gap between evidence-based guide-
lines and clinical practice. Similarly, the Utilization of 
Dapagliflozin and Other Guideline Directed Medical Ther-
apies in Heart Failure Patients: A Multinational Observa-
tional Study Based on Secondary Data (EVOLUTION-HF), 
an observational study spanning Japan, Sweden, and the 
US, revealed that guideline-directed medical therapy 
(GDMT) was often inadequately uptitrated or discontin-
ued within the first 12 months after discharge for HF.
1044
Hospitalization for acute HF is a key opportunity to 
initiate, maintain, and optimize GDMT. Patients who con-
tinued GDMT during hospitalization experienced a sig-
nificantly lower risk of mortality and readmission than 
those who discontinued treatment.
,1045 An integrated anal-
ysis of Japanese acute HF registries found that among 
patients previously diagnosed with HFrEF or HFmrEF, 
greater use of GDMT (ACE inhibitors/ARBs, β-blockers, 
and MRAs) between admission and discharge was associ-
ated with lower rates of all-cause mortality and HF read-
mission.521,522
Recent RCTs have demonstrated the safety and efficacy 
of initiating ARNI and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 
inhibitors during hospitalization for acute HF.568,592 There-
fore, when feasible and in the absence of contraindications, 
it is desirable to continue GDMT during hospitalization 
for acute HF. The STRONG-HF trial examined the effi-
cacy and safety of rapid uptitration of GDMT (RAS inhib-
itors, β-blockers, and MRAs) in acute HF.
142 In the 
high-intensity treatment group, each agent was titrated to 
at least half the recommended dose within 2 days before 
discharge, and up to the full recommended dose within 2 
weeks after discharge. Patients then had follow-up visits, 
[[p66]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1340
KITAI T et al.
including NT-proBNP testing, at Weeks 1, 2, 3, and 6 to 
confirm drug tolerability and safety. There was a signifi-
cant reduction in the combined endpoint of HF readmis-
sion and all-cause mortality at 180 days in the high-intensity 
group compared with usual care, largely driven by fewer 
readmissions for HF.
142 Serious adverse events were similar 
in both groups.142 Although these findings strongly suggest 
that early GDMT uptitration and close follow-up can help 
prevent readmissions, the feasibility of applying the 
STRONG-HF trial protocol in real-world Japanese clini-
cal practice will require further investigation.
 ▋ 4.4  Observation Before Discharge and Immediately 
After Discharge
Residual congestion at discharge is associated with an 
increased risk of readmission and all-cause mortal-
ity.81,82,1047 Thus, it is important to confirm whether conges-
tion persists before and immediately after discharge 
through physical examinations and laboratory tests. A 
single-center retrospective study in Japan indicated that 
echocardiographic assessment and BNP measurements 
before discharge were associated with a lower incidence of 
the combined endpoint of HF readmission and all-cause 
mortality.
1048 Because diuretics and GDMT are often 
adjusted before and after discharge,1049 monitoring serum 
electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine is critical. 
Unless congestion persists, a creatinine increase of up to 
0.3 mg/dL caused by diuretic therapy is not associated with 
worse outcomes. Therefore, diuretics should not be arbi-
trarily reduced or discontinued solely because of mild ele-
vations in creatinine.910,1050
Follow-up after discharge is emphasized in Western 
guidelines for HF,430,1051 although the recommended timing 
varies. In the US, follow-up is recommended within 1 
week, whereas in Europe it is recommended within 1–2 
weeks.2 Given differences in healthcare systems, optimal 
follow-up intervals may vary among countries. Recent 
evidence underscores the importance of rapid GDMT 
titration after discharge;142 therefore, in Japan, follow-up 
within 14 days after discharge is advisable.1058
 ▋ 4.5  Importance of Discharge Support and 
Continuous Care (Transitional Care)
During the transition from inpatient to outpatient status, 
from hospital to home, from an acute care hospital to a 
rehabilitation facility, or even within the same hospital but 
to a different ward with a different level of care, disconti-
nuities in care can increase the risk of HF exacerbation. 
Ensuring coordination and continuity of medical and care 
is therefore essential; these efforts are collectively termed 
“transitional care.”
1052
Early in the hospital stay, it is critical to assess patient 
needs for discharge, as well as the knowledge and under-
standing of HF among both the patient and their family. 
Providing education, optimizing HF medications, ensuring 
early and ongoing follow-up after discharge, and improv-
ing communication and coordination between medical and 
social care have been shown to prevent readmission for 
HF,
1053 reduce mortality,1054,1055 and improve quality of life 
for patients with HF.1055
VIII. Advanced Heart Failure (Stage D)

Patients with heart failure (HF) who exhibit severe symp-
toms that significantly interfere with their daily activities 
are classified as having Stage D (advanced) HF.
1059 This 
stage is characterized by New York Heart Association 
(NYHA) Class III or IV symptoms, despite optimized evi-
dence-based pharmacological and non-pharmacological 
therapies. In addition, these patients often experience at 
least 2 hospitalizations for HF within a year. The progno-
sis for Stage D HF is poor, with a 1-year mortality rate 
ranging from 25% to 75%.
2,4

2. Setting Treatment Goals
 ▋ 2.1 Treatment Goals for Stage D HF
In patients with Stage D HF, specific treatments options, 
such as ventricular assist device (VAD) and heart trans-
plantation, as well as palliative care, are considered. 
Patients who require continuous inotropic infusion or tem-
porary mechanical circulatory support (MCS) to maintain 
hemodynamics should be referred to a heart transplant 
center or a VAD-certified facility.2,4,1060 This enables timely 
discussions about treatment options with the patient and 
their family, and facilitates the establishment of appropri-
ate treatment goals.
The quality of life (QOL) and quality of death for 
patients and their families should be fully evaluated. The 
“I need help” criteria have been proposed for considering 
referral to a heart transplant center or a facility able to 
implant a left ventricular assist device (LVAD).
2,4,1060 These 
criteria was introduced to ensure the timely identification 
of Stage D HF and appropriate referral for advanced HF 
therapies. The 4 main points of the “I need help” criteria 
can be summarized as follows:

When promoting advance care planning, it is recom-

and prognosis, as well as to set and review care goals, in a 
manner that is tailored to the patient’s readiness.
1061
The addition of palliative care to usual management 
improves QOL in patients with advanced HF who have 
difficulty in relieving symptoms. 1062 Consultation with a 
palliative care team can also be considered to provide com-
prehensive support and alleviate a patient’s various symp-
toms.
1062–1064
 ▋ 2.2  Precautions for Setting Treatment Targets for 
Stage D
When establishing treatment goals for patients with Stage 
D HF, it is essential to engage in discussions that consider 
both prognosis and the patient’s QOL. This process 
requires careful consideration of clinical ethics and assess-
ment of the patient’s decision-making ability. In setting 
treatment goals, it is also important to evaluate these goals 
objectively and to support patients in making their own 
decisions. If a patient’s intent cannot be ascertained, it is 
essential to determine whether their family or surrogate 
decision maker can infer the patient’s intent to respect their 
substituted judgment. If the family or surrogate cannot 
infer the patient’s intent, the medical care team should 
thoroughly discuss with them, as the patient’s surrogate, 
what would be in the patient’s best interests. The team 
should always seek the course of action that most benefits 
the patient.
3. Inotropes
Evidence for the efficacy of inotropes in the treatment of 
advanced HF is not well established. Inotropes may 
increase myocardial oxygen demand and calcium over-
load, potentially leading to arrhythmias, myocardial isch-
emia, and myocardial damage, thereby increasing the risk 
of mortality.
977
 ▋ 3.1 Eligible Patients
The following situations represent potential indications for 
inotropes in patients with advanced HF:
•   persistent congestion, low  cardiac output, and  signs 
and/or symptoms of hypoperfusion despite optimiza-
tion of guideline-directed medical therapy and/or 
diuretic therapy
•   symptom improvement and/or palliation in  patients 
ineligible for heart transplantation or destination ther-
apy (DT)
•   hemodynamic  optimization  as  a  bridge  to  MCS  or 
heart transplantation
•   hemodynamic support during or after weaning from 
MCS
•   assessment of  the  reversibility of  organ  dysfunction 
when considering eligibility for heart transplantation 
or DT.

the degree of organ dysfunction is crucial when using ino-

support home intravenous inotropic therapy should estab-

cians, care managers, visiting nurses, pharmacists, and 
other service providers.
4. MCS / VAD / Heart Transplantation
 ▋ 4.1 MCS and VAD
  ▋ 4.1.1 Indication for MCS
Some patients in Stage D (advanced HF) require MCS in 
addition to intravenous inotropes to maintain hemody-
namic stability. The indications for MCS are generally 
determined based on the INTERMACS profile classifica-
tion,
362 which categorizes patients with NYHA Class III–
IV HF based on their clinical status and trajectory. In 
Japan, a similar classification system, known as the 
Japanese registry for mechanical assisted circulatory sup-
port (J-MACS) profile,
5 is used.
  ▋ 4.1.2 Treatment Strategy for VADs
The following outlines a treatment strategy involving the 
use of VADs.
a. Bridge to Transplantation
Bridge to transplantation (BTT) involves implantation of 
a LVAD, which is performed after receiving approval from 
the Eligibility Review Committee for Heart Transplanta-
tion of the Japanese Circulation Society or an in-house 
committee for heart transplantation eligibility at a well-
experienced heart transplantation center. The patient must 
also be listed on the Japan Organ Transplant Network.
b. Bridge to Candidacy
In bridge to candidacy (BTC), an implantable LVAD is 
used in patients who are currently ineligible for heart trans-
plantation due to end-organ damage or other comorbidi-
ties, but who are expected to become eligible for 
transplantation after achieving improvement of end-organ 
dysfunction or comorbidities by hemodynamic improve-
ment. In Japan, BTC using an implantable LVAD is cov-
ered by insurance as a Destination Therapy, as described 
later.
c. Bridge to Decision
Bridge to decision (BTD) refers to the initiation of tempo-
rary MCS, such as with the Impella (a catheter-based per-
cutaneous LVAD), an extracorporeal VAD, or central 
extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), to main-
tain a patient’s hemodynamics in cases of severe cardio-
genic shock while a treatment strategy is decided. 
Conventionally, the term “BTD” is not applied to intra-
aortic balloon pumping (IABP) or peripheral veno-arterial 
ECMO (VA-ECMO).

d. Bridge to Bridge
Bridge to bridge (BTB) refers to a bridging to an implant-
able LVAD after the use of an extracorporeal VAD for 
BTC or BTD, or after the use of Impella, upon receiving 
approval for heart transplantation.
e. Bridge to Recovery
Bridge to recovery (BTR) refers to a situation in which 
patients recover their own cardiac function after VAD 
implantation and subsequently undergo explant of the 
VAD.
f. Destination Therapy
DT is indicated for patients who are not eligible for heart 
transplantation but require permanent circulatory support 
at home with an implantable LVAD. In the US, the Ran-
domized Evaluation of Mechanical Assistance for the 
Treatment of Congestive Heart Failure (REMATCH) trial 
demonstrated that implantable LVADs improved survival 
compared with medical therapy in 2001.
1069 This led to the 
clinical application of DT, and the subsequent develop-
ment of continuous flow (axial flow) pumps from pulsatile 
flow pumps has further improved clinical outcomes. 1070 
Furthermore, the Multicenter Study of MagLev Technol-
ogy in Patients Undergoing Mechanical Circulatory Sup-
port Therapy With HeartMate 3 (MOMENTUM 3) trial 
showed that the HeartMate 3, a fully magnetically levi-
tated centrifugal pump, had favorable outcomes, with a 
5-year survival rate of 58.4%, compared with 43.7% for the 
HeartMate II (an axial flow pump) in a cohort that 
included both BTT and DT patients (where BTT patients 
accounted for 20%).
1071 In 2022, the percentage of the DT 
population in the US increased to 82.3% of all LVAD 
patients.1072 In the US, implantable LVADs are now a 
Class I recommendation for selected patients with 
advanced HF (INTERMACS Profile 2–3) who are depen-
dent on intravenous inotropes or temporary MCS, regard-
less of whether they are a BTT or DT indication.
4 In May 
2021, Japan’s National Health Insurance approved the DT 
indication using HeartMate 3 LVADs.
  ▋ 4.1.3 Temporary MCS
Temporary MCS devices include IABP, (peripheral) VA-
ECMO, central ECMO, Impella, extracorporeal centrifu-
gal pumps, and extracorporeal VAD. When treatment for 
cardiogenic shock is initiated with devices such as IABP, 
VA-ECMO, or Impella CP, but there is difficulty with 
weaning and a decision on the treatment strategy requires 
time, upgrading to the Impella 5.5 (which has a 30-day 
manufacturer’s recommended usage duration and is 
inserted via the axillary/subclavian artery with an artificial 
blood vessel) as a BTD strategy may be considered. For 
patients with small access vessel diameters in which inser-
tion of the Impella 5.5 is difficult, bridging to an extracor-
poreal VAD may be considered.
  ▋ 4.1.4 Implantable LVADs
In Japan, implantable LVADs are indicated for both BTT 
and DT. The HeartMate 3 showed improved 5-year sur-
vival in the MOMENTUM 3 trial, regardless of the indica-
tion for BTT or DT.
1071 For patients with an INTERMACS 
(J-MACS) Profile 2–3 who are dependent on intravenous 
inotropes or temporary MCS and are eligible for BTT or 
DT, an implantable LVAD is recommended to enhance 
both survival and QOL.
a. BTT Eligibility Criteria
In Japan, the eligibility criteria for BTT, which are in line 
with those for heart transplantation, are as follows:
•   patients should be under 65 years of age
•   patients should have NYHA Class IV HF symptoms 
despite receiving or being considered for standard 
guideline-recommended therapy
•   patients need to have an INTERMACS Profile 2 or 3 
and be dependent on intravenous inotropes, IABP, 
Impella, or extracorporeal VAD.
Patients who are less sick (INTERMACS Profiles 4–6) and 
those who experience drug-resistant ventricular arrhyth-
mias and frequent appropriate ICD shock therapies (mod-
ifier A) may be eligible for BTT. Other eligibility criteria 
include medication adherence, continued abstinence from 
alcohol and smoking, understanding of the limitations and 
potential complications of VADs, and securing family 
understanding and support with the patient’s cooperation. 
Additional considerations for eligibility include the expec-
tation that the patient will achieve a high QOL with 
implantable LVAD therapy, the feasibility of long-term 
home treatment, and the potential for social reintegration.
Historically, patients receiving implantable LVAD ther-
apy required support from a caregiver living with them 
permanently until they underwent heart transplantation. 
However, due to advances in LVAD technology resulting 
in improved device performance and safety, this policy was 
revised in 2024, and the required duration of a cohabiting 
caregiver’s support was reduced to approximately 6 
months after the initial hospital discharge.
12 Needless to 
say, it is desirable to have continuous support from a 
cohabiting caregiver beyond this time point. Caregiver 
support, including emotional and financial support, as well 
as accompanying patients on long-distance outings, is gen-
erally still required after 6 months.
Exclusion criteria for BTT include systemic diseases 
with poor prognosis, such as malignant tumors and colla-
gen diseases, with an additional eligibility criterion for 
BTT being a life expectancy of ≥5 years, as determined by 
any comorbidities. Previously, patients with a history of 
malignancy were ineligible for transplantation until 5 years 
of relapse-free survival after confirmation of complete 
remission. However, as of October 2021, this criterion has 
been revised. Now, patients who have undergone curative 
cancer treatment and do not require adjuvant cancer ther-
apy, such as hormone therapy, and whose 5-year relapse-
free survival rate is estimated to be 95% or higher by a 
cancer board at a medical institution accredited at or 
above the Regional Cancer Care Collaboration Base Hos-
pital standard, are also eligible for transplantation. 
Patients with irreversible organ damage, such as cirrhosis, 
are excluded from both transplantation and BTT. Ade-
quate renal function, defined as a creatinine clearance of 
approximately >30 mL/min, is also required.
1073 Another 
exclusion criterion for transplantation is obesity, which is 
defined as a body mass index >25 kg/m
2 in Japan. In addi-
tion, both BTT and DT patients with implantable LVADs 
must commit to lifelong abstinence from alcohol and 
smoking.
b. DT Eligibility Criteria
In addition to patients classified as INTERMACS Profiles 
2–3, those classified as INTERMACS Profile 4 are eligible 
for DT. However, for patients aged ≥65 years, eligibility is 
determined with more careful consideration of hemody-
[[p70]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1344
KITAI T et al.
namics, other organ function, nutritional status, and cog-
nitive function. The eligibility of patients classified as 
INTERMACS Profile 4 is based on findings from the 
ROADMAP (Risk Assessment and Comparative Effec-
tiveness of Left Ventricular Assist Device and Medical 
Management in Ambulatory Heart Failure Patients) 
trial,
1074 which demonstrated that LVAD therapy is more 
likely to improve survival and QOL than optimal medical 
therapy. The J-HeartMate Risk Score (J-HMRS) is 
another risk assessment tool and includes age, nutritional 
status, liver function, and kidney function (Table 7). The 
J-HMRS is based on the HeartMate Risk Score originally 
generated in the US from data on HeartMate II and is not 
based on data from the currently available HeartMate 3. 
The HeartMate 3 has demonstrated superior antithrom-
botic properties and durability compared with the Heart-
Mate II, with favorable 5-year survival rates.
1071,1075 
Although the J-HMRS may not be directly applicable to 
DT patients receiving the HeartMate 3, it is expected that 
older patients, those with liver or renal dysfunction, and 
those with malnutrition will be at higher surgical risk. 
When considering eligibility for DT, it is desirable that the 
patient is not classified as high risk by the J-HMRS. In 
addition, in patients aged ≥ 65 years, implantation is not 
recommended in patients classified as INTERMACS Pro-
file 2; however, using IABP or Impella for preoperative 
hemodynamic stabilization is acceptable if the J-HMRS 
indicates the patient is at low risk.
Other relevant risk scores include the HeartMate 3 Risk 
Score
1076 and the J-MACS risk score 1077 ( Table 7). The 
HeartMate 3 Risk Score was developed from MOMENTUM 
3 trial data1076 and includes left ventricular (LV) diameter 
and right ventricular (RV) function as risk factors. The 
J-MACS risk score was created using data from the 
Japanese registry for implantable LVADs (J-MACS).
1077 
The score derivation cohort only included young patients 
(median 46 years old) undergoing BTT and the score was 
calculated based on the outcomes of LVAD therapy other 
than with the HeartMate 3. However, similar to the Heart-
Mate 3 Risk Score, J-MACS risk score includes risk fac-
tors such as age, history of open-heart surgery, and RV 
dysfunction. In addition, the J-MACS risk score uses 
serum creatinine levels instead of blood urea nitrogen and 
serum sodium levels as indicators of renal dysfunction and 
low cardiac output. When determining eligibility for DT, 
it is desirable that patients are not classified as high risk by 
the J-MACS risk score.
Even for DT, patients are required to have a caregiver 
who can live with them for 6 months after the initial hos-
pital discharge. Continued care from a cohabiting care-
giver or from public services is also encouraged beyond the 
initial 6 months after hospital discharge. For patients aged 
≥65 years, a Mini-Mental State Examination score of ≥24 
and a Trail Making Test-B time of ≤ 300 s before surgery 
are established indicators of the ability to handle the device 
and self-management skills. Patients with neuropsychiatric 
disorders who are expected to have difficulty with self-
management of the device are excluded from LVAD 
implantation as DT.
Because implantable LVADs solely support the LV, 
conditions expected to make discharge difficult due to 
postoperative right HF (e.g., severe preoperative RV dys-
function, significantly small LV) are exclusion criteria for 
DT. Patients with irreversible liver or renal dysfunction, 
such as those requiring maintenance dialysis or those with 
liver cirrhosis, are also excluded. Considering the 5-year 
survival rate shown in the MOMENTUM 3 trial, particu-
larly with respect to comorbidities, patients with a gener-
ally expected prognosis of ≥ 5 years are eligible for DT. 
Patients receiving chemotherapy are excluded. Patients 
requiring immunosuppressants other than low-dose ste-
roids (prednisolone ≤10 mg/day) are also excluded in prin-
ciple, but may be eligible if the underlying disease is 
controlled and the risk of infection due to immunosuppres-
sion is considered manageable.
Finally, it is necessary for both the patient and their 
family to understand and consent to end-of-life care. It is 
desirable an advanced directive is obtained designating a 
surrogate decision maker, ideally before implantation and 
no later than 6 months after implantation.
  ▋ 4.1.5  Recommendations for Temporary MCS and 
Implantable LVAD

IABP did not improve the prognosis of patients with 
cardiogenic shock due to acute coronary syndrome,

venous oxygen saturation and cardiac power output (W; 
calculated as cardiac output (L/min)× mean arterial pres-

in patients with non-ischemic cardiogenic shock. 1078 
Although RCTs have not shown a survival advantage 
with the use of Impella compared to IABP, studies have 
reported that Impella is superior to IABP in improving 
hemodynamics (i.e., increasing mean arterial pressure 
and decreasing lactate levels).
1006 Furthermore, there are 
reports suggesting that the early initiation of LV venting 
in patients receiving VA-ECMO support may lead to suc-

  ▋ 4.1.6 Algorithm for VAD Treatment in Advanced HF
For patients with acute decompensated chronic HF, vari-
ous treatment options, such as intravenous inotropes, 
IABP, Impella, and VA-ECMO, should be initiated based 
on the patient’s condition. If weaning from these support 
devices is feasible, standard treatment is intensified. If 
weaning is difficult, the patient’s eligibility for heart trans-
plantation should be assessed. If the patient has already 
been listed for heart transplantation or is eligible for heart 
transplantation, an implantable LVAD is implanted as 
BTT. Even in cases where the patient is not eligible for 
heart transplantation, an implantable LVAD can be 
implanted as DT if the patient meets the criteria. If neither 
option is viable, best supportive care is provided. For 
patients aged under 65 years who may become candidates 
for transplantation in the future but do not currently meet 
the criteria and who fulfill the requirements for DT, an 
implantable LVAD can be implanted as BTC. If these 
patients subsequently meet the eligibility criteria for trans-
plantation, they can apply for heart transplantation listing 
and can be transitioned to BTT. For patients who may 
become candidates for transplantation but require time for 
evaluation of their neurological prognosis, or who do not 
immediately meet the criteria for DT due to factors such as 
a high-risk J-HMRS, extracorporeal VADs or Impella can 
be used as BTD. In situations where cardiac function has 
not recovered despite the patient receiving adequate circu-
latory support and rehabilitation, eligibility for heart 
transplantation and DT should be re-evaluated to make a 
decision to bridge to implantable LVAD (BTB) or provide 
best supportive care.
 ▋ 4.2 Heart Transplantation
  ▋ 4.2.1 Indications for Heart Transplantation
The underlying diseases eligible for heart transplantation 
include dilated cardiomyopathy, dilated phase hypertro-
phic cardiomyopathy, ischemic heart disease, post-myo-
carditis cardiomyopathy, cardiac sarcoidosis, and congenital 
heart disease. The eligibility criteria are as follows:
PM??c???????
thoroughly considered, the patient requires long-term 
or repeated hospitalization or has irreversible cardiac 
dysfunction with reduced exercise tolerance.
2.  The patient is preferably under 65 years of age.
3.  The patient should have a full understanding of the 
transplant, adequate family support, and be in a 
social environment that allows them to withstand 
heart transplantation.
4.  The patient should be able to receive immunosup-
pressive therapy and undergo various tests, including 
endomyocardial biopsies over a lifetime, after trans-
plantation.
Absolute contraindications include irreversible organ 
damage, such as cirrhosis, or the need for maintenance 
dialysis, as well as active infection, severe pulmonary 
hypertension, substance abuse (including smoking and 
alcohol consumption), and malignancy. Relative contrain-
dications include liver or renal dysfunction, active peptic 
ulcer disease, diabetes with advanced retinopathy, and 
psychoneurological disorders.
1073
  ▋ 4.2.2 Recommendation for Heart Transplantation
In Japan, as of December 2023, 819 heart transplants had 
been performed since February 1999, when the first legal 
heart transplant was performed. Following implementa-
tion of the revised Organ Transplant Law in July 2010, the 
number of transplants increased. Although there was a 
temporary decline in transplants during the COVID-19 
pandemic, 80–100 transplants are performed annually in 
Japan. However, there is still a shortage of donors, and the 
waiting period for transplantation exceeds 5 years. The 
prognosis for the 704 patients in Japan who underwent 
heart transplantation as of December 2022 is favorable, 
with a 5-year survival rate of 92.9% and a 10-year survival 
rate of 88.8%. The leading causes of death after transplan-
tation in Japan are infections (16 cases) and malignancies 
(12 cases).
There are no comparative trials for heart transplanta-
tion. According to International Society for Heart and 
Lung Transplantation registry data, the median survival 
for adult heart transplant recipients now exceeds 12 
years,
1081,1082 demonstrating that heart transplantation 
remains a highly effective long-term treatment for patients 
with advanced HF.
5. Symptom Relief
 ▋ 5.1 Importance of Symptom Relief
In patients with HF, palliative care should be provided 
along with life-prolonging treatment starting from Stage 
C, and HF treatment should be continued even in the ter-
minal stage.1059,1084 In Stage D, symptoms due to organ 
congestion and tissue hypoperfusion are particularly 
severe, and thus additional pharmacological and non-
pharmacological interventions for symptom relief should 
be considered in collaboration with a specialized palliative 
care team. Even in the terminal stage, the perception of 
patients and their families of the prognosis is sometimes 
dissociated from reality. To provide appropriate palliative 
care, it is essential to confirm their wishes, along with a 
comprehensive approach by a multidisciplinary team.
Recommendation and Level of Evidence for Heart 
Transplantation
Recommendation COR LOE
 Heart transplantation should be performed in 
eligible patients with advanced HF to improve 
survival and QOL.

 ▋ 5.2 Symptom Assessment and Intervention
Patients with HF present with a variety of symptoms, 
including dyspnea, pain, fatigue, depression, anxiety, sleep 
disturbances, cognitive impairment, loss of appetite, and 
emaciation.1086 In the terminal stage, it is reported that 
patients with HF experience 6–7 physical and psychologi-
cal symptoms on average,1087 which is comparable to the 
number experienced by cancer patients.1088 In the terminal 
stage, more than half the patients with HF have comor-
bidities such as renal failure, chronic obstructive pulmo-
nary disease, and diabetes, which can limit the use of 
medications. As a result, approximately 70% of patients 
report inadequate symptom relief.
1089 If refractory symp-
toms persist despite continuous symptom relief therapies, 
additional pharmacological treatments, such as opioids, 
and non-pharmacological therapies should be considered. 
Furthermore, if intolerable symptoms persist despite these 
interventions, the use of sedatives can be considered after 
careful evaluation of their appropriateness.
1090
IX. Special Medical Conditions / Diseases

This section presents updated information on hypertrophic 
cardiomyopathy (HCM) as presented in the JCS/JHFS 
2018 Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardio-
myopathies,
406 with incorporation of the latest findings.276,398
 ▋ 1.1 Definition
HCM is a disease characterized by left (LV) or right (RV) 
ventricular hypertrophy and LV diastolic dysfunction 
based on cardiac hypertrophy.
406 HCM should be sus-
pected when echocardiography or cardiac magnetic reso-
nance imaging (CMR) shows a maximum LV wall 
thickness of ≥15 mm (≥13 mm in the presence of a family 
history of HCM). 276,398,406 The diagnosis is made if: (1) 
pathogenic gene mutations have been identified in sar-
coma-related genes (sarcomeric HCM);1096 (2) pathogenic 
gene mutations have not been identified in sarcoma-related 
genes but secondary cardiomyopathy (corresponding to 
1995 World Health Organization [WHO]/International 
Society and Federation of Cardiology “specific cardiomy-
opathy”
1097) that shows a similar phenotype secondary to 
pathological myocardial involvement as a part of systemic 
(multiorgan) disorders is ruled out (sarcomere-negative 
HCM); and (3) genetic testing has not been performed but 
secondary cardiomyopathy has been ruled out.
 ▋ 1.2 Classification
In Japan, the term “dilated phase of HCM” has been used 
to refer to the condition of LV systolic dysfunction with an 
ejection fraction <50% observed during the course of this 
disease. However, there are cases where LV systolic dys-
function is present but LV dilation is not, and in other 
countries the terms “end-stage HCM” and “burned-out 
phase of HCM” are often used. Recently, the term “HCM 
with LV systolic dysfunction” has been proposed.
414
 ▋ 1.3 Update of Diagnosis and Examination
  ▋ 1.3.1 Blood Sampling Test
In cases where HCM is suspected, in addition to routine 
tests, M-protein to diagnose amyloid light chain (AL) 
amyloidosis, α-galactosidase (particularly in men) to diag-
nose Fabry disease, and lactate, pyruvate, and carnitine to 
diagnose mitochondrial disease should be checked.414,1098–1103 
In HCM, natriuretic peptides are also useful for estimating

  ▋ 1.3.2 Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in HCM is thought 
to indicate fibrosis on contrast-enhanced CMR. LGE is 
observed patchily in the mid-wall of the hypertrophic area 
and at the junction between the ventricular septum and the 
RV free wall. In network meta-analysis, the presence of 
LGE is also associated with prognosis.
1104 In particular, the 
presence of extensive LGE is associated with sudden death 
and the development of heart failure (HF).276,398
  ▋ 1.3.3 Genetic Testing and Family Screening
In Japan, genetic testing for HCM has been covered by 
health insurance since 2022, making it increasingly impor-
tant to consider genetic testing in clinical practice.
1105 
Although it remains challenging to predict the prognosis 
based solely on the presence of specific genetic mutations, 
patients with sarcomeric HCM generally have a worse 
prognosis than those with sarcomere-negative HCM.
1106,1107 
Based on clinical findings, scoring systems have been pro-
posed to infer the likelihood of sarcomere gene muta-
tions.
1108,1109 Multiple sarcomere gene mutations are known 
to increase the incidence of cardiac events.1109a
 ▋ 1.4 Treatment
  ▋ 1.4.1 Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death
Prediction of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in HCM 
remains difficult. For example, although the use of 
implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs) in the US is 
approximately twice that in other countries, appropriate 
discharge is infrequent in the US.
1110 At present, it is rec-
ommended that the flowchart for ICD implantation in the 
HCM Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Car-
diomyopathies (2018 revised version) is used in Japan 
(Figure 15).
406 Further research is needed to develop more 
accurate risk prediction scores.

 ▋ 2.2 Diagnosis of Cardiac Amyloidosis
The diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis requires recognition 
of clinical “red flags” suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis 
(i.e., a history of carpal tunnel syndrome or lumbar spinal 
stenosis, low QRS voltage and poor R wave progression in 
the precordial leads on electrocardiography (ECG), and 
echocardiographic evidence of LV hypertrophy in older 
patients with HF). Along with these red flags, the combi-
nation of evaluation using bone scintigraphy (
99 mTc-pyro-
phosphate or 99 mTc-hydroxymethylene diphosphonate) 
and serological assessment for monoclonal protein (1, free 
light-chain measurement; 2, serum immunofixation; 3, 
urine immunofixation) is important to facilitate correct 
diagnosis. A definitive diagnosis of amyloidosis requires 
histological confirmation of amyloid deposits in biopsy 
specimens and immunohistochemical determination of 
their type (AL or TTR). For patients with transthyretin 
amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), TTR genetic test-
ing is performed to distinguish ATTRv from ATTRwt 
cases. Although most older patients have ATTRwt, hered-
itary cases involving TTR mutations (ATTRv), such as 
early-onset forms with peripheral neuropathy (e.g., Val-
30Met) clusters in Kumamoto and Nagano prefectures 
and late-onset forms in non-endemic areas,
1100 have also 
been recognized. Genetic testing is crucial for confirming 
the diagnosis and facilitating early diagnosis and interven-
tion in family members who may be at risk.
 ▋ 2.3 Treatment of Cardiac Amyloidosis (Table 8)
The specific disease-modifying therapy differs depending 
on the type of amyloidosis. For ATTR-CM, the Trans-
thyretin Amyloidosis Cardiomyopathy Clinical Trial 
(ATTR-ACT) demonstrated the efficacy of tafamidis,
1122 a 
TTR tetramer stabilizer. More recently, the Efficacy and 
Safety of AG10 in Subjects With Transthyretin Amyloid 
Cardiomyopathy (ATTRibute-CM) study, a multinational 
Phase III trial evaluating another TTR stabilizer (acorami-
dis), found that acoramidis (800 mg twice daily) signifi-
cantly reduced cardiovascular events compared with 
placebo, as evidenced by a hierarchical composite primary 
endpoint comprising all-cause mortality, hospitalization 
frequency for cardiovascular events, changes in NT-
proBNP, and changes in 6-min walk distance (6MWD).
1121 
Although subgroup analysis of the ATTR-ACT study did 
not confirm the efficacy of tafamidis for reducing cardio-
vascular hospitalizations in NYHA Class III patients, sub-
sequent extension studies suggested a beneficial effect.
1122,1123
For hereditary ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropa-
thy, the A Phase 3 Multicenter, Multinational, Random-
ized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Study to Evaluate 
the Efficacy and Safety of ALN-TTR02 in Transthyretin 
(TTR)-Mediated Polyneuropathy (APOLLO) trial demon-
strated the efficacy of patisiran, a small interfering RNA 
(siRNA) therapeutic agent.
1124 Subsequently, in September 
2022, vutrisiran, a second-generation siRNA agent, 
received approval following the Study of Vutrisiran (ALN-
TTRSC02) in Patients With Hereditary Transthyretin 
Amyloidosis (HELIOS-A), which confirmed vutrisiran’s 
similar efficacy to patisiran in halting neuropathy progres-
sion and reducing TTR levels.
1125 In the APOLLO-B study 
evaluating patisiran in ATTR-CM, the primary endpoint 
(slowing the decline in 6MWD at 12 months) was met, 
although one of the secondary endpoints (a composite of 
death from any cause, cardiovascular events, and change 
from baseline in the 6MWD at 12 months) was not.
1126 The 
HELIOS-B trial, investigating vutrisiran in patients with 
ATTR-CM (12% hereditary; 88% wild-type), reported a 
significant risk reduction in the primary endpoint of death 
from any cause and cardiovascular events over 36 
months.

3. Cardiac Sarcoidosis
This section updates information on cardiac sarcoidosis as 
presented in the JCS 2016 Guideline on Diagnosis and 
Treatment of Cardiac Sarcoidosis by incorporating the 
latest findings and the JCS/JHRS 2024 Guideline Focused 
Update on Management of Cardiac Arrhythmias.
327,1130
 ▋ 3.1 Pathophysiology, Epidemiology, and Prognosis
Cardiac sarcoidosis can cause severe cardiac complica-
tions, including HF due to LV dysfunction and SCD due 
to advanced atrioventricular block or life-threatening ven-
tricular arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia [VT] and 
ventricular fibrillation [VF]).
1131–1133 Recently, relatively 
large-scale epidemiological studies have reported a high 
incidence of VT/VF and sudden death among major 
adverse events associated with cardiac sarcoidosis. 1134,1135 
In addition, studies of ICD implantation for primary pre-
vention have shown frequent early-onset VT/VF events in 
patients with cardiac sarcoidosis compared with patients 
who have dilated cardiomyopathy.
1136 In a multicenter 
retrospective study of 351 patients in Finland, SCD 
occurred in approximately 14% of patients and accounted 
for approximately 80% of causes of death.1134 Similarly, a 
Japanese multicenter retrospective study reported that the 
incidence of VT/VF or SCD within 5 years of diagnosis 
was approximately 20%.1135,1137 HF was present in approx-
imately 15% of patients at diagnosis1134 and hospitalization 
for HF occurred in approximately 13% of patients within 
5 years. 1135 With regard to clinical outcomes, recent 
advances in HF treatment and the widespread use of ICDs 
to prevent sudden death have significantly improved sur-
vival (i.e., 5- and 10-year survival rates of 90–96% and 
81–86%, respectively).
1135,1137,1138
 ▋ 3.2 Diagnosis
Cardiac sarcoidosis is diagnosed according to the 2016 JCS 
Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiac Sar-
coidosis.
327 Although diagnostic criteria differ between 
Japan and Europe or the US, 1139 there are no significant 
differences in clinical outcomes whether or not histological 
evidence is obtained. Therefore, early clinical diagnosis is 
essential.
1140 In diagnosing isolated cardiac sarcoidosis, 
demonstrating active inflammation on either gallium-67 
(67Ga) scintigraphy or 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron 
emission tomography (FDG-PET) is mandatory as part of 
the main diagnostic criteria. Consequently, there are cases 
in which a definitive diagnosis cannot be reached even 
though all other criteria are met, and the likelihood of the 
disease is extremely high. Conversely, some patients may 
be diagnosed without sufficient screening for involvement 
in other organs. Therefore, when diagnosing isolated car-
diac sarcoidosis, it is essential to consult with other speci-
alities and thoroughly investigate the presence of 
extracardiac involvement. If no histopathological diagno-
sis can be obtained from extracardiac lesions, endomyocar-
dial biopsy should be considered to avoid the risk of 
overdiagnosing isolated cardiac sarcoidosis as much as 
possible.
LGE in CMR is a principal criterion in the clinical diag-
nostic criteria. However, recent studies have shown that 
using T
1 and T2 mapping values may enable the detection

 ▋ 3.3 Risk Stratification
Poor prognostic factors include LVEF <40% at initial 
diagnosis, RV dysfunction, a history of VT/VF, and ele-
vated natriuretic peptides.
1135,1145–1149 The representative 
risk factors for VT/VF, the most critical adverse events, are 
as follows: (1) LVEF ≤35%;
5,13 (2) advanced atrioventricu-
lar block;1150,1151 (3) extensive LGE on CMR in the RV or 
LV;1152–1155 and (4) residual inflammation. Notably, VT/VF 
or SCD may occur even in patients with relatively pre-
served LVEF. In such cases, risk stratification using an 
electrophysiological study (EPS), LGE on CMR, cardiac 
18F-FDG-PET, or 67Ga scintigraphy would be use-
ful.1155–1159
Mehta et al. examined the prognostic value of EPS in 76 
asymptomatic patients with histologically confirmed extra-
cardiac sarcoidosis who also had abnormal findings on 
both 18F-FDG-PET and CMR. VT/VF was induced in 8 
of the 76 patients (11%), and 6 of these 8 patients experi-
enced VT/VF or death during a median follow-up of 5 
years, whereas only 1 patient died among the 68 without 
inducible VT/VF.
1160 These results suggest that EPS is 
appropriate for risk assessment.
Recent advances allow quantitative analysis of LGE on 
CMR, and several studies have reported its utility for pre-
dicting VT/VF and sudden death.1153,1161,1162 However, no 
consensus has been reached on an established quantitative 
method. In patients with extracardiac sarcoidosis and pre-
served LVEF, the event risk associated with small LGE 
detected by CMR screening is extremely low.
1163 In patients 
with cardiac sarcoidosis, even after inflammation is con-
trolled with immunosuppressive therapy, the presence of 
LGE involving approximately 20% or more of the myocar-
dial mass is frequently defined as “extensive.” Many stud-
ies have classified such cases as high risk.
1135,1153,1161,1162 
Thus, CMR is a powerful tool for risk stratification in 
cardiac sarcoidosis, although its utility may be limited by 
conditions that prevent LGE assessment, such as perma-
nent pacemaker implantation, intravascular metal implants, 
or renal dysfunction. Although not yet supported by 
robust evidence, fragmented QRS on a 12-lead ECG,
1164,1165 
the T-peak to T-end interval to QT interval ratio, 1166 and 
basal interventricular septal thinning on echocardiogra-
phy1167 have been reported to be significantly associated 
with VT/VF events.
Regarding 18F-FDG-PET and 67Ga scintigraphy, 
although some reports suggest their usefulness for risk 
stratification,
1158,1159,1168 others are negative, 1169 making it 
difficult to rely solely on these modalities. In particular, 
18F-FDG-PET quantification is challenging due to sub-
stantial interinstitutional variability in standardized uptake 
values, hindering its use in determining prophylactic ICD 
implantation. Notably, several studies indicate that FDG 
uptake in the RV or residual inflammation in areas of 
abnormal perfusion is correlated with especially high 
risk.
1159,1168 In cases where refractory inflammation is sus-
pected despite immunosuppressive therapy, cardiac func-
tion, LGE on magnetic resonance imaging, and EPS 
findings should be considered when evaluating the risk of 
SCD.
 ▋ 3.4 Treatment
The principle of treatment for cardiac sarcoidosis involves 
immunosuppressive therapy to control underlying myocar-
dial inflammation, as well as pharmacological and non-
pharmacological interventions to manage HF and fatal 
arrhythmias, and to prevent SCD.
  ▋ 3.4.1 Immunosuppressive Therapy
Because inflammation is the primary pathophysiological 
process in cardiac sarcoidosis, the primary therapy is 
immunosuppression, typically including corticoste -
roids.1170,1171 Corticosteroids are widely used as first-line 
immunosuppressive agents. Their initiation and dosing 
generally follow the protocols outlined in the JCS 2016 
Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiac Sar-
coidosis, with many centers starting at approximately 
30 mg/day and maintaining a dose of 5–7.5 mg/day.
327 
Although steroid therapy is often considered less effective 
in patients with severely reduced cardiac function or in 
those without abnormal myocardial uptake on 
67Ga scin-
tigraphy or 18F-FDG-PET, several reports indicate steroid 
efficacy regardless of these conditions. 1137,1145,1170 In fact, 
granulomatous infiltration has been histologically con -
firmed in myocardial tissue even in 18F-FDG-PET–nega-
tive patients. 17 Therefore, once a definitive diagnosis is 
established, steroid therapy should be initiated in all 
patients without contraindications.

One study showed that after the initiation of steroid 
therapy, persistently elevated troponin levels are signifi-

although it remains unclear whether this reflects ongoing 
active inflammation. In addition, routine repeated assess-

18F-FDG-PET after steroid 
therapy does not improve survival or quality of life, and 
instead increases cumulative exposure to ionizing radia-

scintigraphy or 18F-FDG-PET after steroid initiation is not 
significantly correlated with subsequent adverse events.1174 
Because no definitive biomarkers or imaging modalities are 
currently established for assessing inflammatory activity in 
the myocardium, tapering of the steroid dose is generally 
conducted in a mechanical manner based on the guide-
line.
327 Determining the progression or recurrence of car-
diac involvement is not always straightforward; therefore, 
clinical findings remain central, with imaging results inte-
grated into a comprehensive assessment to guide the man-
agement of steroid dose.
327 Although it may be possible to 
discontinue steroid therapy in some cases, discontinuation 
of steroid therapy has been associated with increased car-
diac mortality,1171 and thus a long-term maintenance dose 
is often continued. Careful monitoring is essential when 
attempting to discontinue steroid therapy.
In Japan, low-dose methotrexate (5–8 mg once weekly) 
is often used as a second-line treatment for cardiac sarcoid-
osis, either alone or in combination with steroids, when the 
steroid response is insufficient or when steroid use is lim-
ited by side effects.
327 The Cardiac Sarcoidosis Multi-Cen-
ter Randomized Controlled Trial (CHASM-CS), is 
currently ongoing to investigate whether the combination 
of low-dose prednisone and methotrexate from the initial 
diagnosis of cardiac sarcoidosis is as effective as standard-
dose prednisone alone.
1175
As third-line options, some trials have investigated inf-
liximab (an anti-tumor necrosis factor-α  antibody), 1176 
rituximab (a B-cell–targeting agent),1177 and anakinra (an 
interleukin-1 receptor antagonist). 1178 A clinical trial of 
namilumab, which targets granulocyte–macrophage col-
ony-stimulating factor, is also in progress (NCT05351554). 
However, none of these agents is routinely used in clinical 
settings for cardiac sarcoidosis.
  ▋ 3.4.2 Management of HF
No clinical trials, including secondary analyses, have spe-
cifically evaluated HF medications in patients with cardiac 
sarcoidosis. Therefore, GDMT follows the same principles 
as in general HF management.
327,1179 Similarly, indications 
for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) should be 
determined as in other cardiomyopathies. 327 However, a 
recent study of 55 patients with cardiac sarcoidosis under-
going CRT (94.5% CRT with a defibrillator [CRT-D]) 
showed no improvement in LVEF at 6 months after 
implantation.
1180 Over a mean follow-up of 4.1 years, 
34.5% of patients died or required left ventricular assist 
device implantation or heart transplantation despite opti-
mal medical therapy and CRT.1180 Progressive myocardial 
fibrosis leading to pacing failure may be a contributing 
factor.1181 In addition, fewer adverse events following CRT 
have been reported in female than male patients, highlight-
ing the need for further investigations into sex-related dif-
ferences.
1182 For indications regarding mechanical 
circulatory support or heart transplantation, see the rele-
vant chapters in this guideline. The recurrence of sarcoid-
osis in transplanted hearts is ≤5%, and the post-transplant 
prognosis is reported to be comparable to that of other 
diseases.1183–1185
  ▋ 3.4.3  Management of Fatal Arrhythmias and the

are common in cardiac sarcoidosis. For atrioventricular 
block, the decision to implant a permanent pacemaker 
should generally be made in accordance with the JCS 2016 
Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Cardiac Sar-
coidosis.

4. Elderly, Frailty, Sarcopenia, and Cachexia
 ▋ 4.1 Characteristics and Epidemiology
HF in the elderly is closely associated with aging-related 
processes, such as functional and structural changes in the 
myocardium, vasculature, and skeletal muscle, as well as 
with frailty.
1200–1203 Recently, the conceptual, pathophysi-
ological, diagnostic, and preventive aspects of frailty have 
drawn increasing attention.1204,1205 Frailty encompasses 3 
domains: (1) physical frailty, in which the physical capacity 
required for daily activities declines; (2) cognitive, mental, 
and psychological frailty, which includes mild cognitive 
impairment and depression; and (3) social frailty, charac-
terized by diminished social connections resulting from 
reduced social engagement (e.g., living alone or going out 
less frequently).
1206 Sarcopenia is primarily characterized 
by reduced muscle mass and strength, whereas cachexia is 
primarily characterized by weight loss. However, these 2 
conditions share multiple pathophysiological and mecha-
nistic features and can coexist in the same patient.
1207 
Notably, sarcopenia generally develops earlier in the clini-
cal course of HF than cachexia.1208 In addition, oral frailty, 
Table 9. Frailty Assessment Methods in Patients With Heart Failure
Method Characteristics
Physical frailty
  CHS criteria (Fried criteria)
Internationally standardized assessment method that diagnoses frailty when three or more of five criteria 
are met (unintentional weight loss, self-reported exhaustion, slow walking speed, weak grip strength,  
and low physical activity), and pre-frailty when one or two criteria are met, based on detailed numerical 
standards.
  J-CHS criteria
Modified version of the CHS criteria adapted for Japanese characteristics, which maintains the same  
diagnostic structure but features simplified assessment methods including shortened weight loss  
observation period and questionnaire-based physical activity evaluation.
Cognitive, mental, and psychological frailty
  Mini-Cog
Brief cognitive screening test that combines a three-word recall task (0–3 points) with a clock-drawing  
test (0–2 points), scored from 0–5 points.
Mini-Cog has the same validity as the MMSE, with a score of ≤2 indicating suspicion of dementia  
(sensitivity 76–99%, specificity 83–93%).
  PHQ-2, PHQ-9
The PHQ-9 is a screening instrument for depression, consisting of 9 questions (0–27 points), with a score 
of ≥10 indicating the possibility of depression.
The PHQ-2 (dual-question questionnaire) is a simple test using the first two items of the PHQ-9.
  GDS
Screening tool for assessing depressive symptoms in older adults, available in a 30-item full version, a 
15-item short version (15-GDS), and an ultra-short 5-item version (5-GDS), tailored for varying clinical  
and research needs.
Social frailty
  Makizako’s 5 questions
Screening tool for social frailty that consists of five yes/no questions about reduced frequency of going  
out, visiting friends, feeling helpful to others, living alone, and daily conversation, where social frailty is 
defined by two or more negative responses and social pre-frailty is defined by one negative response.
Multidimensional frailty
  CFS Overall health screening scale to assess degree of “frailty” (9 levels ranging from very healthy to end of 
life).
  Frailty Index (FI-CD, FI-CGA) More than 30 elderly-specific symptoms, signs, and problems in multiple domains are considered and 
converted to a real number between 0 and 1 to determine frailty.
  Kihon checklist 25-item questionnaire developed by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare in Japan for care  
prevention.
  Simplified Frailty Index 5-item questionnaire assessing shrinking, physical function, physical activity, forgetfulness, and  
exhaustion, with scores of 3 or more indicating frailty, 1–2 indicating prefrailty.
  EFS
11-item multidimensional tool assessing 9 domains (cognition, general health, functional independence, 
social support, medication use, nutrition, mood, continence, and functional performance) with scores of 
0–4 indicating not frail, 5–6 vulnerable, 7–8 mild frailty, 9–10 moderate frailty, and 11–17 severe frailty.

reflecting a decline in oral function, has been proposed as

 ▋ 4.2 Diagnosis and Evaluation
Early detection of frailty is critical, and regular assess-
ments are recommended for adults aged ≥70 years or those 
who have experienced >5% weight loss in the past 
year.
396,1210–1215 The diagnostic criteria for cachexia require 
the presence of a chronic wasting disease (e.g., HF, chronic 
kidney disease), along with a body mass index <21 kg/m2 
or weight loss >2% in the preceding 3–6 months, plus at 
least 1 of the following: anorexia; grip strength <28 kg in 
men or <18 kg in women; or C-Reactive protein level 
≥0.5 mg/dL.
1218 Table 9 summarizes the frailty assessment 
methods in patients with HF.
 ▋ 4.3 Prevention and Control
To prevent frailty in patients with HF, appropriate inter-
ventions targeting key risk factors are essential. These risk 
factors include lifestyle (e.g., physical inactivity), physical 
issues (e.g., polypharmacy, hearing loss), psychological 
factors (e.g., low motivation, depression), environmental 
factors (e.g., living alone, marital frailty), poor oral health 
literacy, and comorbidities. Evidence supporting interven-
tions for general older adults with frailty is accumulat-
ing,
1216 underscoring the need for trials focusing on the 
impact of multifaceted interventions on HF prognosis and 
activities of daily living in patients with HF. Nevertheless, 
intervention strategies should be tailored to each patient’s 
individual circumstances, functional status, values, and 
family environment. For those with oral frailty, establish-
ing regular dental care and undergoing periodic dental 
checkups is strongly recommended. 
5. Pulmonary Hypertension
 ▋ 5.1  Pathophysiology, Definition, and Epidemiology 
of Pulmonary Hypertension Associated With 
Left Heart Disease
In patients with left heart disease, elevated LV filling pres-
sures are transmitted backwards through the pulmonary 
capillaries to the pulmonary arterial circulation, causing 
pulmonary hypertension associated with left heart disease 
(PH-LHD). According to the 2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines 
for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hyperten-
sion, PH-LHD is classified as Group 2.
334 In Japan, based 
on the evaluation of right heart catheterization (RHC), the 
prevalence of PH-LHD is reported to be 20–40%.1220,1221 In 
most patients with PH-LHD, the severity of pulmonary 
hypertension (PH) is proportionate to the elevation in 
pulmonary venous pressure due to left heart disease. How-
ever, some patients develop PH that is out of proportion 
to pulmonary venous pressure and the severity of underly-
ing left heart disease. Such cases may have abnormalities 
in precapillary components (e.g., pulmonary vascular 
remodeling). The former has been termed isolated post-
capillary PH (IpcPH) and the latter combined pre- and 
post-capillary PH (CpcPH).
PH-LHD is known to be a poor prognostic factor in 
patients with HF,
1222,1223 and moderate or severe PH is a 
contraindication for heart transplantation. Its association 
with prognosis has also been reported in patients with 
valvular heart disease, suggesting its role as a prognostic 
factor in transcatheter valve interventions.
1224–1227
 ▋ 5.2 Diagnosis of PH-LHD
The diagnosis of PH-LHD requires confirmation of the 
underlying left heart disease and the concomitant presence 
of PH and elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure by 
RHC. RHC should be performed when patients are clini-

Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1357
JCS/JHFS 2025 Guideline on Diagnosis and Treatment of Heart Failure
cally stable with sufficient treatment of underlying left 
heart disease.224,334,1228 Traditionally, a mean pulmonary 
artery pressure (PAP) ≥25 mmHg has been used as a crite-
rion for PH. In accordance with the ESC/ERS guide-
lines,
334 this guideline recommends using a mean PAP 
>20 mmHg and a pulmonary artery wedge pressure 
(PAWP) >15 mmHg as diagnostic criteria for PH-LHD. 
Although a diastolic pressure gradient (diastolic PAP–
PAWP) ≥7 mmHg is sometimes used to differentiate IpcPH 
and CpcPH, the latest ESC/ERS guidelines recommend 
the use of pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) due to 
poor reliability
1230–1233 and the uncertain prognostic value 
of the diastolic pressure gradient.334,1228 IpcPH is defined by 
PVR ≤2.0 Wood units and CpcPH is defined by PVR >2 
Wood units. The diagnostic algorithm for PH-LHD is 
shown in Figure 18.
Among hemodynamic parameters, PAP and PVR are 
associated with the severity of disease and prognosis.
1233–1237 
In particular, a PVR >5 Wood units is associated with 
prognosis in left heart diseases such as HFrEF. 1235,1238,1239 
The presence of PH in patients with left heart disease can 
be complicated by pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) 
and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension 
(CTEPH), which are the conditions of precapillary PH. 
These conditions should be excluded in cases where PVR 
is higher than that of left heart disease. RHC is recom-
mended to guide treatment decisions and provide prognos-
tic information in cases where the severity of PH is 
disproportionate to the severity of the underlying left heart 
disease, raising suspicion of PAH and CTEPH, as well as 
CpcPH, or in cases of severe HF where heart transplanta-
tion is being considered.
 ▋ 5.3 Treatment of PH-LHD
In patients with PH-LHD, it is recommended that therapy 
for the underlying left heart disease is optimized to reduce 
LV filling pressures or left atrial (LA) pressure. 1240,1241 
Although several RCTs have evaluated PAH-targeted 
drugs in PH-LHD, none has demonstrated a favorable 
impact on its prognosis. Clinical trials investigating the 
endothelin receptor antagonist bosentan in patients with 
PH associated with HFrEF
1242 or HF with preserved ejec-
tion fraction (HFpEF),1243 as well as trials using the phos-
phodiesterase 5 (PDE5) inhibitor sildenafil in patients with 
persistent PH after valvular heart interventions,
1244 failed 
to show prognostic benefits. Similarly, a study examining 
the guanylate cyclase stimulator riociguat in HFrEF found 
no significant reduction in PAP compared with placebo.
1245 
Trials in HFpEF patients with IpcPH using sildenafil 1246 
and riociguat1247 have also shown no clinical efficacy. Con-
sequently, PAH drugs are not currently recommended for 
PH-LHD.
In patients with CpcPH, a single-center trial primarily 
involving those with HFpEF showed no benefit from an 
endothelin receptor antagonist, with worsening fluid reten-
tion.
1248 In patients with HFpEF and CpcPH, PDE5 inhib-
itors were shown to improve hemodynamics, RV function, 
and quality of life in a single-center trial,1249 and observa-
tional studies suggested improvements in exercise toler-
ance.
1250,1251 However, robust evidence from large-scale 
multicenter clinical trials is currently lacking.
Several clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate 
the efficacy of pulmonary vasodilators in patients with HF 
and CpcPH, particularly those with HFpEF. Further stud-
ies are required to clarify their potential benefits.
6. Atrial Cardiomyopathy
 ▋ 6.1 Definition and Classification
Atrial cardiomyopathy is defined as “Any complex of 
structural, architectural, contractile or electrophysiological 
changes affecting the atria with the potential to produce 
clinically relevant manifestations,”
1252 and there is growing 
recognition of its potential to increase the risk of atrial 
fibrillation and HF, particularly HFpEF.1252–1254
Risk factors for atrial cardiomyopathy include aging, 
inflammation, volume or pressure overload, and oxidative 
stress. Prolonged exposure to these factors leads to atrial 
fibrosis and remodeling at the structural, electrophysiolog-
ical, and autonomic levels, ultimately resulting in atrial 
cardiomyopathy.
1253 As atrial remodeling progresses, atrial 
cardiomyopathy emerges in the form of atrial fibrillation 
and cerebral infarction. It is also reported that functional, 
organizational, and electrophysiological changes due to 
atrial cardiomyopathy can cause disruptions in atrial 
blood flow and wall motion, as well as endothelial dysfunc-
tion, thereby promoting thrombogenesis.
1255
The EHRAS working group (for the European Heart 
Rhythm Association, Heart Rhythm Society, Asian Pacific 
Heart Rhythm Society, and Sociedad Latino Americana 
de Estimulacion Cardiaca y Electrofisiologia) has pro-
posed 4 histological and pathophysiological classes of 
atrial cardiomyopathy: (I) primarily cardiomyocyte 
changes (e.g., isolated atrial fibrillation, genetic disease, 
diabetes); (II) primarily fibrotic changes (e.g., aging, smok-
ing); (III) combined cardiomyocyte–pathology/fibrosis 
(e.g., congestive HF, valvular heart disease); and (IV) pri-
marily non-collagen infiltration (with or without cardio-
myocyte changes; e.g., localized atrial amyloidosis, 
granulomatous diseases, inflammatory cell infiltration due 
to myocarditis).
1252

Hypertension Associated With Left Heart Disease

 ▋ 6.2 Evaluation and Causes
Multiple indicators for evaluating atrial function, mor-
phology, and characteristics include the following: (1) elec-
trocardiographic parameters (e.g., P wave timing, duration, 
morphology); (2) echocardiographic parameters (e.g., 
atrial diameter, atrial volume, pulmonary vein blood flow 
velocity waveform, mitral valve blood flow velocity wave-
form, tissue Doppler velocity, LA emptying fraction calcu-
lated from LA volume, LA strain analysis using speckle 
tracking); (3) CMR parameters (e.g., LA strain analysis by 
feature tracking, LGE, T
1 mapping); and (4) hemodynamic 
parameters measured by RHC (e.g., PAWP tracing wave-
form).1256–1258 LA strain analysis enables the assessment of 
each of the 3 functional phases of the atrium: reservoir, 
conduit, and booster pump function. Among these, LA 
reservoir strain reflects LA compliance and exhibits strong 
prognostic utility not only for diagnosing atrial cardiomy-
opathy but also for outcomes in HFpEF.
67,1259,1260 In addi-
tion, exercise stress tests, including passive leg raising, have 
shown promise for the early detection of atrial cardiomy-
opathy.
67,1261
 ▋ 6.3 Treatment
Treatment for atrial cardiomyopathy includes early inter-
vention targeting identified risk factors (e.g., hypertension, 
sleep apnea, atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease) and, 
if HF develops, the administration of standard HF phar-
macotherapies (e.g., diuretics, SGLT2 inhibitors, MRAs). 
A promising future treatment is an interatrial shunt device, 
which is expected to reduce the increase in LA pressure, 
especially during load caused by exercise.
1262 The 
REDUCE LAP-HF II (Reduce Elevated Left Atrial Pres-
sure in Patients With Heart Failure II) trial was a random-
ized sham-controlled comparative study of the efficacy and 
safety of an interatrial shunt device in 626 patients (includ-
ing Japanese participants) with symptomatic HF, elevated 
LA pressure, and an ejection fraction ≥ 40%.
1263 The trial 
yielded neutral results, with no difference between the 
groups in the hierarchical primary composite endpoint of 
cardiovascular death or non-fatal ischemic stroke at 12 
months, rate of total HF events up to 24 months, and 
change in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire 
overall summary score at 12 months. However, subgroup 
analysis revealed that shunt therapy significantly reduced 
the primary endpoint compared with sham among partici-
pants without increased PVR during exercise or without an 
implanted pacemaker.
1264 The RESPONDER-HF (Re-
Evaluation of the Corvia Atrial Shunt Device in a Preci-
sion Medicine Trial to Determine Efficacy in Mildly 
Reduced or Preserved Ejection Fraction Heart Failure) 
trial is currently underway to reassess the efficacy of this 
device in that specific population.
7. Pregnancy, Peripartum, and  
Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
 ▋ 7.1 Pregnancy in Patients With HF
  ▋ 7.1.1 Risk Assessment of Pregnancy With HF
During pregnancy, circulating plasma volume increases by 
approximately 40–50% compared with prepregnancy lev-
els. Furthermore, due to the teratogenic risk of certain 
medications (e.g., angiotensin-converting enzyme [ACE] 
inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers [ARBs], ARNI), 
such drugs must be discontinued. Consequently, preg-
nancy can exacerbate HF, increasing the risk of maternal 
mortality.
1265,1266 Therefore, counseling regarding the 
potential complications and risks of pregnancy and child-
birth is strongly recommended before conception. 
Although various studies have investigated risk assessment 
methods for pregnancy, the Japanese modified WHO clas-
sification is considered most appropriate for evaluating 
risk because it adapts the modified WHO classification to 
reflect the specific circumstances in Japan.
1265 Table 10 
presents cardiac diseases in which pregnancy requires strict 
attention or should be strongly discouraged.
  ▋ 7.1.2 HF Medications to Avoid During Pregnancy
Among the drugs for the treatment of chronic HF, ACE 
inhibitors, ARBs, ARNI, SGLT2 inhibitors, and 
ivabradine are contraindicated during pregnancy and 
therefore need to be discontinued.
1265,1267 MRAs are gener-
ally considered to be safe in the usual dosage. Although 
β-blockers can cause fetal growth retardation and neonatal 
hypoglycemia, necessitating careful monitoring, they are 
not teratogenic and can be administered if it is judged that 
the therapeutic benefits to the mother outweigh the risks.
  ▋ 7.1.3 HF Management During Pregnancy
In the case of acute exacerbation of HF, treatment should 
be performed in the same manner as in non-pregnant 
patients while avoiding drugs contraindicated during preg-
nancy.
1265 Exacerbations of HF often occur in the late 
second or third trimester of pregnancy. Loop diuretics, 
human atrial natriuretic peptide, and catecholamines can 
be used during pregnancy. If administration of catechol-
amines becomes necessary for worsening HF, pregnancy 
interruption should be considered. In addition, patients 
who require bed rest and diuretics due to worsening HF 
are at increased risk of intraventricular thrombosis and 
deep vein thrombosis. In such cases, anticoagulation ther-

 ▋ 7.2 Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
Peripartum cardiomyopathy is an idiopathic cardiomy-
opathy characterized by newly reduced LV systolic func-
tion and HF in women with no history of myocardial 
disease, occurring in the second half of pregnancy or 
within the first few months postpartum. Although there 
are no universally accepted diagnostic criteria, the Japa-
nese Guidelines for the Management of Peripartum Car-
diomyopathy propose the following 4 criteria: (1) 
new-onset of LV systolic dysfunction or HF during preg-
nancy or within 6 months postpartum; (2) no other identi-
fiable cause for LV systolic dysfunction or HF; (3) no 
history of myocardial disease prior to onset; and (4) LVEF 
≤45%.
1265
In Japan, the incidence rate of peripartum cardiomy-
opathy has been reported to be 1 case per 20,000 deliver-
ies,
1268 one of the lowest in the world, likely influenced by 
genetic background, lifestyle, decreased fertility, and med-
ical environment.
1269 The etiology of peripartum cardiomy-
opathy remains unclear, although various hypotheses have 
been proposed. A recent study using animal models has 
highlighted the role of cleaved prolactin in vascular dys-
function as a potential contributor to peripartum cardio-
myopathy.
1270 Bromocriptine, which inhibits prolactin 
secretion, has been reported to be potentially effective in a 
small observational study and an RCT.
1270a,1270b In particu-
lar, antiprolactin therapy has shown promise for patients 
with LVEF <30% at diagnosis.
1270a However, bromocrip-
tine can cause vasospasm and hypertension, and is there-
fore not approved for use in pregnant women in the US. In 
Japan, its package inserts lists gestational hypertension 
(the greatest risk factor for peripartum cardiomyopathy) 
as a contraindication, necessitating cautious clinical judg-
ment. Peripartum cardiomyopathy is also associated with 
a high risk of intraventricular thrombus formation due to 
the combined effects of reduced systolic function and the 
hypercoagulable state of pregnancy.
1271 Therefore, unless 
contraindicated, anticoagulation is recommended for 
patients with severely reduced cardiac function. Because 
there is no evidence for direct oral anticoagulants in the 
setting of LV thrombosis, and their safety during preg-
nancy and lactation has not been established, they are not 
recommended. Warfarin is also contraindicated during 
pregnancy.
In the chronic phase after delivery, patients with HFrEF 
are treated with standard pharmacotherapy, including 
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, β-blockers, and diuretics. In Japan, 
approximately 60% of patients with peripartum cardiomy-
opathy recover normal cardiac function within 1 year, 
whereas approximately 10% either die or require listing for 
heart transplantation and the remaining 30% continue to 
have reduced cardiac dysfunction.
1268 There is no consen-
sus regarding the continuation of chronic HF treatment in 
patients with recovered cardiac function. Even if cardiac 
function is preserved after discontinuation, annual follow-
up for 10 years is recommended.
1272
There is no established consensus on the prognosis of 
subsequent pregnancies following peripartum cardiomy-
opathy. Given the high risk of subsequent pregnancy in 
women with persistent LV dysfunction, including the risk 
of maternal mortality, pregnancy is contraindicated. Preg-
nancy is not always safe even when LV function has nor-
malized, because the risk of recurrence of peripartum 
cardiomyopathy is high.1272 It is therefore imperative that 
women receive detailed counseling regarding the implica-
tions of future pregnancies.
8. Triglyceride Deposit  
Cardiomyovasculopathy
 ▋ 8.1 Pathology
Triglyceride deposit cardiomyovasculopathy (TGCV) 
(Orphanet ORPHA code: 692305) was first described in 
Japan.1273,1274 Long-chain fatty acids are an important 
energy source for living organisms, but in TGCV intracel-
lular lipolysis (breakdown) of long-chain triglyceride (TG) 
is impaired, which results in TG accumulation and defec-
tive release of long-chain fatty acids mainly in cardiomyo-
cytes and vascular smooth muscle cells. Patients with 
TGCV exhibit HF, coronary artery disease, and ventricu-
lar arrhythmia,.
1274–1277 TGCV is categorized as either pri-
mary (ORPHA code: 565612) or idiopathic subtype 
(ORPHA code: 692296). Primary TGCV is an autosomal 
recessive disorder caused by homozygous mutations in the 
patatin like phospholipase domain containing 2 (PNPLA2) 
gene encoding adipose triglyceride lipase, an enzyme essen-
tial for intracellular TG breakdown. In idiopathic TGCV, 
no PNPLA2 mutations are found, and the genetic back-
ground remains unknown. According to the Japan TGCV 
Study Group of the Ministry of Health, Labour and Wel-
fare, the cumulative number of diagnosed cases of TGCV 
as of October 2024 was 991 (15 primary and 976 idiopathic 
cases). Primary and idiopathic TGCV can present with 
either a dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy-like pro-
file.
1276
 ▋ 8.2 Diagnosis
Diagnostic criteria for TGCV have been established by the 
Japan TGCV Study Group  (Table 11).
1277
 ▋ 8.3 Treatment
Typically, TGCV is refractory to current medical and sur-
gical treatments. According to a registry survey conducted 
in Japan, the 5-year survival rate is approximately 70%,
