9. Cardio-Oncology
 ▋ 9.1  Trends in Cardio-Oncology and Basic Principles 
for the Management of Cardio-Oncological 
Diseases
  ▋ 9.1.1 What Is Cardio-Oncology?
Cancer survivors include not only individuals who have 
completed cancer treatment but also those currently under-
going treatment or under follow-up. Notably, 70% of can-
cer survivors are aged ≥ 65 years,1279,1280 placing them at 
increased risk of cardiovascular complications associated 
with cancer treatment. Compared with the general popula-
tion, cancer survivors have a higher incidence of cardiovas-
cular complications; in some cancer types, cardiovascular 
disease is the most frequent cause of death after cancer 
itself.
1281–1285
The field of cardio-oncology addresses a broad spectrum 
of cardiovascular complications affecting cancer survivors. 
In this guideline, we focus specifically on cancer therapy-
related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD), which is closely tied 
to HF.
  ▋ 9.1.2 Basic Principle of CTRCD Management
Various guidelines have proposed different definitions of 
CTRCD.2,4,1286,1287 In this guideline, CTRCD is defined as 
either the onset of symptomatic HF during cancer treat-
ment or imaging evidence of LV dysfunction (LVEF <50% 
with a ≥10% decrease from baseline). The development of 
CTRCD is a critical adverse prognostic factor for cancer 
survivors. In patients experiencing CTRCD, specialists 
from multiple disciplines (oncologists, cardiologists, and 
others) should collaborate to determine whether to con-
tinue or discontinue cancer therapy, balancing the cardio-
vascular risk against the risk of cancer progression if 
treatment is halted.
1288–1290 It is important to recognize that 
the current evidence regarding CTRCD primarily pertains 
to a limited range of agents and cancer types (e.g., anthra-
cyclines and anti-human epidermal growth factor receptor 
2 [HER2] antibodies).
 ▋ 9.2 Monitoring and Treatment of CTRCD
  ▋ 9.2.1 Risk Stratification and Monitoring
Before initiating cancer therapy that may carry cardiovas-
cular risks, a comprehensive cardiac evaluation, including 
ECG, echocardiography, and biomarker measurements 
(e.g. natriuretic peptides and troponin), should be consid-
ered in all patients. Surveillance strategies should be tai-
lored based on the type of anticancer agent and the 
patient’s clinical background, rather than uniformly 
applied to all cancer patients. Specific risk factors depend 
on the patient’s cardiovascular status and the treatment 
regimen. Risk stratification tools, such as the HFA-ICOS 
score,
1291 developed by the Heart Failure Association of 
the European Society of Cardiology Cardio-Oncology

high cardiotoxic risk, such as anthracyclines and anti-
HER2 antibodies, monitoring with echocardiograms and 
biomarker measurements during treatment may facilitate 
early detection of CTRCD. In particular, anthracyclines 
exhibit a dose-dependent increase in cardiovascular risk. A 
cumulative dose of 100–249 mg/m

echocardiography has gained attention as a sensitive 
parameter for detecting subclinical myocardial damage 
caused by anticancer agents and may be considered useful 
for the early detection and risk stratification of CTRCD.
1287
  ▋ 9.2.2 Prevention
Once symptomatic CTRCD develops, the prognosis is 
poor. It is therefore advisable to adopt preventive mea-
sures in high-risk individuals whenever possible. 1288,1296 
Meta-analyses have reported that although ACE inhibi-
tors/ARBs, β-blockers, and MRAs reduce the degree of 
LVEF decline in high-risk patients receiving potentially 
cardiotoxic therapies (e.g., anthracyclines, anti-HER2 
antibodies), clinical outcomes, such as worsening HF or 
mortality, may not show significant improvement. 1297–1301 
Recent studies suggest that SGLT2 inhibitors may lower 
the incidence of HF and improve prognosis following 
CTRCD in patients with diabetes receiving anthracy-
clines.
1302,1303
  ▋ 9.2.3 Treatment and Follow-up
No RCTs have specifically evaluated the effects of particu-
lar drugs on cardiac function or survival in patients who 
have already developed CTRCD. However, observational 
studies highlight the importance of early initiation of 
β-blockers and ACE inhibitors/ARBs.
1293,1294 Once CTRCD 
is diagnosed, discontinuing the causative agent is generally 
recommended, and guideline-directed HFrEF therapy, 
particularly ACE inhibitors/ARBs and β-blockers, should 
be considered. Recent observational and interventional 
studies have reported that cardiac rehabilitation for 
patients with CTRCD can improve cardiopulmonary func-
tion, symptoms, and outcomes.
1304–1306 Thus, cardiac reha-
bilitation should be considered in patients with CTRCD to 
enhance exercise capacity.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been associated 
with various cardiovascular adverse events, particularly 
myocarditis, which has a high fatality rate.
1307–1309 High-
dose corticosteroid therapy is a common treatment option 
in the management of severe myocarditis, and early admin-
istration of adequate doses may be linked to lower rates of 
major adverse cardiovascular events.
1310 Conversely, the 
recent increase in surveillance has demonstrated that non-
severe myocarditis may be more common than recognized 
and have a low risk of cardiovascular mortality.1311
In a large European study of 2,625 patients treated with 
anthracyclines, CTRCD developed in 9%, and 98% of 
those cases occurred within 1 year of therapy comple-
tion.1293 Therefore, in patients who have received highly 
cardiotoxic chemotherapy, it is advisable to perform fol-
low-up echocardiography and biomarker measurements 
within the first year after treatment. Moreover, among 
patients who receive significant cardiac radiation doses, 
long-term follow-up is warranted to detect late complica-
tions such as HF, valvular disease, and arrhythmias.

 ▋ 1.1 Coronary Artery Disease
The prognosis of patients with heart failure (HF) and con-
comitant coronary artery disease remains poor, 1313–1316 
regardless of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). 
Similarly, the prognosis of patients with coronary artery 
disease and concomitant HF is poor. However, early coro-
nary angiography and revascularization may improve out-
comes.
338 Thus, evaluation for coronary artery disease can 
be considered in patients with new-onset HF.
Optimal medical therapy has become essential for 
improving prognosis in patients with coronary artery dis-
ease.1318 In a subanalysis of the STICH trial, which exam-
ined the effect of coronary artery bypass grafting in HF 
with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), the use of optimal 
medical therapy was associated with a reduction in mortal-
ity, regardless of revascularization status.
1319 Therefore, 
optimal medical therapy (e.g., antiplatelet therapy and 
lipid-lowering agents) is recommended for patients with 
concomitant coronary artery disease and HF, similar to its 
use in stable coronary artery disease without HF.
 ▋ 1.2 Valvular Heart Disease
  ▋ 1.2.1  Recent Trends in Valvular Heart Disease and Basic 
Treatment Approach
In our aging society, the prevalence of aortic stenosis (AS) 
and mitral regurgitation (MR) is increasing; however, 
these conditions often remain underdiagnosed.
1320,1321
a. Valvular Abnormalities as the Primary Cause of HF
Severe valvular heart disease presenting with HF is an 
indication for surgical or transcatheter intervention. For 
moderate valvular heart disease accompanied by HF, val-
vular intervention is not currently indicated,
1322 and thus 
intensification of pharmacological therapy for HF remains 
the preferred treatment approach. Moderate mitral steno-
sis (mitral valve area 1.0–1.5 cm2) is an exception that may 
warrant valvular interventions because it can trigger HF 
even at moderate severity. For those patients with a dis-
crepancy between severity and symptoms, searching for 
non-valvular causes of HF, reassessing severity, and per-
forming exercise tests can be considered.
b.  Secondary Valvular Heart Disease Due to Structural 
Alterations in HF
Optimization of pharmacological therapy for HF should 
be prioritized before discussing the potential indications 
for valvular intervention or other non-pharmacological 
therapies, ideally in consultation with a heart team. In 
valvular heart disease with reduced systolic function, con-
tinuation and maximization of pharmacological therapy 
for HFrEF is crucial even after the interventions.
  ▋ 1.2.2 Aortic Stenosis
There is no pharmacological therapy to improve the prog-
nosis of severe AS, and non-pharmacological therapy 
remains the primary treatment approach (see Chapter VI). 
Diuretics may be used in patients deemed unsuitable for 
interventions due to poor general conditions. Nevertheless, 
it is difficult to improve the prognosis with pharmacologi-
cal therapy in patients with severe AS and low blood pres-
sure.
  ▋ 1.2.3 Aortic Regurgitation
The therapeutic principle for severe aortic regurgitation is 
to avoid delaying surgery due to pharmacological treat-
ment, although vasodilators and β -blockers may provide 
some benefit.
1323–1328 In aortic regurgitation with left ven-
tricular (LV) dysfunction, the use of angiotensin-convert-
ing enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor 
blockers (ARBs) can be considered. Patients with LV dys-
function prior to surgery may occasionally experience 
residual or recurrent LV dysfunction after surgery.
1329 For 
patients with residual or recurrent LV dysfunction, con-
tinuation of the guideline-recommended pharmacological 
therapy for HFrEF is recommended.

  ▋ 1.2.4 Mitral Regurgitation
a. Primary MR
In cases of severe primary MR, it is crucial to avoid delay-
ing surgery in favor of pharmacological treatment. How-
ever, if surgical or transcatheter treatment is denied due to 
the patient’s poor general condition, diuretics and vasodi-
lators may be used to improve symptoms.
b. Secondary (Functional) MR
i. Ventricular Functional MR
Because the primary pathophysiology of the disease lies 
within the LV, simply reducing regurgitation does not fully 
address the disease. Therefore, guideline-recommended 
pharmacological therapy for HFrEF is indicated.
1330,1331 
For LV dysfunction presenting after interventional ther-
apy, continuation of guideline-recommended pharmaco-
logical therapy for HFrEF is recommended.1332,1333
ii. Atrial Functional MR
In symptomatic atrial functional MR, pharmacological 
treatment for atrial fibrillation and HF is indicated.
  ▋ 1.2.5 Mitral Stenosis
Heart rate control is particularly important in patients 
with mitral stenosis because tachycardia shortens diastole, 
limiting adequate LV filling and increasing the pressure 
gradient between the left atrium and LV. Pharmacological 
treatment includes diuretics for congestion, β-blockers or 
calcium channel blockers for heart rate control, digitalis, 
and anticoagulation therapy. Although β -blockers are 
effective for heart rate control, their negative inotropic 
effects may worsen exercise tolerance in patients with sinus 
rhythm, which would require particular caution.
1334,1335
  ▋ 1.2.6 Tricuspid Regurgitation
With aging, the prevalence of tricuspid regurgitation (TR) 
associated with atrial fibrillation and device-related TR is 
increasing. TR is a prognostic determinant in many car-
diac diseases.
1336,1337 In patients with functional TR causing 
right-sided HF symptoms such as leg edema, organ con-
gestion, and ascites, the use of diuretics can be considered. 
Although the outcomes of surgery in advanced stages have 
been poor, there is a growing opinion that non-pharmaco-
logical treatment should be considered earlier (see Chapter 
VI for non-pharmacological therapies).
 ▋ 1.3 Arrhythmias and Conduction Disorders
  ▋ 1.3.1 Bradyarrhythmias
In cases of symptomatic bradycardia induced by guideline-
based medications (β -blockers or antiarrhythmic drugs) 
where dose reduction or discontinuation may pose a sig-
nificant disadvantage, permanent pacemaker implantation 
is an option. However, pacemaker implantation exclu -
sively for the prevention of bradycardia induced by 
β-blockers should be avoided.
Retrospective observational studies on patients with HF 
with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) without struc-
tural/functional heart disease who underwent permanent 
pacemaker implantation showed a decrease in LVEF over 
time in approximately 12–14% of patients, reporting high 
pacing dependency and left bundle branch block as risk 
factors for deterioration in systolic function.
1338,1339 It is 
important to note that the potential disadvantage of per-
manent pacemakers may present remotely after their 
implantation in patients with HFpEF. Clinical benefits of 
biventricular pacing (cardiac resynchronization therapy) 
or conduction system pacing (His bundle pacing or left 
bundle branch area pacing) are also gaining attention.

  ▋ 1.3.2 Ventricular Arrhythmias
In patients with ventricular fibrillation (VF) and sustained 
ventricular tachycardia (VT) with hemodynamic collapse, 
prompt electrical defibrillation should be performed, and 
intravenous administration of amiodarone or nifekalant 
can be considered to prevent the recurrence of ventricular 
arrhythmias.
1340,1341 Landiolol has demonstrated its efficacy 
in recurrent life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias resis-
tant to Class III antiarrhythmic drugs in the J-Land II trial 
conducted in Japan.1342
Indication of implantable cardioverter defibrillator 
(ICD) implantation for secondary prevention is referred to 
JCS/JHRS 2019 guideline on non-pharmacotherapy of 
cardiac arrhythmias.719,1344,1345 For patients with reduced 
systolic function, oral amiodarone in addition to β-blockers 
may be considered to prevent the recurrence of life-threat-
ening ventricular arrhythmias after ICD implantation.
1346 
If systolic function is preserved, oral sotalol may be con-
sidered.1347 Multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs) 
have reported the efficacy of catheter ablation, vs. amioda-
rone, in reducing the number of ICD shocks and prognos-
tic improvement in patients with reduced systolic function 
and experiencing electrical storms. Catheter ablation is 
recommended in drug-resistant cases.
1348,1349
Catheter ablation for frequent premature ventricular 
contractions with reduced systolic function is known to 
improve HF symptoms and LVEF, further preventing HF 
hospitalization.
1190,1351,1352 Based on these findings, catheter 
ablation is recommended for frequent (i.e., >10% of 24-h 
total heart beats) and monomorphic premature ventricular 
contractions that are potential causes of HF. Amiodarone 
can be considered for patients at high risk for catheter 
ablation or unsuccessful cases.
 ▋ 1.4 Hypertension
There is no definitive evidence regarding the optimal target 
blood pressure for patients with HFrEF and hypertension. 
The ACC/AHA hypertension guidelines recommend the 
treatment of hypertension in HFrEF to a target blood 
pressure of <130/80 mmHg.
1364 However, blood pressure 
should be managed individually based on the target levels 
for comorbid conditions, such as diabetes, chronic kidney 
disease (CKD), and coronary artery disease. 461 Impor-
tantly, blood pressure management in patients with 
HFrEF and hypertension should be considered an oppor-
tunity to intensify guideline-directed medical therapy 
(GDMT).
9
Similarly, definite evidence on treatment strategies in 
patients with HFpEF and hypertension is lacking. Hyper-
tension is one of the major underlying diseases of HFpEF 
and is strongly associated with worse clinical outcomes;1365 
therefore, blood pressure management is considered essen-
tial. Despite the lack of evidence demonstrating improved 
prognosis, both the US and Japanese clinical practice 
guidelines for the treatment of hypertension recommend 
managing systolic blood pressure (SBP) to a target of 
<130 mmHg.
461,1364 A meta-analysis of RCTs showed an 
association between SBP <130 mmHg and a reduction in 
HF hospitalization.1366 A subanalysis of the PARAGON-
HF trial reported that patients who achieved systolic blood 
pressure of 120–129 mmHg during the study period had 
the lowest incidence of cardiovascular death or HF hospi-
talization.
1367
Based on these findings, this guideline recommends a 
systolic blood pressure <130 mmHg for blood pressure 
management in patients with HFpEF. Importantly, 
patients with HFpEF are more likely to experience exces-
sive hypotension with vasodilators compared to patients 
with HFrEF.
1368 In a subanalysis of the PARAGON-HF 
trial, all-cause mortality was significantly increased in 
patients with HFpEF and SBP <120 mmHg compared to 
those who achieved SBP of 120–129 mmHg.
1367
2. Non-Cardiovascular Comorbidities
 ▋ 2.1 CKD and Cardiorenal Syndrome
  ▋ 2.1.1 Epidemiology
CKD is a common comorbidity in HF, affecting approxi-
mately 35–70% of patients.
1370 Renal function is one of the 
most powerful prognostic determinants in both acute and 
chronic HF.
1371
  ▋ 2.1.2  Pharmacological Management in Patients With HF 
and CKD

Receptor Blockers
Large-scale clinical trials that tested the efficacy of ACE 
inhibitors and ARBs in patients with HFrEF and Stage G3 
CKD demonstrated no significant interaction between 
renal function and the primary endpoints.
1372 However, no 
dedicated RCTs have specifically evaluated the efficacy of

ACE inhibitors or ARBs in patients with HF and CKD

comparable efficacy in this population,1373 the lack of high-
quality data from randomized trials limits the ability to 
draw definitive conclusions about their risk–benefit profile 
in advanced CKD.
b. Beta-Blockers
Unlike other drugs for HF, β-blockers are associated with 
a lower risk of initial renal function decline or long-term 
renal impairment. Notably, compared with placebo, 
β-blockers significantly reduced all-cause mortality in 
patients with HF with mildly reduced ejection fraction 
(HFmrEF) and HFrEF with CKD Stages G3.
1374 A small 
RCT demonstrated that oral carvedilol significantly 
improved survival in patients with HFrEF on dialysis;1375 
however, no such benefit was observed in patients with 
HFpEF.
1374,1376–1378
c. Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibitors
In addition to reducing the risk of cardiovascular events, 
cardiovascular death, or HF hospitalization, angiotensin 
receptor–neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs) are known to sig-
nificantly lower the risk of renal composite events (≥ 50% 
decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], pro-
gression to end-stage renal disease, or death from renal 
disease), and decelerated the decline in renal func-
tion.
1379–1381 However, in the UK Heart and Renal Protec-
tion III (HARP-III) trial, a double-blind study that 
primarily randomized patients with eGFR of 20–60 mL/
min/1.73 m
2 to ARNI or irbesartan, ARNI demonstrated 
neutral effects on renal function and albuminuria com-
pared with irbesartan.
1382 Moreover, previous large-scale 
clinical trials excluded patients with CKD Stages G4 and 
G5 due to concerns about the potential risk of drug accu-
mulation with ARNI.
d. Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) improve 
outcomes in patients with HFrEF regardless of the presence 
or absence of CKD, up to Stage G3.
500,516,1383,1384 However, 
because large-scale clinical trials that focused on patients 
with HF excluded those with CKD Stages G4 and G5, there 
is limited evidence for this population.
1387 Recently, the 
third-generation non-steroidal MRAs esaxerenone and 
finerenone were approved for use in patients with CKD and 
hypertension (esaxerenone) and in those with CKD and 
type 2 diabetes (finerenone). Specifically, in The Finerenone 
in Chronic Kidney Disease and Type 2 Diabetes: Combined 
FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD Trial Programme 
Analysis (FIDELITY), a prespecified pooled analysis of the 
phase III FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD trials in 
patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, finerenone reduced 
the composite cardiovascular endpoint by 14% and hospi-
talization for HF by 22% compared with placebo. In addi-
tion, finerenone reduced the renal composite endpoint by 
23% compared with placebo.
481 A comprehensive meta-
analysis further demonstrated that the use of MRAs reduced 
both all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in patients 
undergoing routine dialysis.1389
e. Sodium–Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors
Sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors sig-
nificantly reduced the composite endpoint of HF hospital-
ization or cardiovascular death in patients with HF and 
CKD.1390 For individual endpoints, SGLT2 inhibitors 
demonstrated a significant reduction in HF hospitaliza-
tions, although they did not achieve statistical significance 
for cardiovascular death, despite a favorable trend. 1390 
These benefits were consistent across patients with and 
without CKD.1390 Of note, the DAPA-HF trial excluded 
individuals with an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, 
whereas the DELIVER trial excluded those with an eGFR

 ▋ 2.2 Anemia and Iron Metabolism
  ▋ 2.2.1 Pathophysiology
Anemia in HF involves a diverse pathophysiology of iron 
deficiency, renal dysfunction, inflammation, and hemodi-
lution due to fluid retention. In particularly, iron defi-
ciency, commonly observed in patients with HF, plays an 
essential role as a primary cause of anemia. Notably, iron 
deficiency is associated with HF symptoms, reduced exer-
cise tolerance, and an increased risk of HF hospitalization 
and mortality, regardless of the presence of anemia.
1397 
Therefore, screening for iron status is imperative in the 
management of comorbidities in HF. Commonly, iron 
deficiency in patients with HF is defined as serum ferritin 
<100 ng/mL or serum ferritin 100–300 ng/mL and transfer-
rin saturation (TSAT) <20%.
662–664,1398–1403
  ▋ 2.2.2 Treatment
a. Iron Supplementation
A meta-analysis including the Ferinject Assessment in 
Patients with Iron Deficiency and Chronic Heart Failure 
(FAIR-HF), Ferric Carboxymaltose Evaluation on Perfor-
mance in Patients With Iron Deficiency in Combination 
With Chronic Heart Failure (CONFIRM-HF), A Ran-
domised, Double-blind Placebo Controlled Trial Compar-
ing the Effect of Intravenous Ferric Carboxymaltose on 
Hospitalizations and Mortality in Iron Deficient Subjects 
Admitted for Acute Heart Failure (AFFIRM-AHF), and 
Effectiveness of Intravenous Iron Treatment vs. Standard 
Care in Patients with Heart Failure and Iron Deficiency 
(IRONMAN) trials showed that intravenous iron supple-
mentation improved the composite endpoint of HF rehos-
pitalization and cardiovascular death in patients with 
HFrEF and HFmrEF with iron deficiency, regardless of 
the presence of anemia.
1400–1402 However, the subsequent 
Randomized Placebo-controlled Trial of FCM as Treat-
ment for Heart Failure With Iron Deficiency/and Sub-
Study (HEART-FID; 3,065 patients with LVEF ≤40%) did 
not show any efficacy of intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 
in the hierarchical composite primary endpoint of 
12-month all-cause mortality, HF hospitalization, and 
6-min walk distance (6MWD) at 6 months, nor in the sec-
ondary endpoint of reduction in HF hospitalization.
1403 A 
meta-analysis including HEART-FID reported a more 
pronounced effect of intravenous iron in reducing cardio-
vascular events in patients with TSAT <15–20%.
1404 Fur-
ther prospective clinical trials are needed, including a 
re-evaluation of the criteria for defining iron deficiency to 
optimize the efficacy of intravenous iron therapy.1405 Con-
[[p92]]
Circulation Journal Vol.89, August 2025
1366
KITAI T et al.
versely, in the Oral Iron Repletion Effects on Oxygen 
Uptake in Heart Failure (IRONOUT-HF) trial in HFrEF 
with iron deficiency, high-dose oral iron supplementation 
(iron polysaccharide for 16 weeks) demonstrated limited 
improvement in iron deficiency and no improvement in 
exercise capacity.
1406 It remains uncertain whether other 
oral iron agents or prolonged administration can achieve 
comparable effects to intravenous iron. The Effect of IV 
Iron in Patients With Heart Failure With Preserved Ejec-
tion Fraction (FAIR-HFpEF; NCT03074591) and Impact 
of Intravenous Iron Repletion on Mechanisms of Exercise 
Intolerance in HFpEF (IRONMET-HFpEF; NCT04945707) 
trials, which are examining the effects of iron supplementa-
tion in patients with HFpEF, are currently ongoing.
Iron overload is known to be associated with oxidative 
stress and malignancy.
1407,1408 A comprehensive assessment 
of optimal iron supplementation should be made through 
regular checks on blood counts and iron status.
b. Red Blood Cell Transfusion
In critically ill patients who are hemodynamically stable, 
those who have recently undergone cardiac surgery, or 
those with cardiovascular diseases, red blood cell transfu-
sion is known to be beneficial when hemoglobin levels are 
less than 7.0–8.0 g/dL.
1409,1410
Conversely, in the Myocardial Ischemia and Transfu-
sion (MINT) trial, a large-scale randomized double-blind 
study that investigated the optimal threshold of blood 
hemoglobin levels for red blood cell transfusion in acute 
myocardial infarction patients with anemia, no statistically 
significant difference was observed between a higher trans-
fusion threshold (e.g., hemoglobin <10.0 g/dL) and a lower 
transfusion threshold (e.g., hemoglobin <7.0–8.0 g/dL).
1411 
However, the group with a hemoglobin threshold of 
<10.0 g/dL tended to have a lower risk of death or myocar-
dial infarction compared with the group with a threshold 
of 7.0–8.0 g/dL.1411
c. Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents
In the Reduction of Events by Darbepoetin Alfa in Heart 
Failure (RED-HF) trial,
1412 a large-scale randomized, dou-
ble-blind trial examining the efficacy of anemia treatment 
with the erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) darbepo-
etin alfa targeting a hemoglobin level of 13 g/dL in patients 
with HFrEF and hemoglobin levels between 9 and 12 g/dL, 
no improvement in all-cause mortality or rate of hospital-
ization for worsening HF was observed with darbepoetin 
alfa compared with placebo. Furthermore, thromboembo-
lism was observed as a complication in the ESA group. 
Therefore, the administration of an ESA with the aim of 
preventing cardiovascular events by improving anemia is 
not recommended in patients with HF unless specific indi-
cations for an ESA exist beyond HF.
d. Hypoxia-Inducible Factor–Prolyl Hydroxylase Inhibitors
The improvement in hemoglobin levels in patients with 
CKD in the non-dialysis phase or on dialysis with hypoxia-
inducible factor–prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors has been 
proven to be non-inferior to that of conventional recombi-
nant human erythropoietin agents.
1412a–1412e However, evi-
dence regarding the efficacy of hypoxia-inducible 
factor–prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors in patients with HF 
has not been fully established. Future accumulation of 
clinical evidence is anticipated.
 ▋ 2.3 Electrolyte Abnormalities
  ▋ 2.3.1 HF and Electrolyte Abnormalities
Patients with HF are susceptible to electrolyte abnormali-
ties due to various organ dysfunctions and polyphar-
macy.1413–1419 A U-shaped relationship between serum 
potassium levels and mortality has been observed, with 
both hyperkalemia and hypokalemia associated with 
increased mortality risk. Serum potassium levels in range 
4–5 mEq/L are associated with the lowest risk of mortal-
ity.
1416–1418
  ▋ 2.3.2 Hyperkalemia
Studies have demonstrated a link between hyperkalemia 
and an increased risk of arrhythmias, hospitalization, and 
mortality,588,1420–1424 which often results in the underuse 
(including dose reduction and/or shortened treatment 
duration) of renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system 
(RAAS) inhibitors (ARNI/ACE inhibitors/ARBs and 
MRAs).
1418,1425,1426 Conversely, some reports suggest reduc-
ing the dose or discontinuing RAAS inhibitors in patients 
with HF due to hyperkalemia is associated with a higher 
risk of subsequent cardiovascular events. 1417,1427–1429 This 
observation indicates that the underdosing of RAAS 
inhibitors could be a potential prognostic indicator in 
patients with HF and hyperkalemia. When hyperkalemia 
is detected in patients taking RAAS inhibitors through 
routine monitoring, imminent intervention with potassium 
binders can be useful in optimizing the use of RAAS inhib-
itors (Figure 19).
1430–1432 Recent studies indicate that the use 
of ARNI and SGLT2 inhibitors is associated with a lower 
risk of hyperkalemia compared with earlier or more con-
ventional regimens without these agents.1433,1434
The effectiveness of new non-polymer gastrointestinal 
potassium binders (patiromer [approved but not yet mar-
keted in Japan] and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate [SZC])

  ▋ 2.3.3 Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia is commonly defined as a serum potassium 
level <3.5 mEq/L.
1441 The most common cause of hypoka-
lemia in patients with HF is drug-induced hypokalemia 
related to loop or thiazide diuretics. Approximately 
40–60% of patients with hypokalemia are known to have

  ▋ 2.3.4 Hyponatremia
Hyponatremia is observed in approximately 20–30% of 
patients hospitalized with acute HF, and is associated with 
an increased risk of HF hospitalization and death.52,1414,1443–1446 
Selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonists (tolvaptan) 
block the V2 receptor, inhibiting arginine vasopressin bind-
ing, limiting water reabsorption, and increasing serum 
sodium concentrations. Continuation of tolvaptan initi-
ated during hospitalization for acute HF showed a long-
term reduction in loop diuretic dose.
1447 However, its 
impact on long-term prognosis remains unknown. A few 
case reports suggest that hypertonic saline administration 
with loop diuretics may be associated with an increase in 
serum sodium levels and diuretic effects.
1448,1449
  ▋ 2.3.5 Hypochloremia
Hypochloremia is commonly defined as a serum chloride 
level <96 mEq/L.1419,1450 In patients with HF, hypochlore-
mia is a prognostic predictor of all-cause mortality inde-
pendent of hyponatremia.
1451–1454 Hypochloremia is 
associated with RAAS activation and resistance to loop 
diuretics.
1455 Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazol-
amide) promote chloride reabsorption and the secretion of 
bicarbonate and sodium in the proximal tubule, exhibiting 
a diuretic effect. In an RCT in patients with acute HF with 
fluid retention (ADVOR trial), acetazolamide administra-
tion improved short-term congestion,
958 but its effect on 
prognosis remains uncertain.
 ▋ 2.4 Diabetes
  ▋ 2.4.1 HF and Diabetes
Diabetes is closely associated with the onset of HF, 
whereas HF serves as one of the important prognostic 
determinants in individuals with glucose metabolism dis-
orders.
1457,1458
  ▋ 2.4.2 Treatment of Diabetes and HF
The impact of intensive glycemic control on cardiovascular 
outcomes in patients with diabetes and HF remains con-
troversial.1459,1460 This is presumably due to overactivation 
of the sympathetic nervous system and inflammation trig-
gered by hypoglycemia, leading to the unfavorable cardio-
vascular effects.1461
a. Biguanides
Studies in Europe and the US have demonstrated that 
biguanides reduce HF hospitalization and mortality in 
patients with diabetes and HF.
468,469,1462–1466 However, in 
Japan, biguanides are contraindicated in patients with 
decompensated HF, severe renal impairment (eGFR 
<30 mL/min/1.73 m2), or those receiving routine dialysis.
b. Thiazolidinediones
Although there are no reports of cardiac dysfunction or 
myocardial injury associated with thiazolidinediones, they 
are contraindicated in patients with symptomatic HF due 
to their potential to induce fluid retention through 
increased sodium reabsorption in the kidneys.
1467–1469
c. Sulfonylureas
Although sulfonylureas have not been shown to have 
direct adverse cardiac effects in patients with diabetes and 
HF, caution is warranted given their potential to induce 
hypoglycemia and weight gain.
d.  Incretin-Related Drugs (Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 
Inhibitors, Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists)
In cardiovascular outcome trials, dipeptidyl peptidase 
(DPP)-4 inhibitors exhibited non-inferiority to placebo in 
the secondary endpoint of HF hospitalization, regardless 
of prior history of HF hospitalization.
1470–1473 These find-
ings implied that DPP-4 inhibitors were a reasonable ther-
apeutic option for managing diabetes and HF. 1470–1472 
However, in the Does Saxagliptin Reduce the Risk of 
Cardiovascular Events When Used Alone or Added to 
Other Diabetes Medications (SAVOR-TIMI 53) trial,
1474 
saxagliptin increased the risk of HF hospitalization com-
pared with placebo. Therefore, DPP-4 inhibitors should be 
used with caution in patients with New York Heart Asso-
ciation (NYHA) Class III-IV or moderate to severe renal 
impairment.
A meta-analysis of 7 cardiovascular outcome trials 
investigating glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor 
agonists demonstrated a significant reduction in the risk 
of HF hospitalization in the GLP-1 receptor agonist 
group.
1475 However, individual trials, with the exception of 
the Harmony Outcome trial (which investigated albiglu-
tide, a drug not approved in Japan), did not show a sig-
nificant reduction in the risk of HF hospitalization.1475 In 
addition, in the Functional Impact of GLP-1 for Heart 
Failure Treatment (FIGHT) trial, which evaluated liraglu-
tide in patients with HFrEF hospitalized for acute HF,1476 
the liraglutide group exhibited a trends toward an 
increased risk of HF hospitalization in patients with diabe-
tes. Conversely, the Research Study to Look at How Well 
Semaglutide Works in People Living With Heart Failure, 
Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes (STEP-HFpEF DM), pub-
lished in 2024, demonstrated that in patients with HFpEF 
and type 2 diabetes and a body mass index (BMI) of 
≥30 kg/m
2, treatment with 2.4 mg semaglutide resulted in 
significant improvements in HF-related symptoms and 
physical limitations, along with weight reduction, com-
pared with placebo.
655
e. SGLT2 Inhibitors
SGLT2 inhibitors have been shown to significantly reduce 
HF hospitalization rates among patients with diabetes at 
elevated cardiovascular risk, independent of pre-existing HF 
status or LVEF.
467–469,1478 However, these trials included a

placebo. In the EMPULSE-HF trial,
1482 the initiation of 
empagliflozin after stabilization of hospitalized acute HF 
(either new-onset or decompensated chronic HF) resulted 
in a significant reduction in the primary endpoint (a com-
posite of all-cause mortality, HF events, time to first HF 
event, and symptoms at 90 days after treatment) among 
patients with diabetes.
Based on these findings, SGLT2 inhibitors can be initi-
ated at any given time point, ranging from the post-stabi-
lization phase of acute HF to the later, chronic phases. 
Although some evidence supports the efficacy and safety of 
SGLT2 inhibitors in older individuals with increased 
frailty,
593,1483 significant variability exists, warranting care-
ful consideration on a case-by-case basis.
 ▋ 2.5 Obesity
  ▋ 2.5.1 Risk of Developing HF
Obesity is an important risk factor and comorbidity for 
HF.
1484,1485 Despite younger age, patients with obesity with 
HFpEF have reduced quality of life and exercise capacity, 
distinct features such as enhanced interventricular interac-
tion and right heart remodeling, and a higher risk of HF 
hospitalization than non-obese patients.
19,1484–1487 Patients 
with obesity often have lower natriuretic peptide levels, 
leading to an underdiagnosis of HF.19,120 Even echocardio-
graphic parameters such as left atrial volume index and the 
E/e′ ratio may underestimate the severity of HF in patients 
with obesity.
19,66,120,1487–1489
  ▋ 2.5.2 Therapeutic Interventions
a.  GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Dual GIP/GLP-1 Receptor 
Agonists
The GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide has demonstrated 
a significant effect on weight reduction. In the STEP-
HFpEF trial, which enrolled patients who had HF with an 
LVEF ≥45% and a BMI ≥30 kg/m
2 without diabetes, once-
weekly subcutaneous administration of 2.4 mg semaglutide 
for 52 weeks improved HF-related symptoms, physical 
limitations (as measured with the Kansas City Cardiomy-
opathy Questionnaire clinical summary score [KCCQ-
CSS]), and 6MWD compared with placebo.
654 The 
STEP-HFpEF DM trial reported that semaglutide 
improved KCCQ-CSS and reduced body weight compared 
with placebo in obese patients with HFpEF (LVEF ≥45%, 
BMI ≥30 kg/m
2) and type 2 diabetes. 655 In the SELECT 
trial, semaglutide reduced both the composite endpoint 
and all-cause mortality by approximately 20% compared 
with placebo in overweight or obese non-diabetic adults 
with a history of cardiovascular disease.
1491 In a subanaly-
sis of the SELECT trial, semaglutide reduced the risk of 
all-cause death or composite endpoint in patients with a 
history of HF, regardless of HFrEF or HFpEF.
1492 Dual 
glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 
receptor agonists are available for patients with diabetes in 
clinical practice. In a Study of Tirzepatide (LY3298176) in 
Participants With Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection 
Fraction (HFpEF) and Obesity (SUMMIT), once-weekly 
subcutaneous administration of tirzepatide in patients with 
HFpEF and obesity (LVEF ≥ 50%, BMI ≥ 30 kg/m
2) 
reduced the composite outcome of cardiovascular death, 
worsening HF, and HF-related symptoms.1493
Inappropriate use of semaglutide as a casual weight-loss 
drug has led to the announcement of guidelines for the 
appropriate use of semaglutide (recombinant) in Japan, 
providing instructions on the appropriate use of semaglu-
tide for the treatment of medically complicated obesity.
b. SGLT2 Inhibitors
The SGLT2 inhibitors empagliflozin and dapagliflozin are

 ▋ 2.6 Dyslipidemia
Dyslipidemia is one of the important comorbidities of 
HF.46 The Controlled Rosuvastatin Multinational Trial in 
Heart Failure (CORONA), which investigated the effects 
of rosuvastatin on reducing cardiovascular events in 
patients with HF due to ischemic heart disease, did not 
show any effect of rosuvastatin in reducing cardiovascular 
death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or non-fatal 
stroke.
1494 The GISSI-HF trial, which included patients 
with HF with both ischemic and non-ischemic heart dis-
ease, also failed to demonstrate any prognostic improve-
ment with rosuvastatin.1495 Therefore, there is no sufficient 
evidence to recommend the use of statins to improve the 
prognosis of HF.
The GISSI-HF trial did demonstrate the benefit of n-3 
polyunsaturated fatty acids (a combination of eicosapen-
taenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid) on all-cause and 
cardiovascular mortality in patients with chronic HF com-
pared with placebo.
613 However, the magnitude of the 
effect was relatively small, and there was no significant 
effect on stroke or myocardial infarction. The n-3 polyun-
saturated fatty acids are not currently recommended for 
patients with HF.
 ▋ 2.7 Hyperuricemia and Gout
  ▋ 2.7.1 Pathophysiology
In Japan, hyperuricemia is prevalent in 56% of patients 
with chronic HF, 1497 and is a poor prognostic factor for 
HF in both HFrEF and HFpEF. 1498,1499 In particular, 
serum uric acid levels ≥9.5 mg/dL are known to be a poten-
tial prognostic marker in patients with HF.1498
  ▋ 2.7.2 Treatment
There is currently no clear evidence that hyperuricemia-
targeted management improves the prognosis of HF. Low-
ering serum uric acid levels with allopurinol, a xanthine 
oxidase inhibitor, did not reduce hospitalization for car-
diovascular disease or all-cause mortality in patients with 
HF.
1500,1501 Patients receiving febuxostat, another xanthine 
oxidase inhibitor, had a higher mortality rate than those 
receiving allopurinol in the Cardiovascular Safety of 
Febuxostat and Allopurinol in Participants With Gout 
and Cardiovascular Comorbidities (CARES) trial,
1502 
which studied patients with gout and cardiovascular dis-
eases, including HF. However, dropouts and treatment 
discontinuations may have affected these results.1502 Sub-
sequently, the Febuxostat versus Allopurinol Streamlined 
(FAST) trial, which included patients with gout and car-
diovascular risk factors, showed that febuxostat had a 
similar safety profile to allopurinol.
1503 Therefore, in 
patients with HF, treatment of hyperuricemia is not rec-
ommended to improve prognosis or prevent cardiovascu-
lar events. However, therapeutic interventions may be 
considered to prevent a decline in renal function and the 
new onset of gout.
1504–1512 Further research is needed to 
establish the target level of serum uric acid for the manage-
ment of hyperuricemia in patients with HF, although a 
target level of ≤6.0 mg/dL is widely accepted, in line with 
guidelines for the management of hyperuricemia and gout.
 ▋ 2.8  Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and 
Asthma
  ▋ 2.8.1 Epidemiology, Pathophysiology, and Evaluation
In Japan, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) 
and asthma are seen in 4.2–14.4% of patients with 
HF.531,1035,1513–1515 The coexistence of COPD with HF is 
associated with increased mortality. 1516,1517 Similarly, the 
prognosis of COPD/asthma is worsened by the comorbid 
HF.1518,1519 Further, COPD/asthma can precede right HF 
and Group 3 pulmonary hypertension. In patients with 
HFrEF and COPD or asthma, measurement of B-type 
natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal pro B-type natri-
uretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is helpful to support the diag-
nosis of HF.
1520–1522
  ▋ 2.8.2 Treatment
a. Treatment of HF With Comorbid COPD or Asthma
Standardized therapies for HFrEF, such as diuretics, 
renin–angiotensin system inhibitors, and β -blockers, are 
well tolerated in patients with comorbid COPD.1521,1523,1524 
Beta-blockers are known to improve prognosis in patients 
with HF and comorbid COPD.585,1525–1527 Nevertheless, the 
use of non-cardioselective β -blockers in patients with 
asthma and cardiovascular diseases including HF may be 
associated with exacerbation of asthma. 1528 Therefore,

 ▋ 2.9 Sleep-Disordered Breathing
The critical and predominant manifestation of sleep-disor-
dered breathing (SDB) is sleep apnea. Active screening for 
SDB is recommended when the medical therapy for HF is 
deemed insufficient, because symptoms of SDB, such as 
excessive daytime sleepiness, are often masked in patients 
with HF.
1533 Sleep apnea is defined by an apnea–hypopnea 
index (AHI) of ≥ 5, defined as the number of apneas and 
hypopneas per hour of sleep.
  ▋ 2.9.1 Pathophysiology
SDB is prevalent in approximately 60–70% of patients with 
HF, regardless of LV systolic function.
1533a SDB is classi-
fied into obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and central sleep 
apnea (CSA). CSA with a Cheyne–Stokes respiration pat-
tern is commonly termed CSA-CSR (CSA with Cheyne–
Stokes respiration). Polysomnography is used to diagnose 
SDB definitively.
1533,1534 OSA is primarily a risk factor for 
HF, whereas CSA is considered a consequence of HF.1533a
  ▋ 2.9.2 Treatment
a. Treatment of OSA Complicating HF
The correction of lifestyle or behaviors that are risk factors 
for OSA is also beneficial for the treatment of HF. Pro-
grams integrating dietary management, increased physical 
activity, aerobic exercise, cognitive behavioral therapy, 
and sleep hygiene education have been proposed.
1535 In 
addition, the use of benzodiazepines should be avoided, 
and the use of non-benzodiazepine hypnotics or orexin 
receptor antagonists should be considered.1534
For OSA in patients with HFrEF, continuous positive 
airway pressure (CPAP) has been suggested to improve 
AHI1536 and LVEF,1537 in addition to improving symptoms 
and exercise tolerance. No large-scale clinical trials for 
patients with HF and OSA have been conducted to evalu-
ate the prognostic improvement of CPAP therapy, 
although some studies suggest potential for improvement 
in survival.
1538,1539 CPAP therapy is generally considered 
effective when used for ≥4 h.1540–1542
For OSA in patients with HFpEF, the evidence is insuf-
ficient. However, the pathogenesis of HFpEF, including 
LV hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and comorbidities, 
is closely associated with SDB; therefore, CPAP is recom-
mended to improve OSA. In addition, CPAP may improve 
structural cardiac abnormalities even in patients with OSA 
without clinically significant cardiovascular diseases. 
Therefore, in patients with HFpEF and moderate or severe 
OSA, CPAP may be beneficial in improving symptoms,

b. Treatment of CSA (CSA-CSR) Complicating HF
CSA is considered a consequence of HF, and optimization 
of GDMT for HF is recommended. In cases where CSA-
CSR persists despite optimal medical therapy, positive 
airway pressure may be considered.
In patients with CSA-CSR in HFrEF, CPAP has been 
shown to improve symptoms, exercise tolerance, and LV 
function,
1544,1545 but not to improve survival. Adaptive 
servo-ventilation (ASV), used for CSR characterized by 
periodic cycles of hyperpnea and apnea, is expected to 
stabilize tidal volume and respiratory rate by adjusting the 
pressure support based on the patient’s respiratory pat-
tern.
1534 However, a large-scale clinical trial (Treatment of 
Predominant Central Sleep Apnoea by Adaptive Servo 
Ventilation in Patients With Heart Failure [SERVE-HF]), 
which investigated the effects of ASV in addition to 
GDMT for patients with HFrEF (LVEF ≤45%) and pre-
dominant CSA, showed no significant difference in the 
primary endpoint, a composite of cardiovascular events 
including death from any cause, lifesaving cardiovascular 
intervention, or unplanned hospitalization for worsening 
HF, between the intervention and control groups.
1546 Sec-
ondary endpoints, including all-cause and cardiovascular 
mortality, were significantly higher in the ASV group.1546
In the Japanese Randomized Controlled Study of Adap-
tive-servo Ventilator in Patients With Congestive Heart 
Failure: Confirmatory Trial of Efficacy on Cardiac Func-
tion (SAVIOR-C),
1547 published in 2015, the effect of ASV 
therapy on improvement in systolic function was investi-
gated in patients with HFrEF regardless of comorbid 
SDB. Despite no significant difference in the improvement 
in LV systolic function between the intervention and con-
trol groups, significant improvements in the secondary 
endpoints of NYHA class and activities of daily living 
(ADL) were observed in the ASV compared with control 
group. Therefore, in 2016, the Japanese Circulation Soci-
ety and Japanese Heart Failure Society issued a joint state-
ment stating that the use of ASV in patients with LVEF 
<45% and predominant CSA should be considered with 
great caution. They recommended that ASV should be 
introduced only when CPAP is ineffective in improving 
sleep apnea or when patients are intolerant to CPAP.
In a subgroup of patients with predominant CSA from 
the Effect of Adaptive Servo Ventilation (ASV) on Sur-
vival and Hospital Admissions in Heart Failure 
(ADVENT-HF) trial published in 2023,
1548 the ASV group 
showed no significant difference in the primary endpoint of 
the composite of all-cause death, cardiovascular hospital-
ization, new-onset atrial fibrillation/flutter, and appropri-
ate defibrillator therapy, or in all-cause mortality, 
compared with control groups. However, quality of life 
was significantly improved in the ASV group.
1548 Taking 
into account the results of the SERVE-HF trial, ASV use 
should not be continued indefinitely after stabilization of 
HF. Despite lacking evidence of prognostic benefit, home 
oxygen therapy (HOT) is known to improve symptoms 
and LVEF.
1549,1550
The treatment strategy for CSA-CSR in HFpEF has not 
been established. No studies have specifically investigated 
the use of CPAP in this population. A randomized study 
that used CPAP or ASV for SDB in HFpEF showed a 
reduction in all-cause mortality and improvements in right 
ventricular function and 6MWD.
1542 However, that study 
was not limited to CSA-CSR, and in patients with CSA-
CSR, ASV was mostly used instead of CPAP. The Cardio-
vascular Improvements With MV ASV Therapy in Heart 
Failure (CAT-HF) study,
628 which examined the effect of 
ASV for SDB in patients hospitalized with acute decom-
pensated HF (ADHF), investigated the effect of ASV spe-
cifically in HFpEF. The composite endpoint of death at 6 
months, hospitalization for cardiovascular events, and 
change in 6MWD was more favorable in the ASV group.
628 
However, the study did not indicate whether CSA-CSR 
was predominant in the HFpEF group. In addition, a 
Japanese study showed that in patients with HFpEF, the 
ASV group had fewer composite endpoints of death and 
worsening HF compared with the control group in a group 
of patients with predominant CSA-CSR;
1551 nevertheless, 
CSA-CSR was not an inclusion criterion of that study. 
SAVIOR-L (Prospective Cohort Study of Adaptive Servo-
Ventilation Therapy on Prognosis in Repeatedly Hospital-
ized Patients With Chronic Heart Failure: Longitudinal 
Observational Study of Effects on Re-Admission and Mor-
tality), a Japanese multicenter study that examined the 
effects of ASV therapy in patients with both HFpEF and 
HFrEF, failed to demonstrate the superiority of ASV ther-
apy over non-ASV therapy.
1552 Therefore, in the absence of 
sufficient evidence, and in accordance with the guidelines 
for SDB,1534 CPAP therapy should precede ASV therapy. 
Further evidence is awaited.
 ▋ 2.10  Depression, Cognitive Impairment, and 
Mental and Psychosocial Issues
  ▋ 2.10.1 Depression and Anxiety
Depression is known as one of the most common comor-
bidities and prognostic determinants in patients with HF, 
reportedly experienced by 36.2% of patients.9 Psychosocial 
interventions, pharmacotherapy, disease management pro-
grams, exercise therapy, cardiac rehabilitation, group sup-
port, and mindfulness-based psychotherapy improve 
mental health, alleviate psychosocial distress, enhance 
wellbeing, promote self-management, improve cardiovas-
cular risk factors, and reduce cardiovascular events, 
including all-cause mortality.
1563–1574
To screen for depression, questionnaires such as the 
Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ)-2 may be recom-

  ▋ 2.10.2 Cognitive Impairment (Including Delirium)
Cognitive impairment is known as one of the most com-
mon comorbidities and prognostic determinants in patients 
with HF.9 Cognitive impairment is highly prevalent in HF, 
??QT–VTD??M?l??L
ment and overt dementia are found in 24% and 15% of 
patients with HF, respectively.1575,1576
Overall, 17% of elderly patients with acute HF have 
comorbid delirium.1577 Delirium may be associated with 
dementia in the long term,1578 and has also been suggested 
to be associated with an increased risk of mortality, 1577 
rehospitalization, and prolonged hospital stay in patients 
with HF. Timely assessment is essential, 1577,1579,1580 and 
early mobilization and environmental adjustments are 
important for preventing delirium.
1581
  ▋ 2.10.3  Psychological Stress and Other Mental and 
Psychosocial Issues to Consider
Psychological stress is known as a risk factor for coronary 
artery disease. A combination of training for stress man-
agement and exercise therapy has been shown to reduce 
composite cardiovascular events, including all-cause mor-
tality.
1570
XI. Disease Management
PM?l?hK?o?
Education, and Self-Care
 ▋ 1.1  Heart Failure Management by  
a Multidisciplinary Team
In recent years, the aging population of heart failure (HF) 
patients has led to increasingly diverse and complex chal-
lenges in HF management.
1585,1586 There is an increasing 
need for a multidisciplinary approach to address the 
diverse needs of HF patients.
1587 Multidisciplinary team 
approach is crucial, because it has been shown to reduce 
hospitalizations and mortality associated with worsening 
HF, and to improve patients’ quality of life 
(QOL).
1040,1048,1053–1055,1588–1593 However, this approach is not 
a one-size-fits-all intervention, but requires patient-
centered, care tailored to each person’s unique needs.2
 ▋ 1.2 Patient Education and Self-Care
A key component of HF management programs is educa-
tion and support to improve self-care.1595–1598 Poor self-care 
practices, such as inadequate salt and fluid management, 
non-adherence to medications, a lack of regular exercise, 
and inadequate infection prevention, significantly increase 
the risk of HF exacerbations.
887,1026,1034 Meta-analyses have 
demonstrated that HF management programs that focus 
on improving self-care reduce the risk of hospitalization 
and mortality,1599–1603 while also improving QOL.1600,1602 In 
Japan, it has also been suggested that self-care support 
improves outcomes for HF patients.1048,1592,1604
  ▋ 1.2.1 Effective Education to Improve Self-Care
Patient education should be provided collaboratively by a 
multidisciplinary team using educational materials and 
taking into account the patient’s level of understanding 
and health literacy.
1599,1605,1606 The “teach-back” method, in 
which patients or their families explain back the informa-
tion provided by healthcare professionals, is useful in 
assessing understanding.1607 The patient and family should 
be encouraged to work together to promote behavior 
change. The effectiveness of education using self-efficacy 
enhancement and motivational interviewing to support 
behavior change has been reported.1595,1608
  ▋ 1.2.2 Education and Support
Table 13 provides details regarding education and support 
for patients with HF, their family members, and caregiv-
ers.
The self-care needs of HF patients can be categorized 
into 3 core concepts: self-care maintenance, self-care mon-
itoring, and self-care management.

a. Self-Care Maintenance
Self-care maintenance encompasses the behaviors neces-
sary to maintain physical and mental health, including 
proper nutrition, medication adherence, exercise, infection 
prevention, psychological care, sleep, sobriety and smok-
ing cessation, and appropriate holiday and leisure plan-
ning.
1610
Excessive salt intake is a common trigger for worsening 
HF.1611 Therefore, salt management should be tailored to 
each patient’s dietary habits.1612 Similarly, individualized 
fluid management is required.1613,1614
Medication adherence is the cornerstone of HF treat-
ment.1603 Meta-analyses have reported that pharmacist-
provided medication instructions and self-care education 
improve medication adherence and reduce the risk of HF 
rehospitalization.1615
b. Self-Care Monitoring
Self-care monitoring is the observation of symptoms and 
signs associated with HF exacerbations.,1610 It enables early 
detection of HF exacerbations, facilitating prompt medical 
consultation and timely initiation of treatment. Using tools 
such as record books or remote monitoring technologies 
can help identify exacerbations early and reduce the risk of 
hospitalization for HF.
1592,1616
c. Self-Care Management
Self-care management refers to coping behaviors in 
response to the onset of symptoms and signs of HF. These 
strategies include adjusting diuretics (additional medica-
tions), resting, restricting salt and fluid intake, seeking 
support from family or caregivers, consulting healthcare 
providers, and seeking medical advice. It is essential to 
ensure that patients and their families or caregivers are well 
informed about the symptoms and signs of acute exacerba-
tions and the appropriate steps to manage them.
  ▋ 1.2.3 Barriers to Self-Care
HF patients face a wide range of health and social chal-
lenges that may affect their ability to perform self-care 
effectively. It is crucial to have a thorough understanding 
of these issues and to continually evaluate the education 
and support provided to patients.
1617,1618 These challenges 
include individual health problems, such as depression, 
cognitive dysfunction, and frailty, as well as broader social 
and environmental factors, including social determinants 
of health, that affect patients’ lives and self-care abili-
ties.
9,1600,1619–1621 Table 14 outlines methods for assessing, 
addressing, and supporting factors that impede self-care in 
HF patients. Careful consideration of these factors is 
required to provide effective, personalized self-care sup-
port.
2. Nutritional Management
 ▋ 2.1 Nutritional Management for HF Patients
In HF management, the importance of personalized nutri-
tional interventions, including the involvement of dieti-
tians, has been emphasized. However, there is limited 
evidence on specific nutritional interventions tailored to 
the severity of HF, highlighting the need for further 
research in this area.
1650,1651
 ▋ 2.2 Nutritional Assessment Methods
Nutritional screening is recommended for all HF patients 
using readily available information such as medical his-
tory, height, and weight. Periodic nutritional status assess-
ments are also recommended to provide appropriate 
dietary interventions, particularly for patients at risk of 
nutritional disorders, including those with swallowing dys-
function, a history of gastrointestinal surgery, and 
decreased appetite and food intake, as well as for those 
who are malnourished.1650 Multiple assessment modalities 
should be incorporated to enable a comprehensive evalua-
tion
1650 (Table 15).
  ▋ 2.2.1 Nutrition Assessment Items
a. Body Measurements
Although nutritional assessment using body weight is the 
simplest modality, it can be influenced by fluid retention; 
therefore, it should be evaluated in conjunction with HF 
symptoms and signs. Body mass index is easy to measure, 
but cannot differentiate between lean and/or fat mass, and 
excess fluid.
1652 To assess long-term nutritional status, it is 
useful to measure arm circumference, triceps skinfold 
thickness, arm muscle circumference, and arm muscle 
area.1650 Because elderly individuals experience physiologi-
cal muscle mass loss with aging, arm muscle circumference 
and arm muscle area should be evaluated along with body 
weight.1650 Increased grip strength is also an indicator of

  ▋ 2.2.2 Nutrition Assessment Tools
Table 15 shows tools for nutritional assessment. Nutri-
tional status assessed by the Mini Nutritional Assessment 
(MNA) is associated with mortality and rehospitaliza-
tion.
1655–1657 Similarly, the Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index 
(GNRI) is associated with cardiovascular death or HF 
rehospitalization rates.1659 In Japan, a GNRI value below 
the cut-off of 92 was associated with increased mortal-
ity.
1660,1661 Furthermore, malnutrition assessed by a combi-
nation of nutrition assessment tools, including the MNA, 
Controlling Nutritional Status, Prognostic Nutritional 
Index, and GNRI, is also known to be associated with 
increased mortality.
1662–1664 The GLIM criteria represent 
the world’s first diagnostic criteria for malnutrition, 1651a 
and nutritional assessment based on these criteria is recom-
mended for HF patients.
 ▋ 2.3 Management of Malnutrition
Conditions indicative of malnutrition, such as sarcopenia, 
frailty, and cardiac cachexia, are associated with a worse 
prognosis,1652,1665,1666 highlighting the importance of nutri-
tional screening, at least once a year, for the early detection 
of malnutrition and the provision of dietary interven -
tions.
1651,1667 A meta-analysis showed that personalized 
nutritional interventions can improve prognosis and 
reduce rehospitalization.
1668 In the Nutritional Interven-
tion Program in Malnourished Patients Admitted for 
Heart Failure (PICNIC) trial, which focused on 6 months 
of nutrition optimization for malnourished, hospitalized 
HF patients, the intervention reduced death and rehospi-
talization rates by 55%.
1669 Similarly, A Trial of an Oral 
Nutritional Supplement in Older Hospitalized Patients 
(NOURISH) demonstrated that protein supplementation 
in malnourished HF inpatients aged ≥ 65 years reduced 
90-day mortality.
1670 In a secondary analysis of the Effect 
of Early Nutritional Therapy on Frailty, Functional Out-
comes and Recovery of Undernourished Medical Inpa-
tients Trial (EFFORT), individualized nutritional support 
from a trained dietitian was associated with a reduction in 
30-day mortality.
1671 In the US, it is recommended that 
patients with malnutrition or cardiac cachexia ingest at 
least 1.1 g/kg protein per day.
1651,1672 Dietary interventions 
for HF patients at high risk of malnutrition should be 
provided by a multidisciplinary team, including a dietitian,

 ▋ 2.4 Dietary Interventions
The Mediterranean diet, Dietary Approaches to Stop 
Hypertension diet, and Japanese dietary patterns have 
been reported to be useful dietary approaches for the pre-
vention of cardiovascular events in HF Stages A and B.1820 
Methodologies for specific dietary interventions for HF 
Stages C and D have not been established.
  ▋ 2.4.1 Energy Intake Requirements
Observational studies of HF patients in Stages B and C 
and in patients with Stage D severe HF on a left ventricu-
lar assist device have estimated the resting energy expendi-
ture of these patients to be 22–24 and 18  kcal/kg/
day,
1672,1674a respectively. It has been suggested that the 
required energy intake for HF patients can be estimated by 
multiplying these values by an activity factor.373
  ▋ 2.4.2 Protein Intake
In addition to the imbalance of protein catabolism and 
anabolism due to HF, patients with HF are at increased 
risk of developing sarcopenia and physical frailty. Consid-
ering the increased protein catabolism in HF patients, it is 
recommended that protein intake be at least 1.1 g/kg/
day,
1675 provided there is no moderate or severe renal dys-
function. For elderly patients, protein intake should be 1.2 
to 1.5 g/kg/day,
1650,1676 provided there is no moderate or 
severe renal dysfunction.
  ▋ 2.4.3 Salt Intake
Excessive salt intake can trigger HF exacerbations, but 
evidence regarding the optimal salt intake for HF patients 
remains inconclusive: the ESC 2021 guideline recommends 
avoiding excess salt (>5 g salt equivalent per day) and the 
AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 HF guidelines recommend avoid-
ing excess salt.
2,9 Individualized dietary interventions to 
reduce salt intake are crucial for patients with HF, taking 
into consideration their dietary habits and socioeconomic 
factors, which can influence their diet.
3. Telemonitoring / Digital Health
 ▋ 3.1 HF Remote Monitoring System
  ▋ 3.1.1 Basic Concept of Remote Monitoring
HF is a syndrome characterized by repeated episodes of 
exacerbation. Typically, signs of worsening can be 
observed days or weeks before an exacerbation.1679 Recent 
meta-analyses indicate that the telemonitoring of these 
early signs may aid in reducing all-cause mortality and HF 
hospitalizations; however, the threshold for intervention, 
the types of interventions, and outcomes vary significantly 
among studies.
736,737,1680–1683
  ▋ 3.1.2 Types of Telemonitoring and Evidence
The use of non-invasive remote monitoring of body weight 
and vital signs has been found to reduce death in meta-
analyses, but the effect has not been consistent.
1684,1685 This 
inconsistency may be due, in part, to the non-specific 
nature of changes in single parameters obtained by these 
devices, because they are not exclusively indicative of HF 
status. Moreover, significant changes cannot be detected 
until shortly before an HF exacerbation.
1686 More invasive 
monitoring systems, such as implantable pulmonary artery 
pressure monitoring (not yet approved in Japan), have 
been shown to reduce HF hospitalizations and deaths in 
patients with severe symptomatic HF refractory to guide-
line-directed medical therapy (GDMT).
523 In recent years, 
digital devices have been developed to non-invasively and 
remotely measure heart sounds and thoracic impedance, 
and are being tested for their ability to non-invasively 
monitor multiple parameters, similar to that of invasive 
devices.
1687
 ▋ 3.2  HF Prevention, Management, and Treatment 
Using Wearable Devices
Wearable devices are body-worn, non-invasive sensors 
that collect biometric data as part of Internet of Things 
(IoT) technology. With their increasing adoption for con-
tinuous health monitoring, these devices are being devel-
oped for remote patient surveillance and diverse healthcare 
applications.
1688 Current medical applications of wearable 
devices in HF management include remote monitoring, 
machine learning-based analysis of collected data, and 
enhanced visualization of analytical results.
1689–1692 How-
ever, to date, no wearable device intended for HF diagno-
sis, prevention, or treatment has obtained regulatory 
approval, and evidence supporting the standalone efficacy 
of wearable interventions in HF patients remain scarce. 
Consumer wearable devices (e.g., Apple Watch, Fitbit) 
also face regulatory constraints regarding the collection of 
medical-grade biometric data when deployed in clinical 
settings.
 ▋ 3.3 Therapeutic Apps for HF
Therapeutic apps, a subset of digital therapeutics delivered 
via smartphone apps, are attracting attention as a third 
therapeutic modality alongside medical and surgical inter-
ventions.1693 These apps facilitate treatment delivery within 
a patient’s daily life, contrasting with traditional facility-
based care. Current HF therapeutics apps leverage this 
advantage through remote monitoring, either through 
standalone smartphone apps or integration with IoT 
devices including wearables. Their primary goals are to 
optimize GDMT implementation and enhance remote car-
diac rehabilitation. Although no therapeutic apps for HF 
management have received regulatory approval, develop-
ment efforts continue. Initial studies have demonstrated 
promising results: one study revealed significant improve-
ments in GDMT medication adherence among HF with

has explored telerehabilitation approaches, incorporating 
cardiologist and nurse telephone support with wearable 
device-linked monitoring apps, 1692 and home-based IoT 
ergometer systems with integrated remote monitoring 
capabilities overseen by hospital cardiologists.1694
 ▋ 3.4 Precautions and Practical Considerations
  ▋ 3.4.1  Information Updates and Human Resource 
Considerations
The use of devices, telemonitoring, and digital health is still 
evolving, with new devices and evidence emerging regu-
larly. As a result, it is crucial to continuously update infor-
mation regarding their use. These interventions require 
human review of device data to guide actionable steps 
because they are not yet fully automated, making adequate 
human resources essential for successful implementation.
  ▋ 3.4.2 Digital Divide
Despite the fact that Japan has one of the highest adoption 
rates of small communication devices, such as smartphones 
and broadband internet, the adoption rate of smartphones 
declines sharply among those aged in their 70s and 80s. In 
addition, nearly 40% of households with an annual income 
of less than 2 million yen do not use the internet.
1695 To 
prevent these groups from experiencing even greater dis-
parities, it is essential to consider individuals’ social back-
grounds and digital literacy, and to design systems that are 
user-friendly.
4. Exercise Therapy and Comprehensive  
Cardiac Rehabilitation
 ▋ 4.1  Components of Comprehensive Cardiac 
Rehabilitation
Comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation for HF patients is 
typically a long-term, multifaceted program delivered by a 
multidisciplinary team in a coordinated manner, rather 
than a series of isolated interventions.373 The goals of car-
diac rehabilitation extend beyond improving exercise toler-
ance and physical function to improve QOL, promote 
wellbeing, prevent rehospitalization, prevent frailty, and 
alleviate depression. To foster a high-quality collaborative 
rehabilitation team, regular multidisciplinary conferences 
for information sharing are essential.
1048,1696
The Cerebrovascular and Cardiovascular Disease Control 
Act in Japan emphasizes the need to enhance rehabilitation 
and ensure coordination across the acute, recovery, and 
maintenance phases. Similarly, seamless coordination 
between hospitals and the community is crucial.
 ▋ 4.2  Significance of Comprehensive Cardiac 
Rehabilitation
Cardiac rehabilitation in HF patients has been shown to 
improve health-related QOL,1623,1697–1699 prevent HF rehos-
pitalization,1599,1623,1700 and prolong survival.1701–1704 Infor-
mation sharing based on systematic evaluation 1696 and 
patient education by multidisciplinary teams have been 
reported to improve not only in-hospital outcomes but 
also survival and HF rehospitalization rates, particularly 
among elderly patients.
1048 Based on these findings, it is 
recommended that cardiac rehabilitation is provided as a 
systematic comprehensive program.
In addition, short-term interventions for patients hospi-
talized due to acute decompensated HF are associated with 
the prevention of declines in physical function/activities of 
daily living (ADL), as well as reductions in mortality and 
the risk of HF rehospitalization.
1705–1707 The effectiveness 
of these interventions is believed to due to the multidisci-
plinary interventions rather than exercise therapy alone.
 ▋ 4.3  Current Status of Comprehensive Cardiac 
Rehabilitation in Japan
According to a survey study from the Japanese Circulation 
Society, the number of patients participating in and facili-
ties providing cardiac rehabilitation have been steadily 
increasing.1708 However, many cardiac rehabilitation pro-
grams are predominantly centered on exercise therapy and 
often lack sufficient multidisciplinary interventions, such 
as disease management support. This raises concerns about 
the overall effectiveness of these programs.
1709 In addition, 
the overall implementation rate of cardiac rehabilitation 
among HF patients in Japan remains low, with only 40% 
of patients receiving cardiac rehabilitation during hospital-
ization and the rate of cardiac rehabilitation for outpa-
tients is even lower, at approximately 7%.
1710
 ▋ 4.4 Exercise Therapy
The clinical benefits of exercise therapy for HF have been 
demonstrated in numerous studies, making it one of the 
most essential non-pharmacologic treatments.373,1594
  ▋ 4.4.1  Early Cardiac Rehabilitation and Early 
Mobilization: Acute to Early Recovery Phase
Hospitalized patients with decompensated HF often expe-
rience physical and mental deconditioning due to excessive 
bed rest. A bedside exercise program is recommended early 
during the hospitalization period (within 48 h of admis-
sion), with caution regarding hemodynamic compromise 
and arrhythmias.
1711–1713 In the acute phase, stepwise initia-
tion of an early mobilization program facilitates a smooth 
transition to cardiac rehabilitation. Even for patients with 
severe HF or those on intravenous inotropes, low-intensity 
aerobic exercise and resistance training can prevent 
declines in skeletal muscle function, maintain skeletal mus-
cle mass, and prevent the loss of exercise tolerance.
1714,1715 
The ACTIVE-ADHF trial, a multicenter RCT, demon-
strated that early initiation of physical therapy, aerobic 
exercise, and physical activity management significantly 
improved physical and cognitive function, as well as post-
discharge QOL in patients with ADHF.
1024 Based on these 
findings, exercise therapy should be carefully introduced 
with attention to worsening HF.
In the early recovery phase, exercise prescription and 
supervised exercise therapy based on an assessment of a 
patient’s overall physical function is recommended. A 
decrease in physical activity during hospitalization, as 
measured by daily steps, leads to a decrement in ADL at 
the time of discharge.
424 In addition, a decrease in ADL 
during hospitalization is associated with HF rehospitaliza-
tion.
1716,1717 In a registry study conducted in Japan, approx-

hospital-acquired disability and approximately 56% had 
disuse syndrome or reduced ADL at discharge.
1030,1718

  ▋ 4.4.2  Outpatient Cardiac Rehabilitation (Exercise 
Therapy in the Late Recovery to Maintenance 
Phase)
Exercise therapy in the late to maintenance phase of HF is 
typically delivered on an outpatient basis as part of a com-
prehensive cardiac rehabilitation program, and improves 
exercise tolerance in both HFrEF and HF with preserved 
ejection fraction (HFpEF) patients.
1719–1724
Several meta-analyses have shown that cardiac rehabili-
tation, focused on exercise therapy, is associated with 
improvements in QOL and survival rates, as well as reduc-
tions in the incidence of a composite endpoint of all-cause 
mortality and all hospitalizations.
1623,1697,1701,1722,1725 Heart 
Failure: A Controlled Trial Investigating Outcomes of 
Exercise Training (HF-ACTION), a large randomized 
controlled trial of HFrEF patients, did not demonstrate a 
primary endpoint of improved all-cause survival, but did 
demonstrate a 15% reduction in the risk of the composite 
outcome measures of all-cause mortality and HF rehospi-
talization after adjustment for confounding factors.
1725 A 
Trial of Rehabilitation Therapy in Older Acute Heart Fail-
ure Patients (REHAB-HF) was conducted to evaluate the 
efficacy of 3 months of outpatient cardiac rehabilitation 
combined with home exercise therapy in elderly HF 
patients with frailty who were hospitalized for acute 
decompensated HF. The study demonstrated that starting 
and continuing exercise therapy during hospitalization 
improved lower extremity function.
1726,1727 When outpa-
tient cardiac rehabilitation is not available, cardiac reha-
bilitation in recovery or community comprehensive care 
wards, or home-based rehabilitation, should be consid-
ered.
1728,1729 To date, clinical trials including patients with 
HFpEF remain scarce,1048 and further research is needed.
  ▋ 4.4.3  Indications and Contraindications for Exercise 
Therapy
Exercise therapy during the recovery and maintenance 
phases is recommended when HF is compensated for and 
the patient’s general condition has improved. For patients 
with relative contraindications to exercise therapy and 
those with NYHA functional class IV, aggressive exercise 
therapy aimed at improving exercise tolerance and physical 
function should be avoided. Interventions to minimize 
declines in conditioning, such as stretching, low-intensity 
resistance training, and ADL training, should be empha-
sized, while taking into account any worsening subjective 
symptoms.
373,1730,1731
  ▋ 4.4.4  Exercise Prescription and Exercise Therapy in 
Practice
When initiating exercise therapy, it is important to under-
take a comprehensive assessment of the patient’s overall 
lifestyle, and to formulate an exercise prescription tailored 
to an individual patient’s needs. Because the safety margin 
for exercise is relatively narrow for patients with HF, it is 
desirable to formulate exercise prescriptions based on car-
diopulmonary exercise test assessments.
In patients who are able to perform moderate-intensity 
exercise training consistently without exacerbation, super-
vised high-intensity exercise training may be consid-
ered.
1732–1734 In elderly patients with reduced physical 
function, frailty, or sarcopenia, exercise therapy based on 
individualized programs can improve physical function 
and reduce the risk of rehospitalization for HF.
1703,1727,1735 
In patients who have difficulty performing regular aerobic 
exercise training, studies have reported the effectiveness of 
low-intensity aerobic exercise using chair exercise aerobics 
or an ergometer with a machine-assist function.
1724,1736 A 
multicomponent exercise program that combines multiple 
types of resistance training with power training, balance 
exercises, and movement training can improve muscle 
strength and muscle power.
373,1737
  ▋ 4.4.5  Cardiac Rehabilitation in Special Conditions and 
Patient Groups
a.  After Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator Implantation 
and Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy
Exercise tolerance improves in HF patients who have 
received an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD) or 
cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), and exercise 
therapy should be considered for these patients.
1738–1742 In 
addition, exercise therapy has been reported to reduce ICD

Comprehensive cardiac rehabilitation is highly indicated in

c. After Heart Transplantation
Exercise tolerance is decreased in many patients after heart

1750 and exercise therapy is recommended

  ▋ 4.4.6  Expected Future Methods in Cardiac Rehabilitation 
(Home and Remote Cardiac Rehabilitation)
a. Conceptual Change
For elderly HF patients with multiple comorbidities, the 
goal of cardiac rehabilitation needs to be shifted from 
improving exercise tolerance and long-term prognosis to 
maintaining and improving physical function and ADL, as 
well as maintaining QOL.
1754
b.  Home-Based Cardiac Rehabilitation and Remote 
Cardiac Rehabilitation
Various methods of providing cardiac rehabilitation have 
emerged, including home-based cardiac rehabilitation, 
outpatient cardiac rehabilitation combined with home 
exercise therapy (hybrid), and cardiac rehabilitation con-
ducted at a local exercise therapy facility. Currently, it is 
possible to have a therapist visit a patient’s residence 
(home-visit rehabilitation). In addition, cardiac rehabilita-
tion using real-time calls and communication via the inter-
net (so-called remote cardiac rehabilitation) may become 
widely available.
1697,1755 A meta-analysis including the 
results of 24 trials in patients with HFrEF reported that 
remote cardiac rehabilitation was equally effective in 
improving survival and exercise tolerance as outpatient 
cardiac rehabilitation.
1756
There are also many information and communication 
technology (ICT) modalities emerging, such as dedicated 
pedometers and activity meters, general-purpose wearable 
devices, and smartphone apps. Home exercise therapy and 
nutritional management using a wearable device improved 
the 6-minute walk distance in Japanese patients with 
chronic HF complicated by frailty.
1757 At present, these 
advanced cardiac rehabilitation modalities are still in the 
research stage and have not yet been widely adopted in 
clinical practice.

Healthcare Providers
HF patients frequently experience socioeconomic chal-
lenges, such as unemployment, poverty, and isola-
tion.1760,1761 The employment rate of patients hospitalized

 ▋ 5.2  Interventions to Support Social Reintegration 
and Return to Work
Enhancing self-care and self-management skills, fostering 
self-esteem related to work, and promoting a sense of self-
worth and self-health are essential prerequisites for HF 
patients to reintegrate into society and find job, as well as 
to maintain employment. The effectiveness of social pre-
scribing, facilitated through interviews conducted by med-
ical professionals with patients and their families, has been 
demonstrated in various studies
