 ▋ 5.3  Programs and Systems to Support Social 
Reintegration and Employment
The Cerebrovascular and Cardiovascular Disease Control 
Act in Japan includes support for balancing medical treat-
ment and work, and cardiac disease was added to the “fee 
for guidance on support for balancing treatment and 
work” in the revised 2022 financial year medical fee sched-
ule.
6. Role of the Certified Heart  
Failure Educator
 ▋ 6.1 Purpose of Establishing the Qualifications
The Certified Heart Failure Educator (Ryoyo-shidoshi in 
Japanese) qualification was established in December 2016 
as one of the human resource development initiatives in the 
Five-Year Plan to Overcome Stroke and Cardiovascular 
Disease formulated by the Japanese Circulation Society 
and Japanese Stroke Association.
1800 The aim of this certi-
fication is to provide comprehensive support for HF 
patients through multidisciplinary collaboration. It equips 
healthcare professionals other than physicians (e.g., such 
as nurses, public health nurses, physical therapists, occu-
pational therapists, pharmacists, nutritionists, certified 
psychologists, clinical engineers, dental hygienists, and 
social workers) with common knowledge and skills related 
to HF. By promoting this common understanding, the 
program facilitates coordinated care and comprehensive 
support for patients with HF.
 ▋ 6.2 Required Role
The Certified Heart Failure Educator is expected to under-
stand the concept and pathophysiology of HF, assess the 
medical condition of individual patients, and provide ther-
apeutic guidance to patients and their caregivers, such as 
family members, to help them acquire the knowledge and 
skills necessary to prevent the onset and progression of 
HF. Certified Heart Failure Educators also play a vital 
role in raising awareness among community members by 
disseminating accurate information about HF, whether or 
not people have heart disease.
To maintain and improve the QOL of HF patients who 
face physical, mental, psychological, social, and spiritual 
challenges, Certified Heart Failure Educators must also 
have a basic knowledge of shared decision making and 
palliative care.
Certified Heart Failure Educators are expected to serve 
as key players in patient-centered team medicine, promot-
ing collaboration among healthcare professionals to pro-
vide treatment and care that meet the preferences and 
needs of HF patients.

Palliative Care
 ▋ 1.1 Definition of Palliative Care
Palliative care is defined as integrated patient/family-cen-
tered care that optimizes quality of life (QOL) for all heart 
failure (HF) patients.
1766 Palliative care is not limited to 
symptom relief at the end of life, also including high-qual-
ity communication, prognostication, coping with uncer-
tainty, shared decision making regarding medically 
appropriate treatment options, advance care planning 
(ACP), attention to both physical and psychological dis-
tress, the relief of symptoms, involvement of caregivers in 
patient care, and attention to the needs of caregivers.
1767 
Consultation with palliative care specialists may be desir-
able for the collaborative care of complicated problems.1768
 ▋ 1.2 Characteristics of Palliative Care for HF
HF follows a progressive course of exacerbations and 
remissions and, as the disease progresses, critical decisions 
regarding the initiation, continuation, and withdrawal of

aid in alleviating suffering at the end of life by allowing 
patients to make decisions based on their wishes.

 ▋ 1.3 Components and Effects of Palliative Care
Quality communication fosters trust and understanding 
between patients and caregivers, conveying prognoses with 
an acknowledgement of uncertainty and clarifying goals of 
care through repeated shared decision making. Symptom 
palliation is provided as required during this process. Sup-
porting caregivers throughout the patient’s illness and after 
the patient’s death is another critical component of pallia-
tive care. A randomized controlled trial has demonstrated 
that palliative care reduced readmissions and improved 
symptoms frequently experienced by patients eligible for 
palliative care (including depressive symptoms), but did 
not improve mortality and QOL.
1769
2. ACP and Decision-Making Support
 ▋ 2.1 Concepts Related to ACP
ACP is a process that supports patients and families in 
understanding a patient’s personal values, life goals, and 
preferences regarding future medical care. Key compo-
nents of ACP include discussing the patient’s values, docu-
menting plans for medical procedures, designating a 
surrogate decision maker, and revisiting the content peri-
odically to reflect changes in preferences.
9,1091,1773
End-of-life discussion is one element of ACP and 
involves clarifying goals and specific preferences regarding 
medical care and the type of support a patient would like 
to receive when death is approaching.
Shared decision making is a collaborative process 
whereby patients and healthcare professionals work 
together to make informed decisions. Based on the prin-
ciple of patient-centered care, shared decision making 
ensures that treatment and care options are discussed, 
selected, and implemented with the patient’s active involve-
ment and in alignment with their preferences and values.
1774
Advance directives are statements of a patient’s inten-
tions regarding medical treatment in case the patient’s 
decision-making capacity is impaired in the future. There 
are 2 primary forms of advance directives: (1) a living will, 
which specifies the types of treatment and care (especially 
life-sustaining measures) the patient wishes to receive or 
decline; and (2) a durable power of attorney for healthcare, 
which designates a substitute decision maker to make 
healthcare decisions on the patient’s behalf if they lose 
decision-making capacity.
1091 There is a difference between 
advance directives and ACP: ACP is the decision-making 
process itself and focuses on sharing the patient’s values 
and wishes between the patient, the surrogate decision 
maker, and healthcare provider.
 ▋ 2.2 Benefits and Harms of ACP
ACP has been shown to increase patients’ sense of self-
control, decrease hospital deaths, and improve communi-
cation between surrogate decision makers and physicians. 
It has also been shown that ACP may improve patient and 
family satisfaction and decrease anxiety and depression 
among bereaved family members by facilitating the imple-
mentation of care that respects the patient’s wishes.
1775–1778 
ACP can also be harmful at times due to its potential psy-
chological burden, failure to observe the principle of no 
harm, and time constraints.1779 Efforts have been made to 
promote ACP based on the assumption that ACP leads to 
end-of-life care consistent with a patient’s preferences. 
However, robust evidence supporting this assumption 
remains insufficient; some reports suggest that documenta-
tion of ACP as an outcome is not a valid quality indicator 
for end-of-life discussions,
1780 and the nature of ACP 
requires continued discussion.

 ▋ 2.3 Selection and Initiation of ACP Subjects
Although there are no high-quality studies examining who 
is most appropriate to initiate ACP, the principle is that 
ACP can be started at an appropriate time and aligned 
with the patient’s readiness. The surprise question is a well-
known and widely used medically appropriate timing 
method, in which physicians ask themselves, “Would I be 
surprised if the patient died within a year?”. The validity of 
the surprise question has been reported to be higher in 
patients aged <70 years with reduced left ventricular ejec-
tion fraction and New York Heart Association Class III/
IV.
1781
 ▋ 2.4 The Decision-Making Process at the End of Life 
The Guideline on the Decision-Making Process for Medi-
cal and Nursing Care at the Last Stage of Life
1782 serves as 
a framework for supporting decision making in Japan, 
regardless of the specific disease, and emphasizes the 
importance of ACP within this process. The main points 
of the guideline are to: (1) understand the individual’s per-
spectives on life and personal values as much as possible; 
(2) engage, through discussions, with the individual and 
their family; and (3) document and share the content of 
these discussions in writing after each conversation.
3. Managing HF Symptoms
 ▋ 3.1  Symptom Progression During the Disease 
Trajectory in HF
Patients with HF experience a wide range of symptoms 
both at discharge following episodes of acute decompensa-
tion and during outpatient care.1783,1784 Palliative care for 
HF is provided concurrently with prognostic therapy start-
ing from Stage C.
1091 As the disease progresses, holistic 
distress interacts and overlaps to manifest as various symp-
toms (Figure 20).
1785 A comprehensive evaluation of the 
interrelationship between symptoms throughout the HF 
trajectory is essential to deliver appropriate care at the 
right time.
 ▋ 3.2 Physical Symptoms and Management
Although assessment of the following HF symptoms is 
important, the use of comprehensive symptom scales, such 
as the Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale, allows for 
an evaluation of the degree to which symptoms are inter-
fering with daily life.
  ▋ 3.2.1 Shortness of Breath (Dyspnea)
Dyspnea is the most frequently observed symptom in HF 
patients and often requires management at the end of life. 
It may be exacerbated by comorbid conditions, such as 
respiratory failure or anxiety, necessitating a comprehen-
sive evaluation of psychological, spiritual, and social dis-
tress alongside clinical assessment (e.g., comorbidities, 
panic attacks, presence of pleural effusion). Nocturnal 
breathlessness may result from increased venous return, 
and elevating the head during rest can provide relief.  Opi-
oids may be used for treatment-resistant dyspnea after 
considering treatment tailored to the patient’s condition, 
such as diuretics, thoracentesis,
  ▋ 3.2.2 Fatigue
Fatigue associated with HF is often a treatment-resistant 
symptom. Contributing factors such as hypokalemia, 
β-blocker use, sleep disturbances, anemia, depression, and 
deconditioning should be considered. Possible interven-
tions include medication adjustments, blood transfusions, 
psychological therapy, and rehabilitation.
  ▋ 3.2.3 Insomnia
Sympathetic nervous system overactivation in HF often 
results in nocturia and insomnia. Instruction on sleep 
hygiene, including moderate daytime exercise, adjustments 
to the bedroom environment, and avoidance of alcohol 
and caffeine before bedtime, is essential. If insomnia per-
sists, the use of non-benzodiazepine or melatonin receptor 
agonists can be considered.
  ▋ 3.2.4 Dry Mouth
Dry mouth is a common symptom among HF patients 
taking diuretics. For patients with severe HF, care should 
be taken to avoid excessive fluid intake. Sucking on ice 
cubes can help reduce fluid intake while alleviating symp-
toms.

  ▋ 3.2.5 Constipation
Constipation is common in HF due to chronic fluid restric-
tion, diuretic use, and intestinal edema. For functional 
constipation without underlying disease, lifestyle modifica-
tion and dietary therapy are first-line recommendations. If 
constipation persists, osmotic laxatives, epithelial function-
altering agents, bile acid transporter inhibitors, and stimu-
lant laxatives should be considered.
  ▋ 3.2.6 Loss of Appetite (Anorexia)
During exacerbations of HF, gastrointestinal reflux, 
abdominal distention from intestinal edema, and other 
factors can lead to anorexia and decreased food intake. 
This can result in malnutrition and, in advanced stages, 
cardiac cachexia. Appropriate nutritional support and 
interventions are crucial.
 ▋ 3.3 Psychiatric Symptoms and Management
Assessments using the Integrated Palliative Care Outcome 
Scale (IPOS) indicate that 18–20% of HF patients experi-
ence anxiety and depression.
1783,1784,1786 In addition to 
hyperactive delirium, there is also hypoactive delirium, 
which can often be mistaken for depression or dementia. 
Hypoactive delirium is reported to be challenging for non-
psychiatrists to diagnose.
2,4,1787,1788 The management of 
psychiatric symptoms, such as depression and delirium, 
should involve collaboration with specialists when neces-
sary.1783
  ▋ 3.3.1 Depression and Anxiety
Depression is a condition characterized by a depressed 
mood that may be triggered by various life events. Con-
versely, anxiety refers to a group of unpleasant emotional 
responses to potential danger or distress that one perceives 
may occur in the future. The diagnosis of depression and 
anxiety should focus on identifying mental and psycho-
logical distress rather than labeling them as mental disor-
ders.
1789 Collaboration with specialists is critical when 
depression and anxiety are suspected. Validated tools such 
as the Patient Health Questionnaires (PHQ-2, PHQ-9) are 
recommended for screening for depression (Table 16).
1789
  ▋ 3.3.2 Delirium
Delirium is a disorder of consciousness caused by physical 
illness, medications, and other factors. Because HF itself is 
a significant risk factor, it is challenging to prevent delir-
ium universally. Non-pharmacological strategies focus on 
addressing and mitigating the underlying contributing fac-
tors. These strategies are typically combined with pharma-
cological interventions where necessary. The Clinical 
Guidelines for the Treatment of Delirium in Japan recom-
mend that non-pharmacological interventions be provided 
early by a multidisciplinary team, including support from 
the patient’s family. These interventions include: (1) 
addressing cognitive function and disorientation; (2) miti-
gating physical factors (e.g., dehydration, infections); (3) 
preventing immobilization; (4) correcting visual and audi-
tory disturbances; and (5) managing sleep disorders. 
Although antipsychotics are the first-line pharmacother-
apy for delirium, effective pharmacotherapy for hypoactiv-
ity delirium remains to be established.
 ▋ 3.4 Use of Sedatives for Intolerable Pain
When intolerable distress persists despite various treat-
ments, including pharmacological and non-pharmacolog-
ical therapies, the use of sedatives may be considered. 1091 
This decision should follow multidisciplinary discussions, 
and through communication with the patient and family. 
For precise management, scales such as the Richmond 
Agitation–Sedation Scale (RASS) should be used to adjust 
the target depth and duration of sedation. After initiating 
sedatives, clinicians should assess the need for continuous 
deep sedation and adjust dosages through titration as nec-
essary.
 ▋ 3.5 Use of Inotropes in Palliative Care
The administration of intravenous inotropes to relieve 
symptoms such as dyspnea and fatigue, and to improve 
QOL under clearly defined goals of care, is reasonable and 
could be a valid option. However, the purpose of inotrope 
administration must be clearly delineated prior to its use, 
because prolonged use has been associated with arrhyth-
mias and worse prognoses.
4 In Japan, reimbursement for 
the use of intravenous inotropes is provided for patients 
with severe HF who are dependent on these therapies. This 
applies when continued treatment with intravenous inotro-
pes at home is expected to improve the patient’s QOL, the 
patient strongly desires such treatment, and both patient 
and facility requirements are met.
4. Clinical Ethics: Withholding and  
Withdrawing Treatment
 ▋ 4.1 Purpose and Methodology of Clinical Ethics
The purpose of clinical ethics is to improve the quality of 
care by recognizing, analyzing, and attempting to resolve 
ethical issues in daily clinical practice. Jonsen’s 4 topics 
approach is a method of identifying problems by dividing 
them into 4 categories, namely medical indication, patient’s 
intention, QOL, and surrounding circumstances, each of 
which encompasses bioethical principles.
1793 The 4 topics 
approach has the advantage of encouraging the consider-

 ▋ 4.2  Debate Over Withholding and Withdrawal of 
Treatment in HF
  ▋ 4.2.1  Situations in Which Clinical Ethics Are Important 
in Heart Failure Practice 
In HF management, clinicians frequently face decisions 
regarding whether to intensify or withhold treatment, rec-
ognizing that it is not always possible to save every 
patient’s life. Although life-saving medical care is often 
delivered throughout the disease course, the appropriate-
ness of continuing such interventions must be balanced 
against factors such as the wishes of the patient and family. 
This process requires careful deliberation to determine the 
best course of action.
Clinical ethics methodologies are particularly valuable 
in addressing complex issues related to end-of-life care. 
These include decisions about withholding or withdrawing 
life-sustaining treatments, such as ventilators and mechan-
ical circulatory assist devices, deactivating implantable 
cardioverter defibrillators, blood transfusion for chronic 
anemia, and the use of sedative drugs. By applying clinical 
ethics frameworks, healthcare providers can navigate these 
challenging situations with greater clarity and sensitivity.
1794
  ▋ 4.2.2 Withholding and Withdrawing Invasive Treatment
When considering decision support in HF, there are vari-
ous guidelines and recommendations regarding the with-
holding or withdrawal of invasive treatment in Japan, with 
the Guidelines for End-of-Life Care in Emergency and 
Intensive Care used in clinical practice.
This guideline provides a definition of the terminal 
phase and states that the continuation of any assistive 
device at the end of life is a life-prolonging procedure.
In such cases, there are three options: (1) maintenance, 
whereby new treatment is withheld; (2) dose reduction, 
whereby there is partial or complete reduction of treatment 
dosage; or (3) termination, whereby treatment is with-
drawn.
When a patient’s wishes are unknown, the Guideline on 
the Decision-Making Process for Medical and Nursing 
Care at the Last Stage of Life recommends that decisions 
should be reviewed for validity by an institutional ethics 
committee.
1782 Establishing an organization to review ethi-
cal issues is also considered advisable.1782 Despite frequent 
encounters with situations requiring clinical ethics aware-
ness in HF practice, there remains insufficient education 
and training for facilitators in clinical ethics.
5. Holistic Care Through  
Multidisciplinary Intervention
 ▋ 5.1 Multidisciplinary Intervention in End-Stage HF
Multidisciplinary interventions for HF patients are known 
to reduce readmissions and improve survival through 
patient education, self-care, and adherence to care 
plans.
1796,1797 However, few studies have evaluated the 
effectiveness of multidisciplinary palliative care in improv-
ing outcomes for end-stage HF. In addition, the methodol-
ogy for identifying and implementing optimal interventions 
remains underdeveloped.
1798 Collaboration among the 3 
specialities of primary care, cardiology, and palliative care 
can enhance patient communication, improve understand-
ing of goal setting, streamline referrals to specialists, and 
provide better end-of-life care.
1797
 ▋ 5.2  Role of Coordinators in Multidisciplinary 
Interventions
Teams function effectively with a clear understanding of 
the organizational, leadership, and coordinator structures. 
In actual multidisciplinary intervention in end-stage HF, 
the coordinator plays an important role. Specifically, the 
coordinator communicates with the patient, ensures that 
medical decisions are made in accordance with the patient’s 
values, goals, and preferences, and coordinates the services 
to be provided. It is desirable for each organization to 
consider who will assume the coordinator role.
1799

and Comprehensive Community Care
In Japan, the Basic Law on Measures against Stroke, Heart 
Disease, and Other Cardiovascular Diseases was enacted in 
2019, and the medical management system for heart failure 
(HF) is continuously evolving and being enhanced within 
local communities.
1800 As shown in Table 17, community 
collaboration and comprehensive community care are 
required for the management of HF patients at every 
stage.482,1040,1801–1804
2. Actual Practice of Regional Cooperation  
and Comprehensive Community Care
 ▋ 2.1 Cooperation With the Family Physician
In Japan, many elderly patients hospitalized for HF are 
managed by a local family physician after discharge, rather 
than a hospital cardiologist.
1805,1806 A Canadian retrospec-
tive observational study demonstrated that when cardiolo-
gists and family physicians collaborated in the outpatient 
follow-up of patients presenting to the emergency depart-
ment with HF exacerbations, the rate of initiation of HF 
medications increased and the prognosis was better.
1807 A 
Japanese registry study reported that when hospital cardi-
ologists and family physicians collaborated in the outpa-
tient follow-up of hospitalized HF patients, there were 
fewer readmissions after discharge than when hospital car-
diologists worked alone.
1805 A Japanese retrospective 
observational study also reported that standardization of 
HF management and collaborative activities in the com-
munity, such as health monitoring using patient diaries, 
standardization of the provision of medical information 
from hospitals to family physicians, and the development 
of HF manuals for local staff, reduced HF rehospitaliza-
tions over time.
1808,1809
 ▋ 2.2 Cooperation With Welfare and Nursing Care
HF patients aged ≥ 65 years with reduced left ventricular 
ejection fraction have a 1.5-fold higher risk of requiring 
long-term support or care certified by the dedicated 
Japanese insurance system than the general elderly popula-
tion,
1810 and approximately half the patients hospitalized 
for HF have been reported to be identified as requiring 
support or care. 48 Family support and the use of social 
resources are important for patients who need help with 
self-care,
1619,1621 such as older patients, those living alone, 
and those with cognitive impairment.1040,1054,1618,1811,1812 The 
use of long-term care insurance services effectively reduces 
rehospitalization for HF and the burden on caregiv-
ers.
1590,1592,1813–1821 One of the goals of community collabo-
ration is to provide care in the patient’s preferred place of 
care. Home palliative care for patients with end-stage HF 
is useful for improving patients’ quality of life and reduc-
ing healthcare costs.
1804 A retrospective observational 
study conducted in Japan reported that the proportion of 
end-of-life care at home increased over time as a result of 
ongoing collaborative activities in the community.1808

Sharing

that inadequate medical information or a lack of informa-

1822 A

cardiologists may be unable to provide sufficient informa-

1823 Of the information most commonly 
requested by family physicians, namely weight before dis-
charge, guidance during hospitalization, physical function, 
and lifestyle function, it was found that cardiologists did 
not provide much of this information.
1823
In a survey of home nursing stations in Japan, the 
majority (66.2%) of nursing staff reported not being very 
satisfied with the information provided by hospitals. 1824 
The information they would like to receive from the 
hospital was reported to include: (1) medications at 
discharge; (2) medical history; (3) degree of water restric-
tion; (4) response to exacerbations; and (5) ideal weight.
1824 
Standardized information sharing is one of the key 
components of transitional care. 1040,1824a Providing 
continuity of care requires information sharing to meet 
local care needs.
 ▋ 2.4 Future Issues
Inadequate knowledge and experience of HF and a lack of 
awareness of HF among community staff have been identi-
fied as issues related to community collaboration and com-
prehensive community care.1825 A survey of care staff in 
Japan indicated that they had little knowledge of HF and 
few opportunities to learn about it.1824,1826
Because face-to-face information sharing is time-
consuming and demanding, the use of digital health tech-
nologies is seen as a way to improve coordination.
1827 It 
has been reported that outpatient visits to a family physi-
cian via telemedicine within 14 days of discharge from 
hospitalization for HF significantly reduced rehospitaliza-
tion for HF within 30 days compared with no outpatient 
visits at all.
1828 However, some studies have found that 
telemedicine was less effective than face-to-face consulta-
tions in initiating HF medications.
1829 It has been suggested 
that prognosis may differ depending on the method of 
telemedicine. In one study, telephone telemedicine 
increased all-cause mortality within 90 days compared 
with face-to-face care, but video telemedicine did not.
1829 
Transitional care using digital medical technology is in its 
infancy, and further research is needed to clarify its clinical 
safety and effectiveness.
XIV. Quality Assessment in Heart Failure Care
The American Heart Association/American College of 
Cardiology were instrumental in the development and 
publication of performance measures and quality indica-
tors (QIs) for healthcare quality assessment.
430,1834 Perfor-
mance measures are systematically developed using 
standardized methodologies and are intended for third-
party evaluation, reporting, and accountability.
1835 In con-
trast, QIs are designed to facilitate internal quality 
improvement and self-assessment at the healthcare profes-
sional and institutional levels.

Compliance with QIs, as advocated in Europe and the

Japan, revealing significant interhospital variation, espe-

1710,1836–1838

Japan in 2020 categorize the appropriateness of drug ther-

rate.

XV. Evidence Gaps and Future Directions
PM?d?e??g?e
 ▋ 1.1 New Devices
Novel therapeutic devices for heart failure (HF) show 
promising potential to revolutionize both treatment and 
monitoring. This section reviews emerging technologies on 
the cusp of clinical implementation, with particular focus 
on devices that could fundamentally alter disease progres-
sion.
  ▋ 1.1.1 CardioMEMS TM HF System
The CardioMEMS HF System enables remote monitoring 
of pulmonary artery pressure through an implanted sensor 
and received US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 
approval in 2014 based on evidence accumulated from US 
clinical studies.
523,524 Following analysis of post-marketing 
surveillance data,1842,1843 the FDA expanded the indication 
of the CardioMEMS HF System in 2022 to include 
patients with New York Heart Association Class II.
  ▋ 1.1.2 Atrial Shunt Devices
The interatrial shunt device creates a controlled passage in 
the atrial septum to reduce left atrial pressure, representing 
a potential therapeutic approach for HF with preserved 
ejection fraction. The device aims to improve exercise tol-
erance by preventing elevated left atrial pressure, especially 
during exercise. In a randomized trial of 44 HF patients 
with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥40%, pulmonary 
artery wedge pressure during exercise was significantly 
lower in the intervention group than in the control 
group.
1844 Although a subsequent larger trial did not show 
improvements in clinical outcomes, including quality of life 
measures,1263 subgroup analyses suggested potential bene-
fits specifically in patients without pulmonary vascular 
disease.
1264 Due to concerns including potential right heart 
burden and decreased left ventricular cardiac output, along 
with being a symptom-directed rather than disease-modi-
fying approach, careful patient selection criteria need to be 
established.
 ▋ 1.2  Genetic Testing, Nucleic Acid Medicine, and 
Gene Editing Therapy
Polygenic risk scores have emerged as tools to estimate 
disease susceptibility by analyzing the accumulated burden 
of common genomic variants found in the general popula-
tion.1845–1847 Targeting therapeutic interventions to patients 
with high polygenic risk scores has been shown to be cost-
effective.1848 Future clinical decision making will require 
comprehensive evaluation of both rare and common 
genetic variants to determine optimal individualized treat-
ment strategies.
Nucleic acid medicines are therapeutic agents engineered 
from nucleotides, which are components of DNA or RNA, 
and their derivatives. These innovative treatments are 
effective when specific underlying causative molecules, 
such as mRNA, have been identified.
1849
Genome editing technology is rapidly advancing around 
the world.1850–1852 This progress has catalyzed the develop-
ment of several cutting-edge therapies for HF, including 
chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, gene ther-
apy, and vaccines.
1853
 ▋ 1.3  Digital Health Interventions and Therapeutic 
Applications in HF Management
Currently, software applications are being developed for 
the management, diagnosis, and treatment of HF using 
digital medicine.1693 Most therapeutic applications run on 
smartphones, although some integrate with wearable 
devices to collect continuous biometric data during daily 
activities.
1693 These applications fall into 2 categories: (1) 
those aiming to optimizing guideline-directed medical 
therapy; and (2) those enhancing telecardiac rehabilitation, 
mainly through the remote monitoring capabilities of 
mobile devices.
2. Clinical Challenges
Finally, in addition to the major technical advances high-
lighted in the previous section, the guideline committee 
members have identified several fundamental challenges in 
the care of HF patients that require attention to further 
advance HF management, as detailed below.

In accordance with “The JAMS COI Management Guidance on Eligibility Criteria for Clinical Practice Guideline Formulation 2023”, all members have submitted their COIs for the past 3 years.
Some members (*) reported under the category of “Amount Category 3” or “Endowed departments established through donations by a company” and therefore do not have a vote in the guideline formulation process, to ensure fairness and transparency 
of the guidelines.
All costs associated with the development of this guideline were borne by the Japanese Circulation Society, and no funding was received from any private companies or for-profit organizations.
